q.t: Firm-seated are eternal Law's foundations; in its fair form are many splendid beauties.
the original idea of regularity, conformity to, or establishment by, eternal order or law, is found throughout
By your high Law firm order is established there where they loose for travel Sūrya's horses.
FROM Fervour kindled to its height Eternal Law and Truth were born

kb.t: Ṛgveda (oral composition c. 1500–1000 BCE; Book X later)
kb.th: The Vedic hymns have a strong word for cosmic and ritual order, *ṛta*, and a hymn of social concord, *saṃjñāna*. Ṛta means regularity, right and truth. Saṃjñāna means one mind and one resolve. Neither is "diversity in wholeness".
h: **Ṛta is a firm-founded, eternal order.** Griffith translates ṛta as "eternal Law". "Firm-seated are eternal Law's foundations; in its fair form are many splendid beauties." His note says that in these verses "the original idea of regularity, conformity to, or establishment by, eternal order or law, is found throughout." ([RV IV.23.8–10, tr. Griffith, p. 425 [scan 440]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biv5WKmg37kZuOT2VjM))

**Ṛta runs the sky and comes first, with truth.** "By your high Law firm order is established there where they loose for travel Sūrya's horses." ([RV V.62.1, p. 546](/q/Biv5WKmg37kZuOT2Vl4)). In the creation hymn, "FROM Fervour kindled to its height Eternal Law and Truth were born" ([RV X.190.1, vol. 2, p. 609 [scan 616]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biv5XDB6CXZ53m6Pp3A)).

**Social concord is unanimity.** The last hymn of the Ṛgveda is addressed to saṃjñāna, which Griffith glosses as "Agreement or Unanimity in assembly". "Assemble, speak together: let your minds be all of one accord," and "One and the same be your resolve, and be your minds of one accord." ([RV X.191.2–4, p. 609 [scan 616]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biv5XDB6CXZ53m6Pp3A))

**The many gods are many names for one.** "To what is One, sages give many a title: they call it Agni, Yama, Mâtarisvan." ([RV I.164.46, p. 227 [scan 242]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biv5WKmg37kZuOT2VgA))
tr: **ऋत *ṛta***. In context it means the regular course of sun, dawn and seasons, the correct performance of the rite, and truth. Its opposite is *anṛta*, falsehood or disorder. **Verdict: does not map.** It is order and truth. It shares one feature with “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”: it holds many things (dawn, waters, cows, heaven and earth) in their courses. But the texts value the regularity, not the variety.

**संज्ञान *saṃjñāna*** ("knowing together, agreement"). In X.191 it is common counsel, a common mind and a single resolve. **Verdict: does not map. It is the opposite pole.** By “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s own terms it is a homogenizing ideal. Indian writers often quote this hymn as a Vedic "hymn of harmony". When it is quoted that way, say that it asks for unanimity.
*ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti* (I.164.46). This is one being with many names. It is a claim about many names, not about many parts.
an: The Upaniṣads turn the many-names theme into the doctrine of one being.
Later *dharma* takes over many of ṛta's functions (social and ritual order).

q.t: The Rik indeed is speech, Sâman is breath, the udgîtha is the syllable Om. Now speech and breath, or Rik and Sâman, form one couple.
And that couple is joined together in the syllable Om. When two people come together, they fulfil each other's desire.
'What is the origin of the Sâman?' 'Tone (svara),' he replied. 'What is the origin of tone?' 'Breath,' he replied.
make honey by collecting the juices of distant trees and reduce the juice into one form,

kb.t: The Upaniṣads (Chāndogya c. 7th–6th c. BCE; Maitrī/Maitrāyaṇī much later)
kb.th: The chanted syllable Om joins unlike partners (speech and breath), and musical tone comes from breath. But the Upaniṣads' image of the final whole is honey, in which the juices of many trees can no longer tell themselves apart, and the "sound-brahman" is a ladder to the soundless.
h: **Om is where a couple is joined.** "The Rik indeed is speech, Sâman is breath, the udgîtha is the syllable Om. Now speech and breath, or Rik and Sâman, form one couple." "And that couple is joined together in the syllable Om. When two people come together, they fulfil each other's desire." ([Chāndogya I.1.5–6, tr. Müller, p. 2 [scan 114]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu6k))

**The Sāman comes from tone, and tone from breath.** "'What is the origin of the Sâman?' 'Tone (svara),' he replied. 'What is the origin of tone?' 'Breath,' he replied." ([Chāndogya I.8.4, p. 16 [scan 128]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu6y))

**In the True, the parts lose their distinctness.** Bees "make honey by collecting the juices of distant trees, and reduce the juice into one form," and "as these juices have no discrimination, so that they might say, I am the juice of this tree or that", so creatures merged in *sat* do not know it. ([Chāndogya VI.9.1–2, p. 101 [scan 213]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu8L))

**Sound-brahman leads to the soundless.** "Verily, there are two Brahmas to be meditated upon: sound and non-sound. Now, non-sound is revealed only by sound." ([Maitrī 6.22, tr. Hume, p. 437 [scan 459]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wp9)). Beyond the varied sound, people "disappear" in the soundless brahman: "There they are unqualified, indistinguishable, like the various juices which have reached the condition of honey." ([p. 438 [scan 460]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1WpA))

**The inner sound has many forms.** With the ears closed, practitioners "hear the sound of the space within the heart. Of it there is this sevenfold comparison: like rivers, a bell, a brazen vessel, a wheel, the croaking of frogs, rain, as when one speaks in a sheltered place." ([Maitrī 6.22, p. 437 [scan 459]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wp9))
tr: **नाद *nāda* / शब्दब्रह्म *śabda-brahman*** (sound; "sound-brahman"). Sound is a real form of the absolute, but the lower one. **Verdict: does not map.** The text gives no relation among sounds, such as consonance or a whole of tones. Sound matters as a means of ascent, and its variety is something to pass beyond.

**मिथुन *mithuna*** (couple, pair), in Chāndogya I.1: speech and breath are joined in Om "as two people come together". **Verdict: partly maps.** It is a union of two unlike partners who complete each other. But it is a pair joined in one syllable, not a many-part whole.

**सत् *sat*** (being, the True) and the honey simile. **Verdict: does not map; it disagrees.** The whole is reached when the parts can no longer say whose juice they are. That is what “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” calls homogenization, and the text presents it as the highest truth.
an: Śaṅkara's Advaita reads the honey and the soundless brahman as non-difference (not traced in the library; the library holds his *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* and Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary).
Kashmir Śaiva thought, including Abhinavagupta, keeps the One but treats the world of difference as its real self-expression. See abhinavagupta.md and.
Saṅgīta theory takes the sound-brahman as its metaphysical ground.
nh: **Nādabindu Upaniṣad**: not in the library as a text (only named in Weber's *History of Indian Literature*). The best PD edition would be the Adyar *Yoga Upaniṣads* (ed. A. Mahadeva Sastri, 1920) or the T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar translation (*The Yoga Upaniṣads*, Adyar 1938).
**Müller's SBE 15** (Upanishads II, with the Maitrāyaṇa) was not found in the library, so Hume (1921) was used for the Maitrī.

q.t: Poetry expresses the intent, song extends the words, sounds depend on the extension, and the musical scale harmonizes the sounds. If the eight types of instruments [original: "八音" - metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, leather, and wood] are in harmony and do not usurp each other's roles, the gods and humans will be in harmony.
If one, knowing how such ease should be prized, manifests it, without regulating it by the rules of propriety, this likewise is not to be done.
IN CEREMONIES A NATURAL EASE IS TO BE PRIZED, AND YET TO BE SUBORDINATE TO THE END OF CEREMONIES,—THE REVERENTIAL OBSERVANCE OF PROPRIETY.
without regulating it by the rules of propriety, this likewise is not to be done.
When those feelings have been stirred, and they act in their due degree, there ensues what may be called the state of HARMONY.

kb.t: The Analects (Lunyu) 論語, 1.12 and 13.23 (compiled c. 5th–4th c. BCE)
kb.th: The Analects says two things about *he* 和. The junzi is "harmonious but not the same" (13.23). And *he* is the most valued thing in the practice of ritual, but *he* that is not regulated by ritual "is not to be done" (1.12). The second line puts a limit on the first.
h: **Harmonious, not the same.** "君子和而不同、小人同而不和。" ([Analects XIII.23, Legge 1861, p. 137, scan 291](/q/BilNtf0qXbKcIO6KMy3))
**Legge reads it as manners.** "The superior man is affable, but not adulatory". His note glosses *tong*: "同, 'agreeing with,'=flattering." ([XIII.23, p. 137, scan 291](/q/BilNtf0qXbKcIO6KMy3))

**Harmony is bounded by ritual.** Youzi: "禮之用，和為貴 … 知和而和，不以禮節之，亦不可行也。" In Legge's English: "If one, knowing how such ease should be prized, manifests it, without regulating it by the rules of propriety, this likewise is not to be done." Legge's chapter heading: "IN CEREMONIES A NATURAL EASE IS TO BE PRIZED, AND YET TO BE SUBORDINATE TO THE END OF CEREMONIES,, THE REVERENTIAL OBSERVANCE OF PROPRIETY." ([Analects I.12, p. 7, scan 161](/q/BilNtf0qXbKcIO6KMvx))

**Zhu Xi: harmony is each rank keeping its own dance.** In the *Zhuzi yulei*: when the Son of Heaven performs his dance, the lords theirs and the officers theirs, "此便是和" (this is harmony); when lords usurp the Son of Heaven's dance, "失禮便不和" (losing ritual is not harmony). ([Zhuzi yulei, juan 21–22 vol., p. 128, Chinese only](/q/Bl0cpAyimC4ZSAO53iq)) (partial: untranslated page)
tr: **Native terms:** *he* 和 against *tong* 同 (13.23). In 1.12, *he* is paired with *li* 禮 (ritual propriety) and limited by *jie* 節 (to regulate, to measure out, as joints divide bamboo).

**What it means here:** in 13.23, getting on with others without merging into them. Legge's "affable … not adulatory" shows that a careful 19th-century reader took it as a matter of conduct between people, not a theory of wholes. In 1.12, *he* is the ease or concord that makes ritual work. Legge translates it "natural ease" and does not use "harmony" at all. *He* is prized, but only as the grace of a ritual order that it must not exceed.

**Verdict: partly maps, and less than its fame suggests.** 13.23 alone supports "harmony is not sameness". Read with 1.12, Analects *he* is concord *within* a ritual hierarchy, and *li* sets the bounds. Zhu Xi's reading makes the bounds explicit: harmony is everyone in their rank. That is order and fitness, not parts that flourish in their own right. It agrees with “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” against homogenization. It does not support the guard clause, and it can be used against it, since usurping one's rank is the paradigm of disharmony.
an: Yanzi (Zuozhuan, Zhao 20) and Shi Bo (Guoyu) give the he/tong contrast its fullest form: see zuozhuan.md, guoyu.md.
The Zhongyong turns *he* inward: feelings that "hit the measure"; and "harmonious without being carried along": (see zhongyong.md).
Xunzi and the Yueji assign union to music and distinction to ritual.
Modern critics ask whether Confucian harmony can resist being used for conformity.

Empedocles, On Nature (Love and Strife)|.a: Empedocles places the rounded Sphere in the strong recess of Harmony. Fragment 27a adds that no faction or fight is found in its limbs.

q.t: But in the strong recess of Harmony, Established firm abides the rounded Sphere, Exultant in surrounding solitude.

Philolaus, fragments (DK 44)|||Greek.a: Philolaus gives harmony a measured extent: a fourth plus a fifth, with the fifth exceeding the fourth by 9/8. The fragment sets the fourth at 4/3, the fifth at 3/2 and the octave in the double ratio. It counts harmony as five 9/8 intervals plus two dieses, and the fifth as three 9/8 intervals plus one diesis.

k.g: the orderly arrangement of the universe

q.t: Indeed, things that are similar and of a similar nature had no need of harmony; but things that are dissimilar, which have neither a similar nature 1 nor an equal function, in order to be placed within the linked whole of the world, must necessarily be bound together by harmony.

Therefore, those things that were similar and related when this structure of things was being born did not need harmony. But those that were dissimilar and neither related nor equal had to be bound together by such a harmony if they were to be contained in the world.

Daodejing (ch. 42)|||Chinese.a: The chapters shown pair opposites that produce, complement and follow one another, and say that sound and voice harmonize with each other. Of the Way, the text says it blunts its sharpness, unravels its tangles, harmonizes its light, and joins with the dust.

q.t: Therefore, Being and Non-being produce each other; difficulty and ease complement each other; long and short shape each other; high and low lean toward each other; sound and voice harmonize with each other; front and back follow each other.
So that it is manifest that swift motion makes a high sound, but slow motion a low sound.
There are three means in music: one is the arithmetic, the second is the geometric, and the third is the subcontrary
And the followers of Archytas used to say that, in consonances, the perception by the ear is of a single sound.
for that which is uttered with a strong impetus of breath is loud and high-pitched; but that with a weak breath, small and low.

kb.t: Archytas of Tarentum (fl. c. 400–350 BCE), fragments via Porphyry
kb.th: Sound is a blow between moving things, high pitch is swift motion, and the mathematical sciences, music among them, are kin. Archytas is the physical and arithmetical foundation of the ratio school.
h: **Swift is high, slow is low.** Many sounds escape us through weakness, distance or excess of size. Of those we hear, the swift seem high and the slow low. "So that it is manifest that swift motion makes a high sound, but slow motion a low sound." He also says "(These mathematical sciences seem to be kindred.)" ([Porphyry in Wallis, *Opera* III p. 237, scan 279](/q/BgOZAX781b89OAfAJ5L))

([Republic X, 617b, scan 483, p. 459](/q/BgTjff0MBbQTZUwcpLH))

kb.th: Concord needs difference. Turning a concord into unison destroys it, and the same goes for a city made too much one. Musical modes carry character into the soul, and consonance pleases as an ordered mixture of opposites. But the soul is not a harmony, and Aristotle reports the Pythagorean "the heaven is a harmony and a number" without endorsing it.
h: **Too much unity destroys the city, as unison destroys a concord.** Against the Republic's common property and families, Aristotle argues that "the less unified is more desirable than the more unified" ([Politics II.2, scan 218](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQEws)). The city must be "one in a way, but not in every way": "For there is a sense in which, as it proceeds, it will not be a city; and there is a sense in which it will be, but being close to not being a city, it will be a worse city. Just as if someone were to make a harmony into a unison, or a rhythm into a single beat." ([Politics II.5, 1263b, scan 224](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQEwy))

**The modes imitate character, so music belongs in education.** The Mixolydian makes listeners mournful and the Dorian makes them "settled", while the Phrygian makes them enthusiastic. "In the melodies themselves, there are imitations of character; and this is clear, for immediately the nature of the harmoniai is distinct, so that those listening are disposed differently" ([Politics VIII.5, 1340a, scan 417](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQF05))

**The soul is not a harmony.** He gives two senses of harmony: a fitting-together of magnitudes, and a ratio of mixed elements. Neither fits reason or perception. If the ratio of a mixture were the soul, flesh and bone would each have one. "Although it is true that harmony is a sort of relation in mixed parts or a combination of parts, we maintain that it is impossible for the soul to be either of these." ([De anima I.4, 407b, Hammond 1902, scan 118, p. 26](/q/BhCV8opeqevMf7Pbdnq)) In the Politics he only *reports* the rival view: "many wise men say: some, that the soul is a harmony; others, that it possesses harmony." ([Politics VIII.5, 1340b, scan 418](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQF06))

**Consonance pleases because it is an ordered mixture of opposites** (Aristotelian *Problems*, a school compilation). "We delight in consonance because it is a mixing of opposites that have a ratio to one another. Now, ratio is order, which is naturally pleasant. And everything mixed is pleasanter than the unmixed" ([Problems XIX.38, scan 173, p. 144](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjimr))

**Any consonance beats a single note, and the octave pleases most.** "Every consonance is pleasanter than a simple sound for the reasons stated. And of these, the octave is the most pleasant. A single note has a simple sound." Singing in octaves joins boys and men: "the most pleasant thing from different sources becomes one and common through the octave." ([Problems XIX.39, scan 173, p. 144](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjimr))

**He reports, and does not adopt, the Pythagorean cosmos of number.** The Pythagoreans "thought that the whole heaven was a harmony and a number", set ten paired opposites, and invented a counter-earth to make ten heavenly bodies ([Metaphysics A.5, scan 404](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjiqa)).
an: Plato's Phaedo had already refuted the soul-as-attunement view, and Aristotle extends that refutation. Alexander of Aphrodisias develops it.
Pseudo-Aristotle's *De Mundo* builds the cosmos and the city from opposites.
Aristoxenus, his pupil, makes the ear the judge of harmony.
Zhmud says "all is number" is Aristotle's gloss on the Pythagoreans, not their own slogan. On the cross-domain metaphor objection: (not checked against Aristotle's own text; see below).
Plotinus answers the proportion theory of beauty. Modern coincidence theories echo XIX.39's coinciding periods.

q.t: Harmony, say its advocates, is a mixture and combination of opposites. The body, too, is composed of opposites. Although it is true that harmony is a sort of relation in mixed parts or a combination of parts, we maintain that it is impossible for the soul to be either of these.

If all the parts of the body are composed of mixed elements, and the ratio of this mixture constitutes harmony and soul, we have the absurd result that we possess many souls distributed through the entire body.

If it is so, it is inconvenient for the mixture of elements to be the soul. For the mixture of elements does not have the same reasons according to which there is flesh and according to which there is bone. Therefore, it will happen that there are many souls here and according to every body.

q.t: Harmony may be illustrated by soup. You have the water and fire, vinegar, pickle, salt, and plums, with which to cook fish.
If you were to try to give water a flavour with water, who would care to partake of the result? If lutes were to be confined to one note, who would be able to listen to them?
Keu is an assenter merely; how can he be considered in harmony with you?
Whatever you say 'Yes' to, he also says 'Yes.' Whatever you say 'No' to, he also says 'No.'

kb.t: The Zuozhuan, "Zuo Commentary" on the Spring and Autumn Annals (compiled c. 4th c. BCE; Zhao 20–21 = 522–521 BCE)
kb.th: Harmony (*he* 和) is not agreement. Yanzi compares it to a soup and to music, where unlike things correct each other. But he says what it is for: a ruler whose judgement is made right, a mind made level, and a government with no contention in it. On the same page Confucius uses *he* for alternating mild and severe rule, and a year later a music master uses it for sound that fits what the heart can bear.
h: **Harmony is not assent.** The marquis says Keu is "in harmony" with him. Yanzi answers: "Keu is an assenter merely; how can he be considered in harmony with you?" The soup needs water, fire, vinegar, pickle, salt and plums. The cook adds what is lacking and takes away what is in excess. Water flavoured with water is no dish, and a lute held to one note is no music. ([Zhao 20, tr. Legge, pp. 684–685, scan 430](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WU))

**Music is made of paired contrasts.** "Then there are [the distinctions of] clear and thick, small and large, short and long, fast and slow, solemn and joyful, hard and soft, lingering and rapid, high and low, the commencement and close, the close and the diffuse, by which the parts are all blended together." The aim follows at once: the superior man listens "that his mind may be composed." ([Zhao 20, scan 430, p. 685](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WU))

**The difference serves a level government.** The minister points out what is wrong in what the ruler approves, and what is right in what he rejects. "In this way the government is made equal, with no infringement of what is right, and there is no quarrelling with it in the minds of the people." ([Zhao 20, scan 430, p. 684](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WU))

**Confucius: harmony is alternation between mild and severe.** Zichan told his successor that only the perfectly virtuous can rule by mildness. The successor was mild, robbers multiplied, and he then "killed them all". Confucius approves: "Mildness serves to temper severity, and severity to regulate mildness;, it is in this way that the administration of government is brought to harmony." ([Zhao 20, scan 430, pp. 684–685](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WU))

**Ling Zhoujiu: harmony is sound fitted to the heart.** King Jing plans to cast the huge bell Wuyi. The music master objects: "The smaller notes must not be too small, nor the greater too great. [This being the case], there ensues a harmony with things without, and admirable music is the result." ([Zhao 21, scan 431, p. 687](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WV)) If the bell is too large, "the king's heart will not be able to endure it." ([scan 432, p. 688](/q/BgRsiMHIbWchDdEV2WW)) The Chinese, printed on scan 430, reads 則和於物.
tr: **Native terms:** *he* 和 (to blend, to tune, to answer in song; in the soup, the cook's verb "mixes", 宰夫和之) against *tong* 同 (same, agreeing). Yanzi also uses *ping* 平 (level, made equable) for the result: the master's mind is "made equable" and the government "made equal". Legge renders *tong* as "assent".

**What it means here:** three different things on two pages. (a) Yanzi: a mixture of unlike ingredients, adjusted until nothing is lacking or in excess. (b) Confucius on Zichan: a balance between two policies over time, which is a mean. (c) Ling Zhoujiu: a fit between sound and the capacity of the heart, which is a measure.

**Verdict: partly maps.** Yanzi's soup is the best ancient match for "diversity in wholeness". Unlike parts are needed, and sameness counts as failure. Two things do not map. First, the guard clause. The ingredients are valued for what they do to the master's mind, not for themselves. The minister's dissent is valued because it makes the *ruler's* approval "entirely correct". Second, the end state is the absence of contention, so the diversity is in the means and not in the outcome. Confucius's use (on the same page) is plainly a mean between extremes, and its "severity" is the killing of robbers.
an: Shi Bo in the Guoyu makes the same he/tong contrast, earlier in narrative time: (see guoyu.md).
Confucius, Analects 13.23: (see analects.md).

The Han writer Liu Liang's "Discourse distinguishing he and tong" reuses the soup and the lute to praise remonstrance: "correcting the unacceptable with the acceptable is he; likes and dislikes that do not differ are tong". It is reprinted with Yanzi's speech in the Ming anthology *Jingji leibian*.
The modern critique that he/tong does not stop harmony being used to demand conformity.

k.g: the cultivation of the mind through music, literature, or contemplation

q.t: For the household and the city must be one in a way, but not in every way. For there is a sense in which, as it proceeds, it will not be a city; and there is a sense in which it will be, but being close to not being a city, it will be a worse city. Just as if someone were to make a harmony into a unison, or a rhythm into a single beat.

It is therefore evident from these points that a city is not naturally one in the way some say; and that which is claimed to be the greatest good in cities, in fact, destroys them. … If, then, the more self-sufficient is more desirable, then the less unified is more desirable than the more unified.
music is able to produce a certain quality of character in the soul. If it is able to do this, it is clear that the young must be led into it and educated in it.

kb.th: Concord needs difference. Turning a concord into unison destroys it, and the same goes for a city made too much one. Musical modes carry character into the soul, and consonance pleases as an ordered mixture of opposites. But the soul is not a harmony, and Aristotle reports the Pythagorean "the heaven is a harmony and a number" without endorsing it.
h: **Too much unity destroys the city, as unison destroys a concord.** Against the Republic's common property and families, Aristotle argues that "the less unified is more desirable than the more unified" ([Politics II.2, scan 218](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQEws)). The city must be "one in a way, but not in every way": "For there is a sense in which, as it proceeds, it will not be a city; and there is a sense in which it will be, but being close to not being a city, it will be a worse city. Just as if someone were to make a harmony into a unison, or a rhythm into a single beat." ([Politics II.5, 1263b, scan 224](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQEwy))

**The modes imitate character, so music belongs in education.** The Mixolydian makes listeners mournful and the Dorian makes them "settled", while the Phrygian makes them enthusiastic. "In the melodies themselves, there are imitations of character; and this is clear, for immediately the nature of the harmoniai is distinct, so that those listening are disposed differently" ([Politics VIII.5, 1340a, scan 417](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQF05))

**The soul is not a harmony.** He gives two senses of harmony: a fitting-together of magnitudes, and a ratio of mixed elements. Neither fits reason or perception. If the ratio of a mixture were the soul, flesh and bone would each have one. "Although it is true that harmony is a sort of relation in mixed parts or a combination of parts, we maintain that it is impossible for the soul to be either of these." ([De anima I.4, 407b, Hammond 1902, scan 118, p. 26](/q/BhCV8opeqevMf7Pbdnq)) In the Politics he only *reports* the rival view: "many wise men say: some, that the soul is a harmony; others, that it possesses harmony." ([Politics VIII.5, 1340b, scan 418](/q/BhIh9YkfTERfSFvQF06))

**Consonance pleases because it is an ordered mixture of opposites** (Aristotelian *Problems*, a school compilation). "We delight in consonance because it is a mixing of opposites that have a ratio to one another. Now, ratio is order, which is naturally pleasant. And everything mixed is pleasanter than the unmixed" ([Problems XIX.38, scan 173, p. 144](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjimr))

**Any consonance beats a single note, and the octave pleases most.** "Every consonance is pleasanter than a simple sound for the reasons stated. And of these, the octave is the most pleasant. A single note has a simple sound." Singing in octaves joins boys and men: "the most pleasant thing from different sources becomes one and common through the octave." ([Problems XIX.39, scan 173, p. 144](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjimr))

**He reports, and does not adopt, the Pythagorean cosmos of number.** The Pythagoreans "thought that the whole heaven was a harmony and a number", set ten paired opposites, and invented a counter-earth to make ten heavenly bodies ([Metaphysics A.5, scan 404](/q/Bjby2leRswtiLndjiqa)).
an: Plato's Phaedo had already refuted the soul-as-attunement view, and Aristotle extends that refutation. Alexander of Aphrodisias develops it.
Pseudo-Aristotle's *De Mundo* builds the cosmos and the city from opposites.
Aristoxenus, his pupil, makes the ear the judge of harmony.
Zhmud says "all is number" is Aristotle's gloss on the Pythagoreans, not their own slogan. On the cross-domain metaphor objection: (not checked against Aristotle's own text; see below).
Plotinus answers the proportion theory of beauty. Modern coincidence theories echo XIX.39's coinciding periods.

q.t: Some of them introduce "alien" matter and exclude sensory perception as being altogether inaccurate, substituting instead intellectual reasons and asserting that there are certain mutual numerical ratios
We, on the contrary, attempt first to establish as foundations all the phenomena which those experienced in music perceive, and then to demonstrate that which follows from them.
For the geometer does not require the power of sensory perception
For the musician, however, the sharpness of sensory perception is nearly the status of a first principle

kb.t: Aristoxenus of Tarentum, Elements of Harmonics (c. 330 BCE)
kb.th: Pitch is a continuous space in which melody sets down stable notes, and intervals are distances in it, judged by a trained ear, not ratios of numbers. Their *functions* are judged by the intellect. That makes him the founder of the "ear" side of the ancient quarrel.
h: **Phenomena first, then proof.** He rejects predecessors who "exclude sensory perception as being altogether inaccurate" and explain pitch by "numerical ratios" and speeds, and also those who pronounce facts like oracles. "We, on the contrary, attempt first to establish as foundations all the phenomena which those experienced in music perceive, and then to demonstrate that which follows from them." ([Marquard p. 47, scan 89](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcEMT))

**The musician is a carpenter, not a geometer.** The geometer never trains his eye to judge whether a line is straight, but "For the musician, however, the sharpness of sensory perception is nearly the status of a first principle" ([p. 49, scan 91](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcEMV)), which refines.

**Speech glides; song stands still.** The voice has two motions through pitch space. The continuous motion belongs to speech. The intervallic motion belongs to song, where "we pursue bringing the voice to a standstill as much as possible", and the steadier each note, "the more accurate the melody appears to our perception." ([Greek leaf p. 14, scan 56](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcELw))

**Consonances are sharp, dissonances loose.** Consonant sizes have no range of variation, or only an infinitesimal one, while dissonant ones "possess this stability to a much lesser degree". Therefore "the most accurate way to 'grasp' a dissonant interval is through the use of consonance", by a chain of fourths and fifths ([Greek p. 80, scan 122](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcEN0)).

**The ear test of the fourth.** He builds ditones by consonance inside a fourth, extends the remainders outward, and brings the outer notes "to the test of hearing". If they sound a fifth, "the fourth consists of five semitones" ([Greek p. 82, scan 124](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcEN2)).

**Fixed and changing functions.** Music "involves both a permanent and a variable element". The same compass takes different names and functions by position ([p. 49, scan 91](/q/BeofsjNckUqTd7OcEMV)).
an: Euclid's *Sectio canonis* answers him by proof (props. 15–16).
Ptolemy (Harm. I.9–11) attacks both his method and his result. Ptolemy keeps his ear as a joint criterion.
Cleonides' *Introductio* (printed in Euclid vol. VIII, scans 244ff.) is an Aristoxenian handbook that passed under Euclid's name. It is held but not claimed here.
Plato's Republic VII had already mocked those who "put their ears before their minds".
nh: **Edition note:** the library's record is catalogued as "Macran 1902". Its title page is **Paul Marquard, *Die harmonischen Fragmente des Aristoxenus*, Berlin 1868**. Even scans are Greek, translated by the library from the Greek. Odd scans are Marquard's German, so their English is English←German←Greek. Each claim says which it uses. Macran's 1902 Greek–English edition was not found as a separate record.

q.t: and the denser ones produce sharper sounds, while the rarer ones produce deeper ones
Wherefore it must be said that sounds are composed of parts, since they are corrected by addition and subtraction.
the consonant ones produce a single blending of the two, while the dissonant ones do not
belong to those numbers which are spoken of by one name in relation to one another, being either multiples or superparticulars

kb.t: Euclid (attrib.), Sectio canonis / Katatomē kanonos (c. 300 BCE)
kb.th: Sound is motion, pitch is the frequency of that motion, and so intervals are numerical ratios. Consonance is the blending of two sounds into one, and the arithmetic of ratios then proves what the ear cannot settle: the tone has no equal halves, and the fourth is less than two and a half tones.
h: **Sound is motion, and so number.** "the denser ones produce sharper sounds, while the rarer ones produce deeper ones". Because a pitch is tuned by adding or taking away motion, "Wherefore it must be said that sounds are composed of parts, since they are corrected by addition and subtraction." ([Heiberg–Menge p. 158, scan 216](/q/BhF8Wi1bknjTcyEODSy))

**Consonance is one blend.** "the consonant ones produce a single blending of the two, while the dissonant ones do not" (μίαν κρᾶσιν), and so consonances are ratios "being either multiples or superparticulars" ([scan 216](/q/BhF8Wi1bknjTcyEODSy), [scan 218](/q/BhF8Wi1bknjTcyEODT0))

**Against the Aristoxenian sizes.** "Thus, the interval BΓ is less than two whole-tones and a semitone, which is the fourth", and "The whole-tone shall not be divided into two equal [parts] nor into more." ([props. 15–16, scan 234](/q/BhF8Wi1bknjTcyEODTG))
**Tuning by consonance.** Prop. 17 finds the lichanos by the same chain of fourths and fifths that Aristoxenus uses ([scan 234](/q/BhF8Wi1bknjTcyEODTG))
an: Aristoxenus's school held the opposite sizes.
Ptolemy accepts the ratio framework, rejects the superparticular rule and agrees on the fourth.
Boethius, *De institutione musica* IV, translates much of the Sectio (not claimed here).

q.t: when the strings of your lute were neither too much stretched nor too loose, but fixed in even proportion, had your lute sound then, was it then in a fit state to be played upon?
Do thou, therefore, O Sona, be steadfast in evenness of determination, press through to harmony of your mental powers.
Therefore, Sona, resolve on an evenness of energy, pierce through to an evenness of the spiritual faculties, and therein take up your object
By avoiding these two extremes, O Bhikkhus, the Tathâgata has gained the knowledge of the Middle Path

kb.t: The lute-string simile: Soṇa Koḷivīsa and the Middle Way (Vinaya Mahāvagga V.1; also AN 6.55; Pali canon, c. 4th–3rd c. BCE)
kb.th: A monk who strives so hard that his feet bleed is reminded of his lute. Strings that are too tight or too loose give no music; strings set "in even proportion" do. Effort, too, should be even. The teaching is about evenness (samatā), the mean between two extremes. It is not about many parts making a whole.
h: **Only strings neither too tight nor too loose can be played.** "when the strings of your lute were neither too much stretched nor too loose, but fixed in even proportion, had your lute sound then, was it then in a fit state to be played upon?" ([Mahāvagga V.1.16, tr. Rhys Davids & Oldenberg, p. 8 [scan 22]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlO3nvM0PcMUKzrwU)). The Pali says the strings are *samē guṇē patiṭṭhitā*, "set at an even pitch" ([Nalanda Pali ed., p. 202 [scan 246]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BkHwzBGaWAMs3raWnig)).

**The same holds for effort.** Over-exerted energy leads to restlessness and slack energy to sloth. So Soṇa is told to resolve on evenness of energy and to penetrate the evenness of the faculties: "वीरियसमतं अधिट्ठह, इन्द्रियानं च समतं पटिविज्झ" ([p. 202 [scan 246]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BkHwzBGaWAMs3raWnig)). The 1882 translators render this: "Do thou, therefore, O Sona, be steadfast in evenness of determination, press through to harmony of your mental powers." ([p. 9 [scan 23]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlO3nvM0PcMUKzrwV))

**A second Vinaya tradition carries the same dialogue.** The Tibetan Vinaya of the Kanjur has Śroṇa and the lute. There the right state of the strings is *ran pa*, "fitting, just right": "When the strings of the lute are neither too tight nor too loose, but are tuned evenly" ([Thadrak Kanjur, 'Dul ba Nga, p. 300 (the library's translation)](/q/Bijfy3OEsYI9E8bmE8q)).

**The simile reached Chinese and Japanese Buddhism.** In the Sutra of Forty-two Chapters a monk who played the "guitar" answers: "“How when they were neither too tight nor too loose?” “Every note sounds in its proper tone.”" ([§34, tr. Suzuki for Soyen Shaku, p. 17 [scan 31]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWxKFVtaHApYWom1n))

**The frame is the Middle Path of the first sermon.** "By avoiding these two extremes, O Bhikkhus, the Tathâgata has gained the knowledge of the Middle Path" ([Mahāvagga I.6.17, p. 94 [scan 138]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhPXIeb5uGyl6M9xHQ2))
tr: **Native terms.** Pali *samatā* (समता), "evenness, sameness, equality", in *vīriya-samatā* (evenness of energy) and *indriyānaṃ samatā* (evenness of the faculties). The strings are *samē guṇē*, "at an even pitch". The verdict for a tuned instrument is *saravatī* ("having sound") and *kammaññā* ("workable"). In Tibetan the word is *ran pa*, "fitting".

**The English word "harmony" here comes from the translators.** Rhys Davids and Oldenberg wrote "harmony of your mental powers" for *indriyānaṃ samataṃ*. Anyone who quotes that line as "the Buddha on harmony" is quoting 1882 English, not the Pali.

**Verdict: does not map** onto “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”, with one partial exception. The image is one string at the right tension between two failures. That is the mean, not diversity in wholeness. The two failures (too tight, too slack) are not homogenization and fragmentation. They are excess and deficiency of a single quantity. The exception is the "evenness of the faculties". Later commentary explains it as balancing five different faculties against each other (faith with wisdom, energy with concentration). That would be diversity in balance.
an: The Sutra of Forty-two Chapters carried it into Chinese and then Japanese Zen teaching.
Huainanzi on strings that resonate is a Chinese string image of a different kind: sympathy between strings, not the tension of one.
Later Theravāda commentary on balancing the five faculties (Visuddhimagga) builds directly on *indriya-samatā*.

Yijing, Wenyan and Xici (like sounds res.a: The Xici says the junzi's good words are answered from a thousand miles away, and bad words are opposed at that distance. It calls words and actions the shuji, the hinge by which the junzi moves Heaven and Earth. It also says two people of one heart can cut through metal, and their words have a fragrance like orchids. The opening of the Xici states that things of the same type congregate, and describes the firm and yielding rubbing together, thunder and wind and rain, and the sun and moon running their courses.

q.t: The Master said: "When the junzi superior person/gentleman dwells in his room, if he sends forth words that are good, they will be responded to from a thousand miles away; how much more so those who are near?

Movement and stillness have their constants, and the firm and the yielding are determined. Things of the same type congregate, and objects are divided by groups, thus good fortune and misfortune arise.
When those feelings have been stirred, and they act in their due degree, there ensues what may be called the state of HARMONY.
Let the states of equilibrium and harmony exist in perfection, and a happy order will prevail
throughout heaven and earth, and all things will be nourished and flourish.
"Heaven and Earth will get their correct place, and the processes of production and completion will go on according to their principles, so that all things will be nourished and fostered."

kb.t: The Zhongyong 中庸, "Doctrine of the Mean" (attrib. Zisi; c. 4th–3rd c. BCE; ch. 1 and ch. 10)
kb.th: Before the feelings arise the mind is in *zhong* 中, equilibrium. When they arise and each "hits the measure", that is *he* 和, harmony. Carried to the utmost, *zhonghe* puts heaven and earth in their places, and all things are nourished. Harmony here is due measure: a mean notion applied to emotion and extended to the cosmos.
h: **Harmony is feeling in due degree.** "喜、怒、哀、樂之未發、謂之中、發而皆中節、謂之和". Legge: "When those feelings have been stirred, and they act in their due degree, there ensues what may be called the state of HARMONY." Equilibrium is "the great root" and harmony "the universal path". ([Doctrine of the Mean 1.4, Legge, p. 351, scan 357](/q/Bem4O0uA6cumtwPdAE1))

**Zhonghe orders the cosmos.** "Let the states of equilibrium and harmony exist in perfection, and a happy order will prevail" ([1.5, scan 357](/q/Bem4O0uA6cumtwPdAE1)) "throughout heaven and earth, and all things will be nourished and flourish." ([p. 352, scan 358](/q/Bem4O0uA6cumtwPdAE2)) Legge reports Zhu Xi's gloss on 位: heaven and earth "will rest in their positions".

**Harmonious without being carried along.** "Therefore, the superior man cultivates a friendly harmony, without being weak., How firm is he in his energy! He stands erect in the middle," (和而不流 … 中立) ([ch. 10.5, p. 359, scan 365](/q/Bem4O0uA6cumtwPdAE9))
tr: **Native terms:** *zhong* 中 (centre; equilibrium; as a verb, to hit the mark), *he* 和, the compound *zhonghe* 中和, and *jie* 節 (measure, joint, due degree). 中節 is literally "to hit the joint/measure". *Yong* 庸 (constant, ordinary) gives the title, which Legge renders "the Mean".

**What it means here:** *he* is a state of one person's emotional life in which each feeling, when it arises, is neither too much nor too little. There is diversity of feeling (pleasure, anger, sorrow, joy), but the harmony lies in each one hitting its measure, not in how they combine. At the cosmic level, harmony means heaven, earth and the myriad things each "rest in their positions". In ch. 10, *he* is a social virtue: getting on with others without drifting into them.

**Verdict: mostly does not map.** Ch. 1 harmony is the mean (Aristotle's *meson* is the nearer Western partner, not Philolaus's harmony of unlikes). It is about proportion and position, not diversity in wholeness. Ch. 1 does say all things "are nourished and flourish" (萬物育), which echoes the guard clause, but the flourishing follows from everything being in its correct place. Ch. 10's 和而不流 does map onto “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s rejection of homogenization, in the same way as Analects 13.23.
an: Xunzi calls music "the binding thread of equilibrium and harmony" (中和之紀): (see xunzi.md).
Zhu Xi's *Zhongyong zhangju* made ch. 1 central to Neo-Confucian self-cultivation. the library holds several Song–Ming Zhongyong commentaries (e.g.
Analects 13.23 is the parallel to ch. 10.

q.t: When (the wind) blows, (the sounds from) the myriad apertures are different, and (its cessation) makes them stop of themselves.
The first notes are slight, and those that follow deeper, but in harmony with them.
Gentle winds produce a small response; violent winds a great one.
the blowing results in ten thousand different sounds. This is to secretly compare the arguments of the world as being unequal.

kb.t: Zhuangzi, "Qiwulun" (Book II, "The Adjustment of Controversies"; c. 4th–3rd c. BCE)
kb.th: The "piping of Heaven" is not a separate music. It is the ten thousand hollows, each sounding differently and of itself when the wind blows. The sage "harmonizes" a quarrel by letting both sides stand and resting in Heaven's equal working. Difference is kept, but the dispute is dropped.
h: **Heaven's music is the many sounds left to themselves.** "When (the wind) blows, (the sounds from) the myriad apertures are different, and (its cessation) makes them stop of themselves." Earlier: "The first notes are slight, and those that follow deeper, but in harmony with them." ([Bk II §1, tr. Legge, p. 178 [scan 206]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRMhna8uenKpEths3a); [p. 177 [scan 205]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRMhna8uenKpEths3Z))

**He (和) here means "answer".** "Gentle winds produce a small response; violent winds a great one." The Chinese is 泠風則小和，飄風則大和, and leading sounds are answered by following ones (前者唱于而隨者唱喁). ([Legge p. 177 [scan 205]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRMhna8uenKpEths3Z); [1699 ed., p. 63](/q/Biiqx8v6fXrwIQS5Dbz))

**The sounds stand for the world's opinions.** A 1699 commentator: "the blowing results in ten thousand different sounds. This is to secretly compare the arguments of the world as being unequal." ([莊子旁注, p. 62 (the library's translation)](/q/Biiqx8v6fXrwIQS5Dby))

**The sage holds both sides.** "Therefore the sagely man brings together a dispute in its affirmations and denials, and rests in the equal fashioning of Heaven … Both sides of the question are admissible." ([Bk II §4, p. 185 [scan 213]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRMhna8uenKpEths3h))

**Harmonizing keeps difference.** "The harmonising of them is to be found in the invisible operation of Heaven". Affirmation "is certainly different from the denial of it:, there can be no dispute about that." Then: "let us forget the conflict of opinions." ([Bk II §10, p. 196 [scan 224]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRMhna8uenKpEths3s))
tr: **天籟 tianlai**, "piping of Heaven": this is the passage's key term. It is not 和. It names the many sounds, each "taking from itself" (咸其自取).
**和 he**: in §1 it is the old musical sense of *answering* sound, call and response. In §4 and §10 it means *reconciling* a dispute. Legge writes "brings together" and "harmonising".

**Verdict: partly maps.** Zhuangzi is a strong witness against homogenization. The hollows stay different, and so do affirmation and denial. But there is no whole that the parts build or strengthen. Reconciliation comes from stepping back to the Tao's viewpoint and forgetting the quarrel, not from joint work. This meets the "diversity" half of “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” and leaves out the "parts and whole strengthen each other" half.
an: Guo Xiang's commentary reads tianlai as "self-so" (自然). the library holds a 1635 Zhuangzi with Guo Xiang (69935b6c2c6394406313403a).
Confucian he (Analects, Zuozhuan) is a social mixing of unlike things. Zhuangzi keeps the unlike things but drops the cook.
Zhang Zai's "Supreme Harmony" takes up the language of qi in motion (see zhang-zai).

Ps.-Aristotle, Problems XIX (on music)||.a: The Problems explain consonance by ratio. A consonance is a collection of sounds that have a ratio to each other. The double-octave is consonant because its extremes stand in a quadruple ratio, while the double-fifth and double-fourth, built from 3:2 and 4:3, yield extremes that are neither multiples nor superparticulars. They say the octave seems to be one sound because of the analogy of equality in the notes, and that the hypate appears to resonate when the nete is stopped because of similarity. Rhythms and melodies are said to resemble moral character because they are movements, as actions are.

q.t: Why do the double-fifth and double-fourth not produce consonance, but the double-octave does? Is it because the fifth is in a hemiolion three-to-two ratio, and the fourth is in an epitritos four-to-three ratio?
Why is the octave the most beautiful consonance? Is it because the ratios are in whole terms, whereas the others are not?
Why is the antiphonon octave response more pleasant than the symphonon consonance? Is it because the consonance becomes more distinct than when one sings against the consonance?
Therefore, music investigates oneness to establish harmony, coordinates instruments to adorn meter, and blends voices to complete artistic patterns.
when music sounds within the ancestral temple and ruler and minister, high and low, listen to it together, all are filled with harmony and reverence.
Thus, music is the great regulator of the realm, the binding thread of equilibrium and harmony, and an unavoidable demand of human nature.
Furthermore, music embodies harmony that cannot be changed; ritual embodies order that cannot be altered. Music unites and harmonizes; ritual distinguishes and separates.

kb.t: Xunzi 荀子, "Discourse on Music" (Yuelun 樂論, ch. 20; c. 3rd c. BCE)
kb.th: Xunzi defends music against Mozi as a tool of rule. Music fixes harmony from a single standard, binds ranks together in shared feeling, and is "the great regulator of the realm". Music "unites the same" and ritual "distinguishes the different". In this text harmony is the uniting, levelling pole, and difference lives in ritual.
h: **Harmony is fixed from the one.** "Therefore, music investigates oneness to establish harmony, coordinates instruments to adorn meter, and blends voices to complete artistic patterns." (故樂者審一以定和者也) Music suffices "to guide people along a single Way". ([Yuelun, juan 14, p. 95 (the library's translation)](/q/Bojb0GnS1vOWqoRET3n))

**One music, a bond for each rank.** When "ruler and minister, high and low, listen to it together, all are filled with harmony and reverence". At home father and son feel harmony and affection, and in the village old and young feel harmony and compliance. ([p. 95 (the library's translation)](/q/Bojb0GnS1vOWqoRET3n))

**Music is the great leveller.** "Thus, music is the great regulator of the realm, the binding thread of equilibrium and harmony, and an unavoidable demand of human nature." (樂者天下之大齊也中和之紀也) The same music serves the king going out to punish and coming home to yield: "none fail to obey". ([p. 96 (the library's translation)](/q/Bojb0GnS1vOWqoRET3o))

**Music unites the same; ritual separates the different.** "Furthermore, music embodies harmony that cannot be changed; ritual embodies order that cannot be altered. Music unites and harmonizes; ritual distinguishes and separates." (樂合同，禮別異) ([p. 100 (the library's translation)](/q/Bojb0GnS1vOWqoRET3s))
tr: **Native terms:** *he* 和; *zhonghe* 中和 ("equilibrium and harmony", the same compound as the Zhongyong); *qi* 齊 (to make even, uniform; the dancers' "advances and retreats achieve uniformity", 進退得齊, p. 96); *tong* 同, used approvingly in 合同 (unite the same) and 同聽 (listen together).

**What it means here:** *he* is shared feeling produced by one music heard together. It is tuned from one standard, makes the realm even, and leaves the ranks in place: reverence for the minister, compliance for the young. the library translation's "unites and harmonizes" for 合同 hides that Xunzi praises *sameness* here, which is what Yanzi and Confucius condemn.

**Verdict: does not map.** Xunzi's harmony is unity and conformity of feeling. Diversity is supplied by a different institution (ritual), which fixes rank. The whole is music-plus-ritual, so one could argue the *pair* is diversity in wholeness, as the Yueji page does. But on that reading the "diversity" is hierarchy, and its parts are asked to obey, not to flourish.
an: Mozi's "Against Music" is the target throughout ("Yet Mozi condemns it: how mistaken!").
The Yueji shares much of this text and the music/ritual division: (see yueji.md).
Against Xunzi's positive *tong*: Yanzi's water-with-water and Shi Bo's "sameness does not continue".

q.t: Being tranquil and pleasant without pride, they attained harmony. … Though there are ten thousand differences, all find convenience in their own nature. … Its Virtue is more abundant than Heaven and Earth and it harmonizes Yin and Yang.

It is like a drum; it has no inherent tone, yet it matches all sounds. The small and large, the long and short of metal and stone instruments are all ordered; different sounds combine to form harmony. The ruler and ministers, from the top down to their official duties, have ranks and distinctions; when affairs differ, they still harmonize.

The harmonious union of Heaven and Earth and the transformative molding of yin receptive cosmic energy and yang active cosmic energy mean that the ten thousand things all ride upon the vital breath of humanity.

kb.t: Huainanzi (Liu An and his court, presented 139 BCE)
kb.th: Things of the same kind resonate with each other, and the Way harmonizes yin and yang in such a way that the ten thousand different things each keep their own nature. The twelve pitch-pipes are generated from Huangzhong by alternate steps of a third.
h: **Sounds of the same kind respond to each other.** "今失調弦者，叩宮宮應，彈角角動，此同聲相和者也" ([Lanming, juan 6, Wikisource](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/淮南子/覽冥訓); the same passage, reading 今夫, is held untranslated in [the library juan 4–7, scan 104](/book/huainan-hongliejie-juan-4-7-contains-dixing-the-topographic-al/page/6a09f7acae0ff9f86740c093))

**Harmony lets ten thousand different things each keep their nature.** "Being tranquil and pleasant without pride, they attained harmony. … Though there are ten thousand differences, all find convenience in their own nature. … Its Virtue is more abundant than Heaven and Earth and it harmonizes Yin and Yang." ([Yuandao, juan 1, scan 21](/q/Bjeg7KdrNlZwai56GPd))

**The twelve lü are generated by alternate descent and ascent (partial: read from a search snippet).** "黃鍾為宮宮者音之君也故黃鍾位子其數八十一 … 下生林鍾林鍾之數五十四 … 上生太蔟太蔟之數七十二" ([Tianwen, juan 3, scan 138, untranslated](/book/huainan-hongliejie-juan-1-3-contains-tianwen-the-12-pitch-al/page/6a09f7a6ae0ff9f86740c012)). The numbers 81 → 54 → 72 → 48 → 64 are the subtract-a-third, add-a-third method, and each pipe is tied to a month.
an: Dong Zhongshu, on the zither's like-to-like response.
Caution on reading ganying as physics.
Zhu Zaiyu replaces the three-part method with equal temperament.
Gao You's commentary is interlinear in the library edition.
nh: No English translation of the Huainanzi is in the library.

Huangdi neijing (Suwen and Lingshu)|||Ch.a: The commentary treats harmonizing Yin and Yang meridians as a matter of sequence. When Yin is abundant and Yang deficient, the practitioner supplements Yang first and then drains Yin. When Yang is abundant, the order is reversed. The commentator ties abundance to the Maikou and Renying pulses and gives the reason that supporting the Zheng Qi, the upright or vital qi, is always the first priority.

q.t: When Yin is abundant and Yang is deficient, first supplement its Yang, and afterward drain its Yin to harmonize them. When Yin is deficient and Yang is abundant, first supplement its Yin, and afterward drain its Yang to harmonize them.
All the modulations of the voice arise from the mind, and the various affections of the mind are produced by things (external to it).
Music is (thus) the production of the modulations of the voice, and its source is in the affections of the mind as it is influenced by (external) things.
they are the instruments by which the minds of the people are assimilated, and good order in government is made to appear.
Hence, the airs of an age of good order indicate composure and enjoyment. The airs of an age of disorder indicate dissatisfaction and anger

kb.t: The Yueji, "Record of Music" (Liji Book XVII; compiled c. 3rd–1st c. BCE)
kb.th: Music is the harmony of heaven and earth and the uniting principle in society, while ceremony is the distinguishing one. Each fails alone: music by itself gives a "weak coalescence", and ceremony by itself gives separation.
h: **Music comes from the mind moved by things.** "All the modulations of the voice arise from the mind, and the various affections of the mind are produced by things (external to it)." ([Liji XVII §1.1, tr. Legge, scan 106, p. 92](/q/BgRlAhI3DcE1ES13xne))

**The music of a state shows its government.** Rites, music, laws and punishments are one set of instruments of rule. "Hence, the airs of an age of good order indicate composure and enjoyment. The airs of an age of disorder indicate dissatisfaction and anger" ([§1.3–4, scan 107, p. 93](/q/BgRlAhI3DcE1ES13xnf))

**Music unites and ceremony distinguishes, and each has its own failure.** "Similarity and union are the aim of music; difference and distinction, that of ceremony. From union comes mutual affection; from difference, mutual respect. Where music prevails, we find a weak coalescence; where ceremony prevails, a tendency to separation." ([§1.15, scan 112, p. 98](/q/BgRlAhI3DcE1ES13xnk))

**Music is the harmony of heaven and earth.** "Music is (an echo of) the harmony between heaven and earth; ceremonies reflect the orderly distinctions (in the operations of) heaven and earth. From that harmony all things receive their being" ([§1.23, scan 114, p. 100](/q/BgRlAhI3DcE1ES13xnm))
an: Xunzi's "Discourse on Music" (Yuelun) shares much of this text.
Mozi's "Against Music" is the opposing position.
Confucius on he vs. tong. Yanzi's soup, which the Yueji's "harmony as union" sits uneasily with.

Cicero, The Dream of Scipio (Republic VI.a: Africanus explains the sweet sound that fills Scipio's ears as the product of the spheres' motion, blending high notes with low. The sound is linked by unequal intervals and distinguished by proportion. He adds that learned men, by imitating it with strings and songs, have opened a return to the heavenly place.

q.t: For such great motions cannot be stirred in silence, and nature provides that the extremes on one side sound deeply, while those on the other sound sharply. For this reason, that supreme course of the starry heaven, whose rotation is faster, moves with a sharp and excited sound, while this lowest one, that of the moon, moves with the deepest.
But those eight paths, of which there is a double power, produce seven sounds divided by intervals, which number is the very bond of existing things.

Ps.-Aristotle, On the Cosmos (De mundo)|.a: The author compares the universe to a city, where civic concord produces unity out of plurality. The arts are offered as imitations of nature: painting mixes white and black, music mixes high and low, and writing mixes vowels and consonants. The text cites Heraclitus on things that agree and differ, and calls God the Coryphaeus who leads the choir of the heavens.

q.t: Perhaps nature has a liking for contraries and evolves harmony out of them, not out of similarities (just as she joins the male and female together, not members of the same sex), and has devised the original harmony by means of contraries.
But the concert which exists from all these things, as they are consonant in heaven and form a choir: as it arises from one, so it terminates in one.

Therefore, the structural arrangement of the universe—I mean of the heaven and the earth and the whole world—Nature itself arranged with a certain harmony of principles that are highly contrary, fittingly tempered, and one and the same harmonious cohesion.

In this way, through this reasoning, the voice from the stage, as if poured out from a center, circulating and striking the cavities of the individual vessels, will arouse an increased clarity and a consonance harmonious to itself.

Indeed, this can be noticed even by cithara players, who, when they wish to sing at a higher pitch, turn themselves toward the doors of the stage, and thus receive the consonance of the voice from their assistance.

the bells are the emblem of the concord and harmony that exist between these things; for neither is the earth without the water, nor the water without the earthly substance, sufficient for the production of anything
since all things are comprised in the number four, namely, a point, and a line, and a superficies, and a solid, and the measures of all things, and the most excellent symphonies of music
it is in reality an ancient discovery of Moses, that out of the same thing opposite things are produced having the ratio of parts to the whole
being in the midst between these two extremities, like a hostage, as it were, to both parties

kb.t: Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – c. 50 CE)
kb.th: Philo reads the Torah through Greek philosophy. The world is a concord of unlike, mutually dependent parts, built on Pythagorean number. Everything is set opposite something else, and the divine Word stands between the opposites and keeps the whole in order.
h: **Concord of parts that need each other.** On the high priest's robe as a model of the world: "the bells are the emblem of the concord and harmony that exist between these things; for neither is the earth without the water, nor the water without the earthly substance, sufficient for the production of anything" ([De vita Mosis II, tr. Yonge, vol. 3 p. 98 [scan 108]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAuN4EehpJvrbfLie4))

**The tetrad holds the musical ratios.** The four-letter Name stands for the tetrad, "since all things are comprised in the number four, namely, a point, and a line, and a superficies, and a solid, and the measures of all things, and the most excellent symphonies of music" (the fourth, fifth, octave and double octave) ([vol. 3 p. 97 [scan 107]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAuN4EehpJvrbfLie3))

**Opposites come from one thing.** Philo lists dozens of opposites and says Heraclitus's principle "is in reality an ancient discovery of Moses, that out of the same thing opposite things are produced having the ratio of parts to the whole" ([Quis rerum divinarum heres, tr. Yonge, vol. 2 p. 135 [scan 147]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAweBMRvXNXEzHIoC3))

**The Word stands between.** The divine Word stands "in the midst between these two extremities, like a hostage, as it were, to both parties", so that creation does not choose "disorder rather than order" ([vol. 2 p. 134 [scan 146]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAweBMRvXNXEzHIoC2))
tr: Philo wrote in Greek: **harmonia ἁρμονία**, **symphōnia συμφωνία** (concord, consonance) and **isotēs ἰσότης**. Yonge's "concord and harmony" probably renders *symphōnia kai harmonia*.

**Verdict: maps in part, and better than most.** Point 1 is diversity in wholeness in a strict sense: unlike parts that produce together what neither can produce alone. Point 3 puts opposition inside unity. Two limits apply. The Word's job is order, peace and preventing "revolt" (point 4), so the whole is ruled from above. Philo also counts the Greek view as Moses's. That is apologetic, and it should not be read as independent cross-cultural evidence: Philo *is* the Greek tradition, read into Jewish scripture.
an: His Logos and number symbolism passed to Clement, Origen and the Church Fathers. His Jewish reception was slight until the Renaissance (Azariah de' Rossi).
Compare Sefer Yeṣira's opposites with a mediating third.
nh: **Not held in English:** Yonge vol. 1 (*De opificio mundi*), where Philo discusses number and the harmony of creation. the library holds the Greek *De opificio* in Richter's edition (1828, vol. 1, book 69944b4d1ba8351377905e27) and Cohn–Wendland (1896). Neither was read. Best PD English: Yonge, *Works of Philo Judaeus* vol. 1 (Bohn, 1854).

Pliny the Elder, Natural History (sympat.a: Pliny the Elder describes the planets as moving against the rotation of the world, so that the air is split, separated, and digested by the contrary beating of the stars. He gives Saturn a cold and rigid nature and Mars an igneous one. Jupiter, placed between them, is tempered by each and becomes salutary.

q.t: Therefore, because of its excessive heat and the coldness of Saturn, Jupiter, which is placed between both, is tempered by each and becomes salutary.
remaining even-minded in success and failure. This equanimity is called yoga.
As manifestations of Brahman, though of different qualities and classes.
to whom pain and pleasure are alike; to whom a sod and a stone and gold are alike
And the natural duty of Sûdras, too, consists in service. (Every) man intent on his own respective duties obtains perfection

kb.t: Bhagavad Gītā (c. 2nd c. BCE – 1st c. CE)
kb.th: Yoga is *samatva*, being the same toward success and failure. The wise see a brahmin, a cow, a dog and an outcaste as alike. The Gītā's balance is evenness of one mind toward opposites. Its picture of a differentiated society is a fixed order of birth-duties.
h: **Yoga is evenness.** "सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते". the library's translation renders this as "remaining even-minded in success and failure. This equanimity is called yoga." ([BG 2.48, Schlegel 1823, p. 14 [scan 50] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiYyE73l7mU3JZJWHn0)). Telang has "(such) equability is called devotion" ([SBE 8, p. 49 [scan 65]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlJ2PBx4HEq6FKsSH)).

**The wise see unlike beings as the same.** "The wise look upon a Brâhmana possessed of learning and humility, on a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a Svapâka, as alike". Their mind "rests in equability", because brahman is "equable". Telang's note: "As manifestations of Brahman, though of different qualities and classes." ([BG 5.18–19, p. 65 [scan 81]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlJ2PBx4HEq6FKsSX))

**The one beyond the guṇas treats opposites as equal.** He is someone "to whom pain and pleasure are alike; to whom a sod and a stone and gold are alike" ([BG 14.24, p. 110 [scan 126]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlJ2PBx4HEq6FKsTG)).

**Society is an allotment of duties by birth.** "And the natural duty of Sûdras, too, consists in service. (Every) man intent on his own respective duties obtains perfection". "One's duty, though defective, is better than another's duty well performed" ([BG 18.44–47, p. 127 [scan 143]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlJ2PBx4HEq6FKsTX)).
tr: **समत्व *samatva* / साम्य *sāmya*** (sameness, evenness). From *sama*, "same, even, level". In 2.48 it is the agent's evenness toward success and failure. In 5.19 *sāmya* is the mind resting in the sameness of brahman. **Verdict: does not map.** It is equanimity. It is a property of one mind, and it is reached by not weighing the difference between opposites. If it is used at all, it fits “Harmony is hierarchical: levels of wholeness”'s "harmony at the level of one mind". It does not fit diversity in wholeness.

**समदर्शन *sama-darśana*** (seeing the same). This is a vision of sameness beneath difference. **Verdict: does not map.** Telang's note keeps the differences ("different qualities and classes"), but they do no work in the whole.

**स्वधर्म *svadharma* / वर्ण *varṇa*** (one's own duty, by class). This is a differentiated social whole. **Verdict: partly maps in structure, but fails the guard clause.** There are unlike parts and one order. But the parts are fixed by birth, ranked, and told not to move. This is the "rank / conformity" reading that “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s guard clause excludes.

**योग *yoga*** (yoking, joining). The Maitrī Upaniṣad glosses it as joining breath, Om and mind. In the Gītā it is discipline, and Telang translates it "devotion". Nothing in the word implies parts in a whole.
an: Buddhist texts that Telang's notes cite constantly (*Sutta Nipāta*) share the equanimity ideal (*upekkhā*). That is the other agent's middle-way page.
Commentators Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Śrīdhara and Ānandagiri appear in Telang's notes. Their readings of samatva were not traced.
Modern critiques of the varṇa passages (Phule, Ambedkar) are the obvious objectors on 18.41–47.

q.t: Disease is the imbalance of the bodily elements; balance is called health.
Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease.
Similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity.
Mind, soul, and body, this trinity, called person, resteth on union like three sticks (standing with one another’s support.) Upon that (trinity) everything rests.

kb.t: Caraka and Suśruta, the Āyurvedic saṃhitās (Caraka redaction c. 1st c. BCE – 2nd c. CE; Suśruta c. 3rd–4th c. CE)
kb.th: Health is *sāmya*, evenness of the body's elements and the three doṣas. Disease is *vaiṣamya*, unevenness. Treatment is action aimed at restoring evenness. Likeness increases a quantity and unlikeness decreases it: "similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity". The person is a tripod of mind, soul and body that hold each other up.
h: **Health is evenness, disease is unevenness.** "विकारो धातुवैषम्यं साम्यं प्रकृतिरुच्यते", "Disease is the imbalance of the bodily elements; balance is called health." Treatment is "प्रवृत्तिर्धातुसाम्यार्था", action aiming at evenness of the elements. ([Caraka, Sūtrasthāna 9.3–4, p. 135 (the library's translation)](/q/BikGiuGd2JWxn8v9m7D))

**Likeness produces oneness and increase; unlikeness produces diversity and decrease.** "Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease." "Similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity." ([Sū. 1.44–45, tr. Kaviratna 1890, p. 4 [scan 14]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biw4tJkL8GnXSdiOJ8o))

**The person is a tripod.** "Mind, soul, and body, this trinity, called person, resteth on union like three sticks (standing with one another’s support.) Upon that (trinity) everything rests." ([Sū. 1.46, p. 4 [scan 14]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biw4tJkL8GnXSdiOJ8o))

**Is anyone evenly balanced? Caraka says the norm is even.** "Some say that there are no creatures that are of equable wind, bile, and phlegm, because of human beings taking food of unequal virtues." Caraka rejects this: physicians want "समवातपित्तश्लेष्माणं", the person with even vāta, pitta and kapha. "Constitutions" named after one doṣa only mean that doṣa predominates. ([Vimānasthāna 6, Sanskrit p. 388](/q/BikGiuGd2JWxn8v9mBI); [Kaviratna p. 519 [scan 678]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Biw4tJkL8GnXSdiOJJW))

**Suśruta's healthy person.** "A person with an uniformly healthy digestion, and whose bodily humours are in a state of equilibrium, and in whom the fundamental vital fluids course in their normal state and quantity... is said to be a healthy person." ([Suśruta, Sū. 15.41, tr. Bhishagratna 1907, p. 232](/q/Biw4rMs4LmzJLZTwx2W))
tr: **साम्य *sāmya* / सम *sama*** (evenness, equality; *samadoṣa*, "even doṣas"). The opposite is **वैषम्य *vaiṣamya*** (unevenness). **Verdict: partly maps.** The three doṣas are unlike (motion, heat, cohesion), and all three must be present. Health is a whole of unlike parts, and none may dominate. That much fits “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”, and it parallels Greek *isonomia* and *krasis*. But the criterion is equal or proper *measure* and return to a norm. The doṣas do not strengthen each other or the whole. They are kept in check. And Caraka treats individual predominance as deviation, not as a valuable variety. The right English is "balance" or "equilibrium". Kaviratna's 1890 footnote uses "harmony" ("a harmony or equability of the three faults"); that is the translator's word.

**सामान्य / विशेष *sāmānya / viśeṣa*** (likeness / particularity). In Caraka's own scheme, likeness makes oneness and unlikeness makes diversity, and both are tools. **Verdict: does not map.** Diversity here is a corrective force that reduces an excess, not a value.

**The tripod (*tridaṇḍa*).** **Verdict: maps best.** Three unlike things, each holding the others up, and "everything rests" on the result. This is the Āyurvedic image closest to "parts and whole strengthen each other".
an: Vāgbhaṭa's *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya* (the library holds the 1891 Sanskrit) restates the doṣa doctrine and treats doṣa-predominant constitutions (*prakṛti*) more positively.
Caraka's own opponents, quoted in Vimānasthāna 6, who deny that anyone is even (item 4).
the library search surfaced a Galen passage (Kühn vol. 14, scan 735) on humours "harmoniously arranged in their qualities".

q.t: just as the Sun among the seven planets is fourth on either side, being the middlemost
for which reasons we do not fully hear this cosmic symphony sounding out something so lush and all-harmonious as the theory describes
That the primary music among sensible things is perceived in the planets, and that our music is an imitation of it.

kb.th: Harmony is a structure of numbers. The true harmonia is the "most perfect" proportion, in which the arithmetic, harmonic and geometric means are woven together (6, 8, 9, 12). The same numbers govern strings and planets.
h: **The harmonic mean is named from the cube.** Nicomachus reports the Philolaic derivation: the cube's 12 edges, 8 corners and 6 faces form a harmonic proportion. "Some believe that this proportion is called "harmonic" in accordance with the views of Philolaus, because it accompanies every geometric harmony. They say that "geometric harmony" is the cube" ([Introduction to Arithmetic II.26, Hoche 1866, scan 153, p. 135](/q/Beog4uqodV9tqIJQHqT))

**Only the four-term proportion deserves the name harmonia.** In it the harmonic and arithmetic means stand between two extremes, and the geometric proportion appears among them. "for this alone could properly and truly be called harmony in a way that the others cannot." ([Introduction to Arithmetic II.29, scan 162, p. 144](/q/Beog4uqodV9tqIJQHqc))

**The seven strings are the seven planets, but the cosmic music is not fully heard.** The Sun is the mese, Saturn the hypate and the Moon the nete. He promises to explain "for which reasons we do not fully hear this cosmic symphony sounding out something so lush and all-harmonious as the theory describes" ([Manual of Harmonics 3, Jan 1895, scan 344, p. 242](/q/Beog4QdFRNhqJWiIwhM))

**The smithy story ends in a universal law of number.** Pythagoras moves the ratios 6, 8, 9, 12 from hammers to strings and then to every instrument: "and in all of them he found the grasp of harmony through number to be consistent and unerring" ([Manual of Harmonics 6, Jan 1895, scan 350, p. 248](/q/Beog4QdFRNhqJWiIwhS))
an: Iamblichus copies the smithy story and comments on the *Introduction*.
Boethius's *De institutione arithmetica* is a Latin adaptation of the *Introduction*, and *De institutione musica* follows Nicomachus in Book I.
Archytas named the three means before him.
Ptolemy rejects the Pythagorean habit of fitting numbers without the ear.
The physics of the hammer story.
