q.t: say that music is a harmony of opposites, a unification of the many, and a shared mindset of those who think differently
Indeed, God is the harmonizer of the discordant, and this is the greatest work of God: to make enemies into friends
Guided by numbers, he applied such ratios to vessels.
for its goal is to unite

kb.t: Theon of Smyrna, Expositio rerum mathematicarum ad legendum Platonem utilium (c. 125 CE)
kb.th: A Platonist handbook of the mathematics needed to read Plato. Its musical part preserves the Pythagorean formula that music is "a harmony of opposites, a unification of the many", together with early reports of ratio experiments.
h: **Music as the harmony of opposites.** The Pythagoreans "say that music is a harmony of opposites, a unification of the many, and a shared mindset of those who think differently". Its goal is "to unite", and "God is the harmonizer of the discordant, and this is the greatest work of God: to make enemies into friends". The one power is harmony in the cosmos, *eunomia* in the city and temperance in the home ([Hiller p. 12, scan 34](/q/BeogB3blhPrPtxPckPS)).

**Ratios tested on apparatus.** Lasus and the circle of Hippasus tied consonance to speeds of motion. Hippasus is said to have struck equal vessels, one empty and the other filled by fractions, to get the octave, fourth and fifth ("Guided by numbers, he applied such ratios to vessels.") ([p. 59, scan 81](/q/BeogB3blhPrPtxPckQD)).

**Both schools' units side by side.** The Aristoxenians call the quarter-tone the smallest singable diesis. The Pythagoreans give that name to what is now called the semitone ([p. 55, scan 77](/q/BeogB3blhPrPtxPckQ9)). Not made a claim.
an: Nicomachus and Iamblichus carry the same Pythagorean material. Hiller's apparatus cross-refers Philolaus and Nicomachus.
Boethius's *De institutione musica* uses the same tradition.

q.t: Then indeed the soul, stripped of the motions of the celestial harmony, returns to its desired nature
He who had all judgment and power over the mortal and irrational living things of the world, emerged through the harmony and went out.
having fallen into the harmony, he was put at risk and made a slave
For the friendship and the blending of opposites and unlikes has become a shining light

kb.t: Corpus Hermeticum and Asclepius (Greek treatises c. 1st–3rd c. CE; Latin Asclepius c. 4th c.; Ficino's Latin 1463)
kb.th: In the Hermetica "the harmony" (ἁρμονία) is first a *structure*: the seven planetary governors and their zones, the machinery of fate. Man was made above it, fell into it and became its slave; the soul's salvation is to climb back through it, giving each zone back its power until it stands outside the harmony altogether. Beside this sits a warmer picture of cosmic order: the planets shine because of a "friendship and blending of opposites and unlikes", and the Asclepius defines music as knowing the order of all things gathered into one divine song.
h: **The ascent through the harmony is a stripping.** After death the soul rises up through the harmony (διὰ τῆς ἁρμονίας), and at the first zone "he gives up the energy of growth and waning"; at the seventh it gives up "the lie that lies in wait" (ἐνεδρεῦον ψεῦδος). Only when it has been stripped (γυμνωθείς) of the harmony's workings does it reach the eighth nature and become one of the Powers ([CH I.25–26, Greek MS, scan 162](/q/BejFoukEepZzy8QxSza)). Ficino's Latin: "Thus the remainder then hastens back through the harmony" ([p. 22](/q/BeeLnC21tompzKeTFCQ)); "the soul, stripped of the motions of the celestial harmony, returns to its desired nature" ([p. 23](/q/BeeLnC21tompzKeTFCR)).

**Man fell into the harmony and was enslaved there.** The archetypal Man, given a share in each governor's order, "emerged through the harmony and went out" to look down on Nature ([CH I.14, 1532 ed., p. 15](/q/BcORHXQ0k51dBviJCN8)). Loving her, he descended: "having fallen into the harmony, he was put at risk and made a slave" ([CH I.15, 1481 ed., p. 19](/q/BeeLnC21tompzKeTFCN)).

**The planets shine by a friendship of opposites.** The seven worlds are full of light but not of burning fire: "For the friendship and the blending of opposites and unlikes has become a shining light" ([CH XI.7, Greek MS, scan 210](/q/BejFoukEepZzy8QxT0M)). Ficino's Latin is *amicitia contrariorum dissimiliumque commixtio*; the Source Library English renders it "For it is the harmony … of opposites and the blending of dissimilar things that established this light", with a note that *amicitia* literally means "friendship" ([1481, p. 64](/q/BeeLnC21tompzKeTFD6)). The word *harmonia* is not in either text here.

**Many unlike motions keep one order.** "For although the movements are many and various, and the bodies themselves are dissimilar, there is yet one single order of speed". The text argues that this order proves a single maker, because with more than one "the one who was weaker would surely envy the more powerful, and from this, a kind of discord would arise" ([CH XI.9, 1481, p. 65](/q/BeeLnC21tompzKeTFD7)).

**Music is knowing the order of all things.** "To know music is nothing else but to know the order of all things and what the divine reason has allotted. For the order of individual things, brought together into one by a craftsmanlike reason, will produce a certain harmony sweet-sounding and most true in a divine song" (*concentum quendam melo divino*) ([Asclepius 13, 1532, p. 134](/q/BcORHXQ0k51dBviJCP3); garbled in the [Vatican MS, p. 328](/q/BeliJaVZekOCgmHY5NY)).
an: Ficino translated CH I–XIV in 1463 and built his astral music on cosmic attunement, but kept the Poimandres ascent as a model of liberation.
Macrobius gives the Platonist version of the planetary ladder, in which the spheres furnish faculties rather than vices.
Plato's Sirens on the spindle are the older image of a sounding planetary order. The Hermetica turn it into a system of fate.
Augustine (City of God VIII) attacked the Asclepius on idols; not read here.

q.t: He said that the body of music consists of unequal parts that nevertheless harmonize
it is necessary for sense and intelligence to concur in judging the parts of music, so that they neither go before—which happens to headlong senses—nor are left behind—which happens to the slow.

What has been said should suffice to show that neither harmonics, nor rhythmics, nor any other of the specific musical sciences is self-sufficient on its own to understand character or to judge the other aspects of music.
Therefore, he did not judge music by the sense of hearing, but by harmonic proportion.

kb.th: A dialogue-history of Greek music that ends as an argument about judgement. Harmony is unlike parts sounding together (citing Aristotle). Sense and intellect must "run together", and no technical science, whether harmonics or rhythmics, suffices to judge character.
h: **Unlike parts that agree.** Aristotle (reported) said harmony's body "consists of unequal parts that nevertheless harmonize" (ἐκ μερῶν ἀνομοίων συμφωνούντων μέντοι), in the terms 6, 8, 9, 12 ([Volkmann p. 28, scan 38](/q/Beog4ilO9qyg1zHlzWw)).

**Sense and intellect run together.** "it is necessary for sense and intelligence to concur in judging the parts of music, so that they neither go before … nor are left behind". Judgement works on continuous sequences, not isolated notes, and "neither harmonics, nor rhythmics, nor any other of the specific musical sciences is self-sufficient on its own to understand character" ([pp. 41–43, scans 44–45](/q/Beog4ilO9qyg1zHlzX3)).

**Pythagoras against the ear, and a trained ear lost.** Pythagoras "did not judge music by the sense of hearing, but by harmonic proportion". Yet now that the enharmonic is out of use, "most people do not possess even a casual perception of enharmonic intervals" ([p. 45, scan 46](/q/Beog4ilO9qyg1zHlzX4)).
an: Its material on Pythagoras and the ear parallels Aristides III. Its sense–intellect rule refines Ptolemy's.

q.t: The criteria of harmony are two: hearing and reason. But they function in different ways. Indeed, hearing judges according to matter and affection; reason, according to form and the cause
it follows by right that sensible perceptions must be defined and limited by rational ones
the Pythagoreans (not sufficiently obeying the warning of Hearing in all things where they ought) adapted to the differences of sounds those Proportions which are often incongruous with Phenomena
The Aristoxeneans, however, attributing too much to those things perceived by sense, abused Reason as if it were a side-issue

kb.th: Harmony is a rational cause of well-proportioned motion, to be found by hearing and reason together, and it shows most clearly in human souls and the heavens.
h: **Two criteria, with different jobs.** Hearing finds what is close to right; reason finds what is exact, and sense must be bounded by reason. "The criteria of harmony are two: hearing and reason. But they function in different ways. Indeed, hearing judges according to matter and affection; reason, according to form and the cause" ([Harmonics I.1, Wallis 1682, scan 33, p. 1](/q/BhF4qDI1tKL5iu6SUVd))

**Both schools erred.** The Pythagoreans ignored the ear and the Aristoxenians slighted reason. A harmonicist must keep rational hypotheses "which in no way conflict with the senses", as an astronomer does with the phenomena. "the Pythagoreans (not sufficiently obeying the warning of Hearing in all things where they ought) adapted to the differences of sounds those Proportions which are often incongruous with Phenomena" ([Harmonics I.2, scan 40, p. 8](/q/BhF4qDI1tKL5iu6SUVk))

**Harmonia is a power in all moving things, clearest in souls and the heavens.** "the power of harmony is a species of the cause according to reason, which concerns the symmetry of motions" ([Harmonics III.4, scan 269, p. 237](/q/BhF4qDI1tKL5iu6SUZR))

**Virtue is concinnity and justice is a consonance.** Ptolemy maps reason, spirit and appetite onto the octave, fifth and fourth. "the concinnity of sounds is a certain virtue of them, and discordance is a vice; and, conversely, the virtue of souls is a certain concinnity of them, and vice is discordance" ([Harmonics III.5, scan 273, p. 241](/q/BhF4qDI1tKL5iu6SUZV))

**The double octave is a circle like the zodiac.** Unrolled at an equinox, the zodiac fits the two-octave system, and neither has "any beginning by nature, but only by convention" ([Harmonics III.8, scan 282, p. 250](/q/BhF4qDI1tKL5iu6SUZe))
an: Against Aristoxenus's ear-first criterion.
Boethius takes over the reason-over-sense ranking and draws much of Book V from Ptolemy.
Porphyry wrote a commentary on the Harmonics.
Kepler reworked Book III's programme on observed planetary ratios in Harmonices Mundi, and edited an appendix on Ptolemy.
nh: Not found in the library: Düring's 1930 critical edition.

Galen, On Temperaments|||Hellenistic & L.a: Galen, in the Linacre translation, calls the middle of all extremes eucraton (well-tempered) and symmetron (well-proportioned), with the equality of the portions of the elements as its norm. In each genus or species the symmetra are the mean, equally distant from the highest and lowest limits, and the human is the mean in temperament among animals. Health has a latitude, and an intemperies within it counts as health until some function is manifestly harmed.

q.t: The norm and judgment of this was the equality of the portions of the elements. For this reason, the middle of all extremes, rendered to a precise degree, is called eucraton well-tempered and symmetron well-proportioned, or temperate and mediocre.

Furthermore, in every genus or species, those things which are called symmetra symmetrical/well-proportioned in Greek are the mean. Indeed, they are those which are equally distant from the highest and lowest limits in that genus and species.

Therefore, as great as the interval is between that which performs its function most perfectly and that which has some action manifestly harmed, so great is the latitude of both health and distemperantia bad temperament that exists within health.

Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus (the.a: Clement says the Word harmonized the cosmos and the small world, man, soul and body, with the Holy Spirit. He describes fire softened by air as a Dorian harmony blended with a Lydian, and the sea and land held to their boundaries. He also says the union of many, receiving divine harmony from polyphony and dispersion, becomes one concord following the Word as dancer and teacher.

q.t: But the one from David and before him, the Word of God, disregarding the lyre and the cithara, the soulless instruments, but having harmonized this cosmos and indeed the small world, man, both his soul and body, with the Holy Spirit, sings to God through this many-voiced instrument and sings along with the instrument, the human being.
The union of many, having received divine harmony from polyphony and dispersion, becomes one concord, following the one dancer and teacher, the Word, and finding rest in Truth itself,

The dissonant notes are those that have an interval of twenty microtones. For example: rishabha and gandhara, dhaivata and nishada. Thus, when the vadi, samvadi, and vivadi are established, the remaining ones are called anuvadi.
A note is a vadi because it speaks, samvadi because of consonance, vivadi because of dissonance, and anuvadi because it follows.
two lutes with identical strings and rods should be set to the shadja-grama. One should make one of them follow the madhyama-grama.
Through this method of observing microtones, the twenty-two microtones of the two gramas should be understood.

kb.th: Aesthetic experience (rasa) is the tasted result of combining unlike components, and in music each note has a role relative to the others: speaking, consonant, following, or dissonant. Bharata measures consonance by counting shrutis.
h: **Rasa arises only from a combination.** No single element produces a sentiment. Rasa comes from the joining of determinants, consequents and transient states, just as a taste comes from many condiments. "The birth of rasa [occurs] through the combination of vibhāva, anubhāva, and vyabhicārin." ([Nāṭyaśāstra ch. 6, scan 137, p. 71](/q/BgOdORO6NftNlNHmxZp))

**Rasa is called rasa because it is tasted.** Refined spectators taste the durable states the way refined diners taste a seasoned dish. The causation runs one way, from bhāvas to rasa. "Just as people of refined mind, eating food prepared with various condiments, taste the flavors and obtain joy and other [emotions], in the same way, refined spectators taste the sthāyibhāvas" ([ch. 6, scan 137, p. 71](/q/BgOdORO6NftNlNHmxZp))

**Consonance is a distance counted in shrutis.** The vādī is the focal note. Notes nine or thirteen shrutis apart are samvādī, for example Sa–Ma and Sa–Pa. "There, the note that is the focal point is the vadi; and those that are separated by nine or thirteen microtones are consonant to each other." ([ch. 28, vv. 20–21, scan 383, p. 327](/q/BgOdORO6NftNlNHmxdn))

**Dissonance has a named role in the system.** Ri–Ga and Dha–Ni are vivādī, and every other note is anuvādī, "following". "A note is a vadi because it speaks, samvadi because of consonance, vivadi because of dissonance, and anuvadi because it follows." ([ch. 28, scan 384, p. 318](/q/BgOdORO6NftNlNHmxdo)). In this edition the vivādī interval is printed as "twenty" shrutis.

**The 22 shrutis are shown by experiment, using two identical vīṇās.** "Through this method of observing microtones, the twenty-two microtones of the two gramas should be understood." ([ch. 28, scan 385](/book/natyashastra-muni/page/6990653d726f64800c10a6d8))
an: Śārṅgadeva restates the shruti allocation and the vīṇā demonstration, and adds rakti as the criterion for dissonance.
Mataṅga's Bṛhaddeśī, quoted by Kallinātha.
Abhinavagupta's commentary on the rasa-sūtra.
nh: Ghosh's English translation, vol. 2 (ch. 28 onward), is not in the library.

Censorinus, The Birthday Book|||Roman.a: Censorinus names six numerical ratios that agree with one another, and says each of the first five yields a symphonia (fourth, fifth, octave, octave and fifth, double octave). He says Pythagoras held that the world was made by musical reason, and that the seven wandering stars sound a melody too loud for human ears. The days of gestation (6, 8, 9, 12) are set out as the fourth, fifth and octave.

q.t: From all the countless variety of numbers, few and countable ones were found that would agree with each other to create music. There are six of these in all: epitritus ratio of 4:3, hemiolios ratio of 3:2, duplaris ratio of 2:1, triplaris ratio of 3:1, quadruplus ratio of 4:1, and epogdous ratio of 9:8.

To this is added that which Pythagoras handed down, that this whole world was made by musical reason. And the seven wandering stars between heaven and earth, which moderate the births of mortals, have a movement that is euruthmon rhythmic/well-proportioned, and have movements congruent to musical intervals, and return various sounds according to their own altitude, so concordant that they sing a most sweet melody.

These eight, when they are added to the first six, make the first symphonia, the diatessaron fourth. At the third stage, nine days are added, now making the flesh. When these are compared to those first six, they make a one-and-a-half ratio and the second symphonia, the diapente fifth.

When the same symmetry remains, yet a face appears beautiful at one time and not at another, how can one avoid saying that beauty is something placed upon the symmetry, rather than the symmetry itself?
Hence the whole is at last beautiful, not if every thing is as a stone, but if every part conferring a proper tone rightly conduces to one entire harmony
If therefore we should say that virtue is harmony, but vice dissonance, shall we adduce an opinion conformable to that of the ancients?

For it is not only necessary that they should sing together, but that each should sing well with an appropriate music, as far as pertains to his own part of the performance; so that then also in the soul there is harmony, when each part performs that which is adapted to it.

kb.th: The cosmos is one living being whose unequal and even discordant parts sound one harmony through sympathy. Beauty, though, is not symmetry: proportion is beautiful only because of something beyond it.
h: **Beauty is not the symmetry of parts.** He rejects the view held "by almost everyone": on that view simple things such as colour, sunlight, gold, lightning or a single tone could not be beautiful. "When the same symmetry remains, yet a face appears beautiful at one time and not at another, how can one avoid saying that beauty is something placed upon the symmetry, rather than the symmetry itself?" ([Enneads I.6.1, Greek MS 1464, scan 67](/q/BgTrHRPLpc8xmD3v47v))

**The whole is one harmony because its voices are unequal.** Providence puts lesser and discordant parts into the whole, as a pipe needs a weaker voice beside the strong one. "Hence the whole is at last beautiful, not if every thing is as a stone, but if every part conferring a proper tone rightly conduces to one entire harmony" ([Enn. III.2.17, Taylor 1794, scan 269, p. 190](/q/Bi8TVXMpLHijB36Kair)). "so that even the tune which a soul sings discordant to herself is melodious to the whole" ([scan 270, p. 191](/q/Bi8TVXMpLHijB36Kais))

**Virtue is the soul's harmony, but each part needs its own excellence first.** "For it is not only necessary that they should sing together, but that each should sing well with an appropriate music, as far as pertains to his own part of the performance; so that then also in the soul there is harmony, when each part performs that which is adapted to it." ([Enn. III.6.2, Taylor 1817, scan 220, p. 125](/q/Bi8TYwtni7t7sPx5omC))

**Magic works by cosmic sympathy.** Enchantments work through the cosmos's "breathing together" and through concord and opposition among things united in one living being. "And in the whole universe, because it is friendship and a bond, he is the first sorcerer" ([Enn. IV.4.40, Greek MS 1464, scan 296](/q/BgTrHRPLpc8xmD3v4Bc))

**The universe is a single living being under one harmony.** "For if a movement occurs in one place, it also causes a movement elsewhere. Often this movement is of a different kind, but it is not grasped by sensation; there is a single voice, and it is fitted under a single harmony." ([Enn. IV.4.41, Greek MS 1464, scan 297](/q/BgTrHRPLpc8xmD3v4Bd))
an: Behind him: Plato's harmonized soul and the Stoic sympathy of the whole. Heraclitus's concordant-discordant.
Proclus: beauty as good order. This partly restores the order Plotinus put second.
Ficino translated the Enneads into Latin (1492) and built natural magic on IV.4 in *De vita* III. Not yet a claim; the closest existing claim is.
Early modern sympathetic resonance turned Plotinus's metaphor into experiment. The Chinese parallel is.
Taylor's Neoplatonist translations made him available in English: (Taylor on the Timaeus).
nh: MacKenna's English (1917–30) was not looked for. Ficino's Latin Enneads (Florence 1492) was not found as a separate the library book.

q.t: For it was not possible for those troubled by passions to attain the healing that comes from reason. For pleasure is the strongest lure
either offering harmony to each soul according to similarity or according to opposition
showing that the extremity in music must be grasped intellectually through numbers rather than sensibly through hearing
demonstrating that sensible music falls far short of the precision of intelligible music.

kb.t: Aristides Quintilianus, De musica (c. 3rd–4th c. CE)
kb.th: An eclectic encyclopaedia. Books I–II are largely Aristoxenian: technical harmonics, and music as education that reaches where reason cannot. Book III turns Pythagorean and Platonic: the extremity of music is grasped "through numbers rather than … through hearing".
h: **Feeling reaches where reason cannot.** "For it was not possible for those troubled by passions to attain the healing that comes from reason. For pleasure is the strongest lure". Children's songs and dances could not be forbidden, so they were healed "little by little and imperceptibly" ([Jahn p. 41, scan 114](/q/BgOYQKMuh0EM5T4W8Ys)).

**Two therapies: likeness and opposition.** The musician offers harmonies "to each soul according to similarity or according to opposition" (ἢ καθ’ ὁμοιότητα … ἢ κατ’ ἐναντιότητα) ([p. 57, scan 130](/q/BgOYQKMuh0EM5T4W8Z8)).

**Numbers over hearing (Book III).** Pythagoras praised the monochord, "showing that the extremity in music must be grasped intellectually through numbers rather than sensibly through hearing", and the Timaeus numbers show that "sensible music falls far short of the precision of intelligible music." ([p. 70, scan 143](/q/BgOYQKMuh0EM5T4W8ZL))
an: Meibom printed him among the *Antiquae musicae auctores septem*. Martianus Capella's Book IX draws on the same material (not checked).

Iamblichus, On the Pythagorean Life|||He.a: Iamblichus says the stars move at different speeds, magnitudes, and intervals, yet are arranged in a most musical proportion to one another. This yields a movement and revolution he calls favorable and beautiful. In chapter 26 Pythagoras names the lyre strings for the numbers six, eight, nine, and twelve, and builds the eight-stringed scale on the double, sesquialter, sesquitertial, and sesquioctave ratios.

q.t: Rather, using a certain ineffable and difficult-to-conceive divinity, he directed his hearing and braced his mind to the celestial harmonies of the cosmos, hearing—as he indicated—alone by himself and understanding the harmony and consonance of the totality of the spheres and the stars moving according to them
yet arranged according to a most musical proportion to one another, a movement and revolution is accomplished at once most favorable and in various ways most beautiful.

And when he had filled in the intervening spaces with proportional sounds according to the diatonic genus, he organized the eight-stringed scale [original: octochordum] with concordant numbers: namely the double [2:1 ratio, the octave], the sesquialter [3:2 ratio, the perfect fifth], the sesquitertial [4:3 ratio, the perfect fourth], and the ratio that separates these two, the sesquioctave [9:8 ratio, a whole tone].
they resemble a Balance, on the one hand the guilty, on the other hand the purified, and Aleph the Air is like the Tongue of a Balance standing between them.
from the air was formed the chest, again placed as a mediator between the others.
God also made every thing, one opposite the other;

kb.t: Sefer Yeṣira, "Book of Formation" (anonymous; c. 3rd–6th c. CE, date disputed)
kb.th: The world is built from ten numbers (*sefirot*) and twenty-two letters. Its basic pattern is a pair of opposites held by a mediating third, and the same pattern is repeated in the world, the year and the human body.
h: **The three mothers are a balance.** "they resemble a Balance, on the one hand the guilty, on the other hand the purified, and Aleph the Air is like the Tongue of a Balance standing between them." ([Sefer Yeṣira III.1, tr. Westcott, p. 19 [scan 19]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bev0BKuyaMfdk7OnBWF))

**The Hebrew names the mediator.** The Mantua 1562 text reads "שלש אמות אמ"ש יסודן כף זכות וכף חובה ולשון חק מכריע בינתים" ([Mantua 1562, scan 222, search snippet](/book/6988a5a0a23e0a8ef27fec91?page=222)) (partial)

**One pattern at three levels.** Fire and water are opposed in the World, the Year and Man. Air, the temperate season and the chest are "again placed as a mediator between the others." ([III.3–4, p. 19](/q/Bev0BKuyaMfdk7OnBWF))

**Everything has its opposite.** "God also made every thing, one opposite the other;" good opposite evil, and each distinguishes the other ([Mantua 1562, p. 191, the library translation](/q/BgBkzZa23vYwy2xY75D))
tr: **lashon ḥoq makhriaʿ beinatayim לשון חק מכריע בינתים**: "the tongue of decree that decides (tips the balance) between them". The image is the needle of a pair of scales. *Makhriaʿ* means to decide or to make one side prevail. It is a judge's word.
**zeh le-ʿummat zeh זה לעומת זה** ("this opposite that"): paired opposites that define each other.
There is no word for "harmony" in the text. The structure is **opposition + mediator**, applied across levels.

**Verdict: partly maps.** Two opposed parts and a third that holds them in one structure fits "dissonance belongs inside" and fits idea 3 (one pattern across levels). But the mediator *decides* between merit and guilt. It does not let both flourish, so this is balance as adjudication. The parts are also elements and moral pans, not agents, so the guard clause has nothing to apply to.

kb.th: The world is beautiful the way a poem is, by ordered contraries, and its parts flourish in their own places. Yet what delights the senses in music is equality and likeness, which is number.
h: **The world is a poem adorned with antitheses.** God orders the ages "like a most beautiful poem" from contraries, the wicked included. "so the beauty of the age is composed by a certain eloquence not of words, but of things, through the opposition of contraries" ([City of God XI.18, Dombart 1877, scan 498, p. 486](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHq)). Latin: "ordinem saeculorum tamquam pulcherrimum carmen etiam ex quibusdam quasi antithetis honestaret" ([scan 497, p. 485](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHp))

**Each part flourishes in its place and contributes to a common whole.** Fire, cold and wild beasts offend us only because they are inconvenient to us. "they flourish in their own places and natures and are disposed in a beautiful order, and how much they contribute to the beauty of the universe of things for their own portions as if to a common commonwealth" ([City of God XI.22, scan 502, p. 490](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHu))

**What pleases the senses pleases by equality.** In sound, form, light, colour, smell and taste: "Nihil eni ẽ horũ p̃stantiu q̃ nob nõ eq̃litate aut similitudine placeat. ubi autẽ eq̃litas aut similitudo ibi nũerositas" ([De musica VI.13.38, 15th-c. MS, scan 104](/q/BhNl3G6Fzzirc8jmjUW)). In plain Latin: nothing pleases us except by equality or likeness, and where there is equality or likeness there is number. **The felt power of singing is a moral risk.** He wept at the Church's songs, approves of them for weaker minds, and still judges it sin to be moved more by the singing than by the words. Martianus Capella, The Marriage of Philo.a: Martianus describes a grove whose high and low sounds are joined in the middle by double, sesquialteral, sesquitertian and sesquioctave intervals, and Cyllenius says the heavenly spheres harmonize in a similar way. The music book assigns the fourth to the epitritus ratio, the fifth to the hemiolios ratio and the octave to the diplasia, the double ratio. It counts the diesis as the fourth part of a tone and sets out five principal modes with their attached modes.

q.t: But the middle of the structure, through the connection of double, sesquialteral ratio of 3:2, and sesquitertian ratio of 4:3 intervals, as well as sesquioctave ratio of 9:8 without indistinct joints, though limmata small musical intervals intervened, sang in harmony. Thus it happened that the grove resounded with the whole harmony and the song of the gods in the congruence of modulations.
But this symphony is in the epitritus ratio of 4:3, the perfect fourth ratio. An epitritus is called that which has both the number three and a third of three, which is one, as four is to three.

That which is called the disdiapason double octave has fifteen sounds, fourteen intervals, twelve tones, doubled semitones, and forty-eight diesis intervals; and it is in quadruple ratio, such as twelve is to three. The tone, moreover, is in the ratio of eight to nine.

kb.th: In his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, the world soul is woven from the numbers that make musical consonance. It drives the heavens, which therefore sound in intervals that are "unequal, but proportioned". Every soul comes from that music and carries its memory into the body. That is why everything alive is caught by song, and why we cannot hear the heavens: the sound is too great for us.
h: **The soul carries heavenly music into the body.** "For this reason, every soul in this life is captured by musical sounds", barbarian nations included. "This is because the soul carries into the body the memory of the music of which it was conscious in heaven" (*quia in corpus defert memoriam musicae*) ([II.3.7, p. 593](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKjt)). This is the original of d'Ailly's report. It confirms that report and refines it: d'Ailly follows Macrobius almost word for word. Macrobius adds that the same songs can either rouse people to virtue or loosen them into soft pleasure.

**The world soul is musical, so its sound is unequal but proportioned.** Book II explains "why the soul is interwoven from numbers creating music" ([II.2.24, p. 592](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKjs)). "Therefore, everything that lives is rightly captured by music, because the celestial soul, by which the universe is animated, took its origin from music". Driving the spheres, "it effects a sound which is distinct by uneven intervals, but nevertheless distinct by a ratio in due proportion" (*intervallis... disiunctus imparibus, sed tamen pro rata parte ratione distinctis*, Cicero's phrase) ([II.3.11, p. 594](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKju)).

**Nine Muses: eight songs and their concord.** "Theologians also wished for there to be nine Muses: the musical songs of the eight spheres, and one greatest harmony which is composed of them all". Calliope is the ninth, "which the harmonious entirety of sounds composes" (*sonorum concors universitas*) ([II.3.1–2, p. 592](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKjs)).

**We do not hear the spheres because the sound is too great.** "we do not clearly perceive by hearing the music born from the perpetual revolution of the heaven because the sound is greater than that it may be received by the narrowness of human ears", as the people at the Nile cataracts cannot hear the roar ([II.4.14, p. 598](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKjy)). The same page gives the diatonic genus to Plato's cosmic music.

**The descent through the spheres furnishes the soul.** The soul is clothed in an ethereal covering at each sphere, "and therefore, through as many deaths as it passes spheres, it arrives at this which is called life on the earth" ([I.11.12, p. 530](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKis)). In each sphere it "produces the individual motions which it is going to have in exercise": reasoning in Saturn, action in Jupiter, spirit in Mars, sense and imagination in the Sun, desire in Venus, speech in Mercury, growth at the Moon ([I.12.13–14, p. 533](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKiv)).

**A diversity that agrees with itself.** In the smithy story "the high notes harmonized with the low notes", and Pythagoras collected "all the numbers by which the diversity of weights was contained in agreement with itself" (*consentiens sibi diversitas ponderum*) ([II.1.9–12, p. 584](/q/Bh4JidBMyNOVLnhiKjk)).

Proclus, Commentaries on the Timaeus and.a: Proclus reads the harmony of the world soul as present in the cosmos, the intellect and the soul, with intellectual harmony giving rise to psychic harmony and that to sensible harmony. He matches the harmonic mean to the Same and the arithmetic mean to the Other. The hemiolic, epitritic and epogdoic ratios are bonds within the means, joined to the leimma and the fourfold octave.

q.t: For since there is harmony in the cosmos, in the intellect, and in the soul, for this reason Timaeus says it participates in harmony and is harmony. The cosmos participates in harmony according to a decade, but the soul according to a tetrad, while it pre-exists in the intellect in a monadic way.

It must therefore be stated that the harmonic mean binds together all the identity within the soul and grants the indissoluble communion to the celestial [bodies], distributing greater powers and motions to the larger circles and smaller ones to the smaller; for the containing [bodies] move more quickly than the contained.

This is why the ancients sometimes posit eight Sirens [mythological figures representing cosmic order] and nine Muses [deities of the arts and sciences] overseeing the universe, depending on whether there are eight or nine portions of the cosmos, from which harmony comes to all things.

For since they refuse to be mixed with one another and each strives, in a sense, to arrive as a complete whole, and as one obstructs the other, both are transmitted to the senses in an unpleasant way.

Cassiodorus, Institutions II.5 (on music.a: Cassiodorus defines music as the science of numbers related to sounds, such as double, triple, and quadruple, which are called relational. A symphony is the temperament of a low sound to a high one, or a high to a low, producing melody in voice, percussion, or breath. He lists six symphonies, beginning with diatessaron, diapente, and diapason, and says the Psaltery holds the modulation of the heavenly virtues.

q.t: Music is a discipline or science that speaks of numbers related to sounds; such as double, triple, quadruple, and similar things, which are called relational.
Harmony is to be valued,¹ and an avoidance of wanton opposition to be honoured.
Hence there are some who disobey their lords and fathers, or who maintain feuds with the neighbouring villages.
But when those above are harmonious and those below are friendly, and there is concord in the discussion of business, right views of things spontaneously gain acceptance.
when the lord speaks, the vassal listens; when the superior acts, the inferior yields compliance.

kb.t: Shōtoku Taishi, Seventeen-Article Constitution (604; in the Nihon shoki, 720)
kb.th: "Harmony is to be valued." Article 1 opens Japan's first written code of conduct for officials. Harmony here means concord, the end of faction and dispute, inside a fixed order where the lord is Heaven and the vassal Earth. It invites discussion and admits that hearts differ, but its answer to difference is agreement and deference.
h: **Harmony against faction.** "Harmony is to be valued,¹ and an avoidance of wanton opposition to be honoured." The trouble it names is men who "disobey their lords and fathers, or who maintain feuds with the neighbouring villages." ([Nihongi XXII.10, tr. Aston, p. 129 [scan 569]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSD))

**Harmony is concord across rank, reached in discussion.** "But when those above are harmonious and those below are friendly, and there is concord in the discussion of business, right views of things spontaneously gain acceptance." ([p. 129 [scan 569]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSD))

**The order is cosmic and fixed.** "The lord is Heaven, the vassal is Earth." So "when the lord speaks, the vassal listens; when the superior acts, the inferior yields compliance." ([Art. 3, p. 129 [scan 569]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSD))

**Hearts differ, and then everyone should follow the many.** "For all men have hearts, and each heart has its own leanings. Their right is our wrong, and our right is their wrong." But the article ends: "though we alone may be in the right, let us follow the multitude and act like them." ([Art. 10, p. 131 [scan 571]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSF))

**The text glosses its own first article.** Private motive breeds resentment, and a resentful man "will assuredly fail to act harmoniously with others." "Therefore in the first clause it was said, that superiors and inferiors should agree together." ([Art. 15, p. 132 [scan 572]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSG))

**Weighty decisions are not for one person.** "Decisions on important matters¹ should not be made by one person alone. They should be discussed with many." ([Art. 17, p. 132 [scan 572]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOmsvA1KqZRvAPTFSG))
tr: **Native term.** *wa* 和 (Chinese *he*), in 以和爲貴 "take *wa* as precious". Aston notes the phrase is "From the "Lunyu," or "Analects" of Confucius." In Analects I.12 it reads "有子曰、禮之用、和爲貴": in the *use of ritual*, *he* is to be prized. Youzi adds that *he* not regulated by ritual "is not to be done". Legge translates *he* there as "a natural ease", not "harmony" ([Legge, Analects I.12, p. 9 [scan 15]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bem4O0uA6cumtwPdA8V)).

**What it means in context:** concord, non-contention, the absence of factions and feuds, and "superiors and inferiors" agreeing together (Art. 15). Its opposite is *faction*, which is fragmentation. It has no opposite on the side of homogenization.

**Verdict: partly maps, and mostly does not.** It names one of “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s two failures, fragmentation (feuds, factions, private resentment). It has nothing to say about the other, homogenization. Its one pluralist sentence (Art. 10) ends by telling the dissenter to follow the multitude. There is no clause that the parts should flourish. Unlike Confucius' *he* versus *tong*, Article 1 does not separate harmony from sameness. Harmony as concord within a hierarchy.
an: The source is Analects I.12. Confucius' own *he er bu tong* is the stronger pluralist statement that Shōtoku did not take up.
The later use of *wa* as a slogan of national unity (Meiji to wartime *kokutai* writing) is a well-known reception.

Isidore of Seville, Etymologies III (mus.a: Isidore divides sound into three kinds: vocal (harmonic), breath (organic) and struck (rhythmic). He defines symphony as the temperament of low and high sounds and names diaphonia, discordant voices, as its contrary. He also defines euphonia as sweetness of voice. He explains the zither's strings as harmonizing among themselves, and offers a link between its seven strings and the seven movements of the sky.

q.t: There are three parts of music, that is, harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. Harmonic is that which discerns high and low in sounds.

Harmonic is the modulation of the voice and the concord or adjustment of many sounds. Simphonia symphony is the temperament of modulation from low and high concordant sounds, whether in voice, or breath, or impulse. By this, indeed, the higher and lower voices are harmonized so that whoever is dissonant from it offends the sense of hearing.
But it is called seven-stringed either because they fill the whole voice or because it sounds in accordance with the seven movements of the sky.

For those things which in the parts of the universe seem opposed and contrary to one another, and dissonant from each other, are, in the most general harmony of the universe itself, considered fitting and consonant.

Thus, the beauty of the whole created universe, of similar and dissimilar things, is established by a certain wondrous harmony, compacted into a certain ineffable unity from diverse genera and various forms
so in the concord of the universe, things that are dissonant when viewed singularly are unified according to the uniform will of the Creator from the diverse subdivisions of the one nature
For the almighty Creator of the universe, lacking nothing and tending toward the infinite, could create and did create not only things similar to Himself, but also things dissimilar.

kb.th: In the *Periphyseon* (*De divisione naturae*) the universe is a harmony made from like and **unlike** things. God made the opposites on purpose, and what sounds dissonant in a part is consonant in the whole, as voices far apart in pitch make one organ melody. The doctrine runs all the way through. Punishment, vice and even a whipped slave in a royal house are counted as voices in the final "one harmony of the universe", and that restored harmony will have no dissonance at all.
h: **Dissonant in the parts, consonant in the whole.** God is "the opposition of opposites, and the contrariety of contraries" and gathers all into one concord: "For those things which in the parts of the universe seem opposed and contrary to one another, and dissonant from each other, are, in the most general harmony of the universe itself, considered fitting and consonant." ([Periphyseon I, p. 42](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLo3))

**The universe as organ melody.** "Thus, the beauty of the whole created universe, of similar and dissimilar things, is established by a certain wondrous harmony, compacted into a certain ineffable unity from diverse genera and various forms". He compares this to how *organicum melos* is made "ex diversis vocum qualitatibus & quantitatibus": "so in the concord of the universe, things that are dissonant when viewed singularly are unified according to the uniform will of the Creator" ([III.6, p. 104](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLov)).

**God made the unlike on purpose.** The Creator "could create and did create not only things similar to Himself, but also things dissimilar"; had he made only the like, "He would seem to have failed in the creation of dissimilar and opposite things" (same page).

**Punishment belongs to the harmony.** "I am not moved when I hear that a most beautiful harmony will come from the punishments of evil wills and the rewards of good ones", because "grave and acute sounds, and their intermediates, create a certain symphony among themselves by their own proportions and proportionalities" ([V, p. 282](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLrn)). On the same page evil does not exist; vices are "illicit", and ferocity is good in a lion.

**Harmony is in the proportions, and the end has no dissonance.** "nothing else pleases the soul or creates beauty except the rational intervals of diverse voices". The sweetness comes not from the sounds but from "the proportions of sounds and the proportionalities which... the interior sense of the soul alone perceives and judges". The restored universe "will modulate a harmonious music without any dissonance" ([V, p. 281](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLrm)).

**The royal house.** Punishment and reward can coexist, he argues, as a great royal house holds at once "the one struck with lashes as a slave, the one exalted with honors as a master". So too "in one harmony of the universe, restored and reverted into its causes, the whole rational creature" is gathered ([V, p. 285](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLrq)). Answering those who complain that God makes some masters and others servants, he says that "temporal and transitory goods of this life are not truly good" ([V, scan 293](/q/BgOVhBjfgvqIr1HjLrp)).
an: Plotinus' providence argument and Augustine's world-poem of antitheses are the direct models for point 4. Eriugena also cites Dionysius the Areopagite on the non-existence of evil.

The *Periphyseon* was condemned in 1225 by Honorius III, partly for its pantheist reading of "God is in all things". Gale's 1681 edition was placed on the Index in 1685.

Musica enchiriadis|||Medieval Latin.a: The passage explains that organum is called diaphonia because it consists of a "concordantly dissonating concert" of voices singing together. It places organum among the symphonies, the consonances, and lists the double octave and the octave with the fifth or fourth as composite consonances. Examples of organum at the fourth, fifth, and octave follow.

q.t: Now let us pursue that which is properly called Symphonia and is so, that is, how the same voices behave when singing together. For this is what we call diaphonic chant or usually Organum. It is called Diaphonia because it does not consist of uniform singing, but of concordantly dissonating concert.

he perceives what is in truth incompatible as compatible, and what is compatible as incompatible, and this only occurs in the minority.

a human is not sufficient with what he alone measures, without also having the measures of the perception of others. Therefore, nothing of these is complete without the testimonies of the rest of humanity, just as it is in the science of astronomy.

kb.th: Musical consonance is graded by perfection and tested first by the pleasure of a healthy, shared ear. The good city is a harmony of unequal, ranked parts, like the organs of a body.
h: **Pleasure is the measure of what is natural to hearing.** Perception that is perfected is followed by pleasure, so the pleasures common to all or most people set the standard. "it is necessary that the pleasures resulting from them be used as measures for what are perfections for the sense" ([Great Book of Music, Intro. Art. 2, p. 108](/q/BiUf4DgCxcvgv4qlcLn))

**One ear is not enough.** Some people hear the incompatible as compatible, so the standard needs others: "nothing of these is complete without the testimonies of the rest of humanity, just as it is in the science of astronomy." ([Great Book of Music, p. 108](/q/BiUf4DgCxcvgv4qlcLn))

**But "humanity" is drawn by latitude.** Only peoples between latitudes 15 and 45 count as the natural standard. Peoples to the far south and north are "outside what is on the natural course for man" ([Great Book of Music, p. 109](/q/BiUf4DgCxcvgv4qlcLo))

**Consonances are graded, and practice can overrule theory.** "these agreements vary in their perfection. The best and most perfect is the agreement of the "all,"" (the octave). Practitioners drop the octave-plus-fourth because melodies do not use it; the Pythagoreans drop it on their own principles. ([Great Book of Music, p. 181](/q/BiUf4DgCxcvgv4qlcMy))

**The city is a body of unequal, competing parts.** "The Virtuous City resembles a completely healthy body, whose limbs all assist one another to fully produce and preserve the life of the creature." The ranks run down to "limbs that only serve, but do not rule anything at all." ([Musterstaat ch. XXVII, p. 86](/q/BmiNukILiokqVv8wELK))

**Music tempers character (Latin, attributed).** The Latin *De ortu scientiarum* gives music's use as "tempering the characters of living beings that exceed balance" and healing the body through the soul ([De ortu scientiarum ch. 4, p. 19](/q/BmiNvomCLskZTbm0qLL))
an: Ibn Sīnā followed and condensed al-Fārābī's music theory (his own music text is not held; see the Ibn Sīnā page).
Rodericus Zamorensis, *Speculum vitae humanae* (1468), cites Alfarabi for the claim that harmony aids contemplation.
His parallels are Plato's *Republic* and *De Mundo*'s city of unlike parts. The difference is that al-Fārābī's body is explicitly ranked under a chief organ.
nh: **Not found:** *Iḥṣāʾ al-ʿulūm* / Latin *De scientiis*, including its section on music. A search for "De scientiis" returned only later Latin works. *Kitāb al-īqāʿāt* (on rhythm) was not found either.
**Held, read in part:** *Der Musterstaat* (Dieterici's German translation, 1900), scans 176–178, read two steps from the Arabic. The Arabic text is not held.

k.g: mental equilibrium or the weight of the spirit
a state of proportion or symmetry

q.t: This continues until one reaches the limbs that only serve, but do not rule anything at all.
The fundamental disposition of everything, however, is proportion Ebenmaass equilibrium, balance, or justice.

q.t: the bamm is sixty-four strands of silk, the mathlath is forty-eight strands, the mathna is thirty-six strands, and the zir is twenty-seven strands.

In sum, there is no string or fret among these strings and frets that does not have a proportional relationship to the others. However, some of these proportions are excellent and noble, while others are less so.
The tone of the zir strengthens the bile humor, increases its power and effect, and opposes the phlegm humor, refining it.

When these tones are arranged in melodies suitable for them, and those melodies are used during times of the night and day whose nature is contrary to the nature of prevailing diseases and occurring ailments, they soothe them, break their intensity, and alleviate the pain of the sick.

kb.t: Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ (Brethren of Purity) (fl. 10th c., Basra)
kb.th: Music is proportion that acts on bodies and souls. The oud's strings are built in ratio and tuned to the elements and humours. The human body is a web of ratios. Souls delight in music because they are *like* it, and through it they recall the harmony of the spheres.
h: **The oud is built in proportion.** The strings are 64, 48, 36 and 27 silk strands thick, each 4:3 of the next: "there is no string or fret among these strings and frets that does not have a proportional relationship to the others." ([Rasāʾil, music epistle, scan 102](/book/rasa-il-ikhwan-al-safa-epistles-of-the-brethren-of-purity-al-safa/page/69b6363a8ab57a1de53a762e))

**Strings act on humours, by contraries.** Each string answers to an element and strengthens one humour against another: "The tone of the zir strengthens the bile humor, increases its power and effect, and opposes the phlegm humor, refining it." Melodies played at times contrary to a disease "soothe them, break their intensity, and alleviate the pain of the sick." ([music epistle, scan 108](/q/BhPTycM4I0HGIyYWZFU))

**The body is a web of ratios.** "every limb of the human body, it is proportional to the whole body by one ratio, and proportional to some other limb of the body by another ratio." ([music epistle, scan 115](/q/BhPTycM4I0HGIyYWZFb))

**Souls delight in music by likeness.** In a reported saying, souls rejoice in measured melody "because of the similarity, proportionality, and homogeneity between them." ([music epistle, scan 124](/q/BhPTycM4I0HGIyYWZFk))

**The spheres sound, and music reminds souls of them.** "Their tones are proportional and harmonious, and their melodies are balanced" ([music epistle, scan 103](/book/rasa-il-ikhwan-al-safa-epistles-of-the-brethren-of-purity-al-safa/page/69b6363a8ab57a1de53a762f))

**The same art heals or corrupts, depending on use.** The sages used "sad melodies that soften hard hearts". Where religious law forbids music, it is because of its use "on the path of amusement and play" ([music epistle, scans 105–106](/q/BhPTycM4I0HGIyYWZFS))
an: They cite Pythagoras hearing the spheres, then Nicomachus, Ptolemy and Euclid (scan 105). Compare and, and see.
Aristotle denied that the spheres sound; the Ikhwān insist they do.
The strings–humours doctrine is usually traced to al-Kindī, whose music treatises the library does not hold (see the al-Kindī page).

q.t: the imposition of limitations of time and place through the rule of "belonging to oneself" or "belonging to another,"
how can there be one rasa if love varies according to its base—is due to their lack of knowledge. This love is one and the same.
And love and other states are indeed manifestations caused by a specific coloring of obstruction.
the mirror, even though it is composed of those various reflections, shines forth as having a nature that has transcended those reflections

kb.th: Rasa is consciousness freed from obstacles, a single impersonal relish ("wonder", "repose", "dissolution"). Ownership ("mine / another's") and the particular object drop away in it. Calm (*śama*) is the self's nature, and the other emotions are that calm under a coloured tint. Unlike components are needed to reach rasa. The rasa itself is a unity in which their difference no longer counts.
h: **Rasa is obstacle-free consciousness.** "लोके सकलविघ्नविनिर्मुक्ता संवित्तिरेव चमत्कारनिर्वेशरसास्वादभोगसमापत्तिलयविश्रान्त्यादिशब्दैरभिधीयते". Consciousness free of all obstacles is called wonder, relish, absorption, dissolution, repose. One obstacle is "the imposition of limitations of time and place through the rule of "belonging to oneself" or "belonging to another,"". The first obstacle is removed by "तदपसारणे हृदयसंवादो", the agreement (*saṃvāda*) of hearts. ([Abhinavabhāratī on NS 6, p. 835 (leaf 628) (the library's translation)](/q/BeogWPC23sgJFYAyanL))

**Drama is a collection of rasas.** "रससमुदायो हि नाट्यम्", "Drama is indeed a collection of essences." ([on NS 6.33, p. 684 [scan 861] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogWPC23sgJFYAyanl))

**One rasa, however many objects love has.** To the objection "how can there be one rasa if love varies according to its base", he replies that it "is due to their lack of knowledge. This love is one and the same." ([on NS 6, śṛṅgāra, p. 709 [scan 886] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogWPC23sgJFYAyaoA))

**Calm is the self; the other emotions are tinted calm.** "तदिदमात्मस्वरूपमेव तत्त्वज्ञानं शमः। तथा च यत्कालुष्योपरागविशेषात्मान एव रत्यादयः।", "And love and other states are indeed manifestations caused by a specific coloring of obstruction" (better: "of impurity", *kāluṣya*). ([on NS 6, śānta section, p. 771 [scan 948] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogWPC23sgJFYAyapA))

**The mirror holds its reflections and is not changed by them.** This is from the commentary on his *Paramārthasāra*, by Yogarāja, not Abhinavagupta: "the mirror, even though it is composed of those various reflections, shines forth as having a nature that has transcended those reflections". ([Yogarāja on Paramārthasāra, p. 37 [scan 46] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiYzOChj0YakHVwz0fe))
tr: **रस *rasa*** (taste, relish). After Abhinavagupta it is a single, generalised (*sādhāraṇīkṛta*) relish of a durable emotion, free of "mine" and "yours". **Verdict: partly maps, and on the decisive point it does not.** It needs unlike components (Bharata's determinants, consequents and transient states:). That is the "diversity" half. But the valued state is *viśrānti*, repose, and *laya*, dissolution. In it the particular lover, object and owner no longer matter, and the plurality of emotions is a tint on one calm. On “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s own terms that is homogenization at the top, reached by way of diversity. The bharata.md verdict ("supports the definition well") should be softened to "partly".

**हृदयसंवाद *hṛdaya-saṃvāda*** ("agreement of hearts"). This is the same *saṃvāda* that names the consonant note. **Verdict: partly maps.** It is the sympathetic agreement of many spectators with the shared object. It is a real social whole, but its form is agreement or likeness of response, not difference.
**शम / शान्त *śama / śānta*** (calm, the tranquil rasa). **Verdict: does not map.** It is the one underlying nature, and the many emotions are its modifications.

**प्रतिबिम्ब *pratibimba*** (reflection), in Yogarāja. **Verdict: partly maps.** The whole really contains the many ("composed of" the reflections), and that is closer to “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” than the Upaniṣadic honey. But the parts are appearances in the whole, and they neither strengthen nor change it.
an: Bharata's rasa-sūtra, which he comments on.
Earlier rasa theorists he refutes on these pages: Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa, Śaṅkuka, Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka (whose *bhoga* and *bhāvakatva* he adapts).
Mammaṭa and Viśvanātha systematise his view; Jagannātha later revises it.
The *Tantrāloka* (the library holds the KSTS Sanskrit with Jayaratha, vol. 1, and a second record) gives the metaphysics of the One appearing as many.

Picatrix (Ghāyat al-ḥakīm)|||Arabic.a: The Picatrix advises looking in all works for benevolence and things mutually loving one another, and avoiding things that hate one another and are contrary by nature. In the planetary passage, the planets' sympathetic essence appears toward one another, and the nearer they are to apogee, the greater their effect. In opposition of the apogee they work sympathetically through a friendly subject, which the text calls the reason of the world.

q.t: That in all your works and effects you look for benevolence and things mutually loving one another: and you beware of adversities and of things hating one another: and which are contrary to one another by nature.

The more they are in their apogee, the greater will be their effect, because their sympathetic [original: "simapate"] essence appears toward one another with certainty; and if they are in the opposition of the apogee, they work sympathetically through a friendly subject, and this is the reason of the world, and they perform a greater work.
Complexion is a quality which arises from the reciprocal action and passion of contrary qualities found in the elements
for the equality of the bone is that dryness should abound in it more; and of the brain, that moisture should abound in it the most; and of the heart, that there should be more heat in it

And each one of them, by comparison to its own species, is temperate: which, by comparison to another, is not temperate. For the body of an Indian, when it becomes like the complexion of a Slav, will either fall ill or die.
You must know, however, that every individual ought to have a complexion solely proper to him

kb.th: Health is a temperament, a balance made from unbalanced parts. It holds within a range, and it differs from one people and one person to another. The pulse has a musical nature, and a trained hand can feel its proportions.
h: **Complexion arises from contraries.** "Complexion is a quality which arises from the reciprocal action and passion of contrary qualities found in the elements" ([Canon I, fen 1, doctr. 3, ch. 1, p. 11](/q/BhDcpRW2e2OipKeRupi))

**The body balances by weighing unequal members.** The heart is hot, the brain cold, the liver moist, the bones dry: "When, therefore, they are weighed and equalized, he will be close to certain equality." Each member's own "equality" is an excess of one quality ([Canon I, p. 12](/q/BhDcpRW2e2OipKeRupj))

**Temperance is relative.** Indians and Slavs each have a healthy complexion of their own: "by comparison to its own species, is temperate: which, by comparison to another, is not temperate." Also, "every individual ought to have a complexion solely proper to him" ([Canon I, p. 12](/q/BhDcpRW2e2OipKeRupj))

**The pulse has a musical nature.** "musical nature is found in the pulse, for just as the art of music is completed by the addition of sounds according to the proportion accompanying them between the high and the low … so is the disposition of the pulse" ([Canon I, fen 2, doctr. 3, p. 141](/q/BhDcpRW2e2OipKeRuro))

**Feeling those proportions takes training.** Against Galen's claim that pulse proportions follow the musical ratios: "it is easy for him who is accustomed to the grade of touching, and who knows the nature of sounds by art" ([Canon I, p. 141](/q/BhDcpRW2e2OipKeRuro))
an: Galen is the source he answers on the pulse.
Pietro d'Abano's *Conciliator* (1472) discusses consonance in the pulse with reference to Avicenna.
Ficino's tempering of body and soul by music inherits this medical frame.
nh: **Not held:** the music section of the *Shifāʾ* (*Jawāmiʿ ʿilm al-mūsīqī*). the library's *al-Shifāʾ* record (69c1b7acfe4b8f25b9200ccf) mentions music only as a branch of mathematics (scan 26). The *Najāt* is not held, and neither is the *Dānishnāma*'s music section.

q.t: Furthermore, the alternation of ratios only applies to things within a single genus. This is because the ratio is preserved during the original and alternated states. The ratio exists within one specific shared meaning with a common intelligible reality.

q.t: Otherwise, if one is similar but cannot differ, that similarity is merely following vulgar habits and practicing what is wrong. If one differs but cannot be similar, that difference is merely disrupting the regular order and violating principle.
Because the myriad things are originally one, they can harmonize differences. Because they can harmonize differences, it is called stimulus. If there were no differences, there would be no harmony.
In all things, those capable of mutual resonance are the nature of ghosts and spirits receiving and giving. Those incapable of resonance are also transformed by the body of ghosts and spirits.

kb.t: Zhang Zai, Zhengmeng ch. 1 "Taihe" (Supreme Harmony) (1020–1077; Zhengmeng c. 1076)
kb.th: Supreme Harmony is the Way. It holds opposed tendencies (rising and sinking, motion and rest) in mutual stimulation, and what is not turbulent "like wild horses" is not Supreme Harmony. Opposites become enemies, and "enmity must be resolved by he". No two things made by creation are alike.
h: **Harmony contains contest.** 太和所謂道，中涵浮沉、升降、動靜相感之性，是生絪縕相盪、勝負屈伸之始: "Supreme Harmony is what is called the Way. Within it are the natures of floating and sinking, rising and falling, motion and rest, which stimulate each other; it is the beginning of their mingling and pressing, victory and defeat, contracting and stretching." And 不如野馬絪縕，不足謂之太和: "what is not like wild horses swirling does not deserve the name Supreme Harmony." (my reading) ([張子全書, p. 79](/q/Bl15zIrFQzUg2SuP1VH))

**Opposition ends in harmony.** 有象斯有對，對必反其為；有反斯有仇，仇必和而解: "where there are images there are opposites; opposites must act against each other; where there is opposition there is enmity; enmity must be resolved by harmony." The same passage: 造化所成，無一物相肖者, "of all that creation makes, no one thing resembles another." ([p. 93](/q/Bl15zIrFQzUg2SuP1VV))

**A Qing commentator names both failures.** "if one is similar but cannot differ, that similarity is merely following vulgar habits and practicing what is wrong. If one differs but cannot be similar, that difference is merely disrupting the regular order and violating principle." ([Wang Zhi, 正蒙初義, p. 85 (the library's translation)](/q/Bl160BFfaPJBBqbkRYD))
tr: **太和 taihe**, "Supreme Harmony": the whole of qi in motion, before and through its condensing into things. It is not a social term.
**和而解 he er jie**: "resolved by harmony". 解 means untie or dissolve, and a Ming gloss reads 和 here as 和諧 (性理羣書句解, the library vol. 3 p. 138).

**The test: is the conflict preserved or dissolved?** Both, at different levels. The *things* stay unique: "no one thing resembles another". The *enmity* is undone, and the very next line says that love and hate "both come from the Great Void and in the end return to" desire for things and to dispersal (故愛惡之情同出於太虛而卒歸於物欲). The resolution goes back into the undifferentiated qi, not forward into a structured whole.

**Verdict: partly maps.** Zhang Zai is the strongest pre-modern Chinese text in this group for "dissonance belongs inside": contest and turbulence are part of the definition of taihe. He also insists on uniqueness. But the whole is the Great Void, a medium, not a body whose parts strengthen it. The opposition is resolved by dissolving it. The Qing commentary in point 3 comes closest to “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”, and it is a commentator's gloss, not Zhang's own words.
an: Zhu Xi annotates the first line: 此以太和狀道體，與發而中節之和無異, "this uses Supreme Harmony to describe the substance of the Way; it is no different from the harmony of feelings that 'issue and hit the measure'" ([p. 80](/q/Bl15zIrFQzUg2SuP1VI)).

A comment in the collected preface material, in the wording of Zhu Xi's recorded sayings, objects that Taihe and Taixu are "only talk of qi" and drift toward "a great wheel of rebirth" ([p. 78](/q/Bl15zIrFQzUg2SuP1VG)).
Wang Fuzhi's 張子正蒙注 is the major later defence of Zhang. It was not found or searched in the library.
nh: No English translation of the Zhengmeng was found in the library. Claims 1–2 are "partial" (my reading of the Chinese OCR). Point 2 was read from a search snippet only, because the page-text call was rate-limited.

q.t: When harmony reaches its peak, it is natural that the ancestral spirits arrive. The way harmony arises in the human heart is visible through such expressions.
When the underlying intent was calm and harmonious, one chanted it with calm and harmonious sounds. When the intent was sorrowful and longing, one chanted it with sorrowful and longing sounds.

They sing joyful words to sorrowful tunes, and sing mournful words to joyful tunes. Therefore, although the wording may be poignant, it fails to move human emotion, because sound and meaning do not harmonize.
This is because the listener applies everything he hears to whatever is dominant in his heart.
The enjoyment of the ear is secured in listening to harmonious voices.

kb.t: al-Ghazālī, Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn, Book of Listening (Kitāb ādāb al-samāʿ wa-l-wajd) (1058 – 1111)
kb.th: Music is permitted or forbidden according to the listener. What a person hears is shaped by what already fills the heart, so the same poem helps one gathering and harms another.
h: **The listener hears what dominates his heart.** In the Book of Knowledge, al-Ghazālī anticipates his Book of Listening: love poetry does not harm an elite gathering "because the listener applies everything he hears to whatever is dominant in his heart. This will be verified later in the Book of Listening and Ecstasy" ([Iḥyāʾ, Kitāb al-ʿilm, p. 36 [scan 46], the library translation](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BilO2Qx43lTdoCI7rnK))

**Each faculty has its proper pleasure.** In the *Kīmiyā-yi saʿādat* (Homes's English): "The enjoyment of the ear is secured in listening to harmonious voices." The heart's pleasure is knowing things as they are ([Alchemy of Happiness, tr. Homes, p. 34 [scan 46]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bem2FvbK83HMg6lArfC))
tr: **samāʿ سماع** ("listening"): hearing music and poetry, judged by its effect on the heart. **wajd وجد** is the ecstasy it can produce.

**mawzūn موزون** ("measured") is the word usually used for the measured, pleasing sound that al-Ghazālī says the ear enjoys. "Harmonious voices" is Homes's English, translated from a Turkish version of a Persian text, so it cannot carry a terminological argument.

**Verdict: does not map.** *Samāʿ* is about the listener's state and its moral and spiritual direction, not about parts forming a whole. The relevant structure is a match between the sound and what is already in the heart. That is closer to "likeness" (cf. the Ikhwān) than to diversity in wholeness. The same page also limits the audience: Junayd would not speak to more than twenty, and al-Ghazālī calls for harsh suppression of ecstatic claims among common people. Licence to listen depends on who you are.
an: Rūmī's reed is heard by each "from his own opinion". The Mevlevi order made *samāʿ* a ritual (see rumi.md).
Jurists who forbade music are his opponents in the Book of Listening. Not read.
nh: **Book of Listening (Iḥyāʾ book 18): not held.** the library Iḥyāʾ (Beirut 1982, book 69e8b2a72ff2a8dc09e7860d) is volume 1, the quarter of worship. Best public-domain edition: D. B. Macdonald, "Emotional Religion in Islam as affected by Music and Singing", *JRAS* 1901–1902 (three parts). Not held.
