q.t: For even the symphony softens hard hearts and leads them into the humor of compunction and calls the Holy Spirit.
The mind and rationality of man have great strength to sound in His voices and to excite sluggish souls to vigilance in symphony.
clearly leads the faithful to that unanimity where there is no discord
and the symphony not only in the unanimity of exultation in the way of righteousness, but presents the joy, yes, which by concord raising the voices from the way of justice fallen

kb.th: For Hildegard harmony (*symphonia*) is sung praise that moves the soul. It softens hard hearts, wakes the sluggish and brings the fallen back. Its goal is a unanimity "where there is no discord". In the body, health is a concord of humours in which each is tempered by the others, under the rule of one.
h: **Song acts on the soul.** In Scivias III.13: "For even the symphony softens hard hearts and leads them into the humor of compunction and calls the Holy Spirit." Human mind and reason "have great strength to sound in His voices and to excite sluggish souls to vigilance in symphony" ([scan 399](/q/Bij5sl3VKqSYAfaGOjf)).

**Many kinds of praise, one mind.** The blessed praise God "in wonderful diverse genres of musical praises" ([scan 398](/q/Bij5sl3VKqSYAfaGOje)). The harmony "clearly leads the faithful to that unanimity where there is no discord" ([scan 399](/q/Bij5sl3VKqSYAfaGOjf)).

**Concord brings back the fallen.** The symphony belongs not only to the righteous: "by concord" it raises "the voices from the way of justice fallen", like the shepherd and the lost sheep (scan 399). At the end of the Ordo Virtutum the Virtues tell the penitent Soul: "We wish to lead you back and we do not wish to desert you … therefore it befits us to sound in harmony" (*in symphonia sonare*) ([p. 126](/q/Bij9OWeSKgR1jn9ko44)).

**The Devil does not sing.** Every role in the Ordo is sung except the Devil's. His lines are headed *strepitus* (noise) and printed as prose: "The clamor of the Devil to that soul: Foolish! Foolish! What does it profit you to labor?" ([p. 110](/q/Bij9OWeSKgR1jn9ko3o)).

**Health is a concord of humours under one ruler.** If the elements "hold no concord within him, they make him sick and kill him". A humour keeps health when "it is tempered by the others in such a way that it is forced to maintain its right proportion". Then "when one holds the upper hand in the "regiment" …, the other is subject to it in servitude" ([Causae et curae, p. 53](/q/Belt89ZyPJytzr7q09T)).

**Nothing exists by one quality.** "There is no creature that can exist through only a single quality; it must possess several." At the end of time the purified elements "will raise a song in harmony" (*Gesang im Einklang*) ([p. 11](/q/Belt89ZyPJytzr7q08n)).
an: She shares the softening-by-song topos with the Ikhwān and with Ficino's music as a cure of soul and body. Neither is likely to be a direct source.
The Devil-without-song can be set beside Ficino's three planets that "have voices indeed, but not songs". In both, some voices stay outside harmony.
the library holds later lives and chronicles that mention her (*On the Lives of the Saints*, 1581, 6a0854a615c643eb1af533fd; the Hirsau chronicles, 69b51e7947b06ecd58190d25).
nh: **Not held:** the letter to the prelates of Mainz (1178/79), with its account of Adam losing the angelic voice and music as a way to recall it. Searches for Mainz/prelates/Adam's voice/symphonia found no edition of the letters. The *Symphonia armonie celestium revelationum* (the song cycle) is also not held as a separate edition, and neither is the *Liber divinorum operum* (only an excerpt in Manly P. Hall, 1972).

Bartholomaeus Anglicus, On the Propertie.a: Bartholomaeus Anglicus states that music treats voices and sounds and finds musical proportions in the duodenary number compared with six and other mean numbers. He names the sesquitertia as diatessaron, the sesquialtera as diapente, the double as diapason, and the epogdoon as the tone. Citing Boethius, he calls music the modulation of numbers and says all created things are formed by numerical reason, which was the exemplar in the Creator's mind. A well-proportioned medium color delights and comforts the sight, and an extreme color weakens it, as Aristotle says.

q.t: These, eight to six and nine to twelve, provide a sesquitertia four-to-three proportion, and thus they make the proportion of the diatessaron perfect fourth. Six to nine and eight to twelve provide a sesquialtera three-to-two proportion and create the diapente perfect fifth symphony. Twelve to six are considered a double proportion, which they sing as the diapason octave symphony.

So also it is to be seen in music, which music is the modulation of numbers noted for us, as Boethius says, as by the diatessaron a musical fourth, and diapente a musical fifth, and diapason an octave, and in other musical sounds that are not named without a preceding number.
Likewise, a well-proportioned medium color delights the sight and comforts it; an extreme color, however, weakens the sight and saddens it, as Aristotle says.
Through sound, letters are manifested; from letters, words; from words, speech; Through speech, all worldly interaction is carried out; therefore, the world is dependent upon sound.
There is no song without Sound, nor are there musical notes without Sound. > There is no dance without Sound; therefore, the world is composed of Sound.
Those two notes which have an interval of either twelve or eight || 48 || Microtones between them are mutually Consonant.
The second string should have a pitch slightly higher than the first. By saying "slightly," he clarifies the meaning: "so that no other intermediate sound is heard between them."

kb.t: Śārṅgadeva, Saṅgītaratnākara (fl. first half of the 13th c.)
kb.th: Musical sound is born from a union of unlike elements (breath and fire), and the human world rests on it through speech. Within a melody, consonance sustains the character the main note creates, and dissonance destroys its charm (rakti).
h: **Song, instruments, dance and the human world all depend on nāda.** "Through sound, letters are manifested; from letters, words; from words, speech; Through speech, all worldly interaction is carried out; therefore, the world is dependent upon sound." ([Saṅgītaratnākara 1.2.1–2, scan 54, p. 22](/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONvi)). The stronger claim, that the world is *composed* of sound, belongs to Mataṅga, whom Kallinātha quotes ([scan 55, p. 23](/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONvj)).

**Nāda is a union of breath and fire.** Mind strikes the bodily fire, the fire drives the breath, and the breath sounds at five places in the body. "The syllable na is known as the name of breath, and the syllable da is known as fire. Because it is born from the union of breath and fire, it is called Nada." ([1.3.6, scan 96, p. 64](/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONwO))

**Consonance and dissonance are judged by their effect on the melody.** Notes with eight or twelve shrutis between them are samvādī. The commentary says the vivādī "means destroying the aesthetic delight produced by the Sonant and other notes" ([1.3.47–49 with commentary, scan 124, p. 92](/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONwq))

**The 22 shrutis are distributed unequally across the notes.** "the note Shadja, which possesses four microtones, is to be placed on the fourth string. Rishabha, with three microtones, on the seventh." ([1.3.10–16, scan 107, p. 75](/book/sangita-ratnakara-ocean-of-music-sarngadeva/page/69906540726f64800c10a76a))

**Bharata's experiment becomes a fixed and a mobile vīṇā.** Lowering the mobile vīṇā further is forbidden because it destroys rakti. "The second is the "Mobile Vina" (Chala-vina); on that instrument, one should shift the strings." ([1.3.17, scan 107, p. 75](/book/sangita-ratnakara-ocean-of-music-sarngadeva/page/69906540726f64800c10a76a))
an: Bharata, whose ch. 28 he systematises.
Commentators Siṃhabhūpāla and Kallinātha, printed in this edition. Their objections appear in.
Mataṅga's Bṛhaddeśī, quoted as a source.

Ps.-Albertus Magnus, The Marvels of the.a: The author holds that every nature, particular or general, has a natural friendship and enmity toward some other. Each species has something to be feared and destructive, and something exalting, gladdening, and concordant. He gives the hare and dog, the cat and mouse, the lion and quadrupeds, the eagle and birds, and man and all animals. Some pairs hold for the whole species and all time, and others for the individual and a limited time. Enmity between living things continues in their parts and hairs after death.

q.t: Likewise, it has something exalting, gladdening, and concordant. This is by nature—as the sheep [fears] the wolf; and the sheep recognizes the wolf not only when it is alive, but even when it is dead; not only through sight, but even through taste.

And of all there is certification that those which hate each other during life, that their parts, indeed their hair and all, hate each other after they die. Whence the sheepskin is consumed by the wolf skin, and a drum made of wolf skin makes the one of sheepskin go silent
Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it.
Every one became my friend from his own opinion; none sought out my secrets from within me.

On account of the (diverse) place (object) of view, their statements differed: one man entitled it "dál," another "alif." If there had been a candle in each one's hand, the difference would have gone out of their words.
I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward (spirit) and the state (of feeling).

kb.th: For Rūmī, music is the sound of a part separated from its whole and longing to return. He defends a diversity of outward forms of worship. He also treats plurality itself as a veil that true sight removes.
h: **The reed laments separation.** The *Masnavī* opens with the reed-flute (*ney*): "Every one who is left far from his source wishes back the time when he was united with it." ([Masnavi I, Proem, tr. Nicholson, p. 5 [scan 25]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWvTPxLvYYcdnj0Fl))
**Each hearer hears his own state.** "Every one became my friend from his own opinion; none sought out my secrets from within me." ([same page](/q/BgTWvTPxLvYYcdnj0Fl))

**Difference comes from partial sight.** In the dark house, each person who touched the elephant described a different part. "If there had been a candle in each one's hand, the difference would have gone out of their words." ([Masnavi III.1259–68, tr. Nicholson, p. 52](/q/BeltTVAElmnnLS2s85k))

**God looks at the inward, not the form.** God rebukes Moses for silencing the shepherd's uncouth prayer: "I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward (spirit) and the state (of feeling)." On the same page: "The religion of Love is apart from all religions" ([Masnavi II.1759–70, p. 312 [scan 331]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWvTPxLvYYcdnj0Kh))

**Plurality is to be seen through.** "But if thou keep thy gaze (fixed) upon the Light, thou wilt be delivered from dualism and the numbers (plurality) of the finite body." ([III.1257, p. 52](/q/BeltTVAElmnnLS2s85k))
tr: **samāʿ سماع** ("listening"): the Sufi practice of listening to music and poetry, including the Mevlevi turning. It is a means of union, not a theory of concord.
**ney نی** (reed): music as **firāq فراق** (separation) and longing for **waṣl وصل** (union).
**waḥdat وحدت** (oneness) as against **kathrat کثرت** (multiplicity). Nicholson's "numbers (plurality)" probably renders a word of this family.

**Verdict: partly maps, and mostly the other way.** The shepherd story is a clear defence of diverse outward forms held together by one inward aim. That part maps. The governing picture, though, is union with the source. The reed's music is longing for it, and the many views of the elephant are a defect of seeing. A whole made of many is not the goal. In “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”'s terms, the end state looks like the "union/likeness" pole. Rūmī is often quoted as a pluralist. The text supports tolerance of form, not diversity as the good.
an: al-Ghazālī is a forerunner on *samāʿ* (see al-ghazali.md). Homes's 1873 notes on al-Ghazālī describe Mevlevi turning sceptically (Homes's note, p. 118 [scan 130]). That is a 19th-century Western view, not al-Ghazālī's.
The elephant parable also appears earlier, in Sanāʾī, and in Buddhist sources (Udāna). Not checked in the library.

k.g: A more general doctrine concerning all unions

q.t: But the sense of hearing is in no way able to perceive this. But the reason shows this to it
Let the fourth ratio also be divided into two ratios, a larger and a smaller, so that the larger is similarly as close as possible to double the smaller, so that it is sweet to coincide.

The fourth concordance is observed in the epitrits sesquitertian/4:3 ratio; the fifth in the hemiolios sesquialter/3:2 ratio; the octave in the double; the octave and fourth in the double-sesquitertian, that is, double under the third; the octave and fifth in the triple; and the double octave in the quadruple.

kb.th: A Byzantine compendium of ancient harmonics, mostly Ptolemaic. On the quarrel, it keeps Ptolemy's division: sense checks coarse differences, and reason shows the smallest.
h: **Reason shows what hearing cannot.** In the smallest differences between sounds, "the sense of hearing is in no way able to perceive this. But the reason shows this to it" (ἀκοὴ οὐδαμῶς διαισθάνεσθαι τοῦτο δύναται) ([MS Laur. Plut. 28.11, scan 45](/q/BhNl2rvP2hMPzWgfgxZ)). (partial)

q.t: That the heaven has commensurable or incommensurable motions of the signs, and furthermore that certain planets dominate this or that nation, is entirely unproven.

They have erred, as experience has taught, wishing to bring certainty where only rhetorical probability can be had, as Master Nicolaus Oresme deduces, and after him the Lord Cardinal Petrus de Alliaco

For such a proportion is alien to any consonance and is more suitable to the horrid darkness of hell than to the movements of heaven. In these movements, the sweetest music is believed to resonate according to the testimonies of many philosophers, declaring the glory of God.

kb.th: In the one work the library holds, harmony is not his word: what he holds is that a commonwealth, like a body, lives only by due proportion among its parts. His theory of incommensurable celestial motions survives here only at second hand.
h: A kingdom is like a human body, and a body where one member swells with humours while the rest dry out cannot last: "for such a body cannot live for long except by due and equal proportion" ([p. lxxviii](/q/BhE4ka76WF3U5QcECIY)). A prince who hoards riches "is like a monster in nature, like a body whose head is so large that the remainder of it is so weak that it cannot sustain it" (same page).

The ratio of gold to silver coin is set by nature, not by the prince: "Nevertheless, this proportion must follow the natural custom or value of gold to silver in preciousness." ([p. xxx, ch. 10](/q/BhE4ka76WF3U5QcECHm)). A prince who could change it at will could "unduly attract to himself the wealth and substances of his subjects" ([p. xxxi](/q/BhE4ka76WF3U5QcECHn)).

Second-hand: a comment printed with d'Ailly's treatises says that whether the heavens' motions are commensurable is "entirely unproven", "as Master Nicolaus Oresme deduces" ([fol. 154v](/q/BiPv46BJOiGP6KrpOEy)). d'Ailly's own chapter on the question, which does not name Oresme, says of the ratio between two unknown motions that "it is more likely that it is irrational than rational" and calls the question "a neutral problem" ([p. 36](/q/BiPv4CE1dXM10UOxnGO)).
an: Pierre d'Ailly, De legibus et sectis, chs. 9–10: argues the commensurability question the same way, without naming Oresme on the pages read (read, p. 35–37).
The commentator in the 1483 d'Ailly volume (probably Gerson; not verified) names Oresme and then d'Ailly as the authorities for "unproven" (read, fol. 154v).
Pico, Disputationes, and Gessner's Bibliotheca cite Oresme as an opponent of astrology.
nh: **Not held:** Tractatus de commensurabilitate vel incommensurabilitate motuum celi; Ad pauca respicientes; De configurationibus qualitatum; Livre du ciel et du monde; De proportionibus proportionum. Searches for "commensurabilitate", "De configurationibus", "Livre du ciel" and "Oresmius" found no copy.

q.t: Indeed, luxury and its enjoyments completely dampen that group feeling which leads to sovereignty; the tribe that has lost it no longer has the strength to attack its neighbors
As for the inhabitants of the central climates, one finds in them a character of measure and propriety shown in their physical and moral state

The three climates—the fifth, the fourth, and the third—stand between them; thus they have a large share of temperateness, which is the temperament of the mean. The fourth is the most temperate of them, to the utmost limit of moderation, as we have previously mentioned.

kb.th: Societies hold together by *ʿaṣabiyya*, group feeling. It grows from kinship and likeness, needs one dominant element to bind a mixture, and is used up by the prosperity it creates. This is a theory of cohesion, and it is not a theory of harmony as diversity.
h: **Group feeling rests on kinship.** Clients of a great house drop their own lineage, because "ils savent que la parenté est l'élément essentiel de l'esprit de corps, et que les grandes maisons doivent à cet esprit leur consistance et leur illustration" ([Muqaddima I, tr. de Slane, p. 285 [scan 409]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiwGSG72y7Cn5eDsoWn))

**A whole needs one dominant part.** *ʿAṣabiyya* is like the temperament (*mizāj*) of a body: "un mélange d'éléments qui se neutralisent ne saurait former un tempérament: pour que cet effet se produise, il faut absolument que l'un des éléments prédomine sur les autres." So one family must "tenir ensemble les autres, les absorber" ([p. 341 [scan 465]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiwGSG72y7Cn5eDsoXh))

**Group feeling decays.** "Indeed, luxury and its enjoyments completely dampen that group feeling which leads to sovereignty; the tribe that has lost it no longer has the strength to attack its neighbors" ([p. 295 [scan 419], the library translation](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiwGSG72y7Cn5eDsoWx))

**The temperate mean ranks peoples.** "As for the inhabitants of the central climates, one finds in them a character of measure and propriety shown in their physical and moral state". Prophecy, laws, sciences and arts are placed among them ([p. 173 [scan 297], the library translation](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiwGSG72y7Cn5eDsoUz))
tr: **ʿaṣabiyya عصبية** (de Slane: *esprit de corps*, *esprit de tribu*): solidarity from shared blood or adopted kinship (clientage). It is a unity through **likeness**. Its strength is measured by the power to dominate and defend.
**mizāj مزاج** (temperament): a mixture of the four elements. On Ibn Khaldūn's account it exists only because one element **dominates**. A balanced mixture of equals would cancel out.
**iʿtidāl اعتدال** (equilibrium, the temperate mean): the middle climates, and their people's "measure and propriety".

**Verdict: does not map.** ʿAṣabiyya is cohesion by likeness, and its best wholes are made by absorbing the other parts. Iʿtidāl is the mean between extremes, and it is used to rank peoples. Neither term means "diversity in wholeness where the parts flourish". The closest point of contact is negative: Ibn Khaldūn describes the fragmentation that follows when group feeling is lost.
an: His climate theory has the same shape as al-Fārābī's latitude band for the "natural" ear, and as the Ikhwān's humours.
On the same page he rejects the genealogists' claim that Black Africans' colour comes from descent from Ham. His alternative is climatic, and it still ranks peoples.
The ranked whole has a parallel in al-Fārābī's city as a body.
nh: **Chapter on the craft of singing** (*ṣināʿat al-ghināʾ*, Muqaddima ch. V), with pleasure from *tanāsub* (proportion): **not held**. the library has de Slane vol. 1 only (book 69ef3e3a72c1376fdf2b0d3d) and an Arabic Muqaddima (1858, book 69e8b29f2ff2a8dc09e78458) that also covers only the first part. The edition needed is de Slane, *Prolégomènes* vol. 2 (Paris, 1865; PD).

k.g: a deep, intuitive sense of wonder or aesthetic resonance

q.t: if one makes yang in the qi of yang, or yin in the qi of yin, there will be no harmony, and there will be no realization.
It is said in the secret teachings that all things should be known as the realization of the boundary where yin and yang harmonize.
the hearts of the ten thousand, as well as the actor's behavior, will harmonize and become deeply intimate
One should determine this by the mood of the Noh.

kb.th: A performance succeeds where yin and yang meet. On a bright, restless (yang) day the actor must bring calm (yin). At night (yin) he must bring liveliness (yang). Matching like to like gives "no harmony" and no success. Harmony is also the moment when the audience's hearts and the actor's movements become one. Jo-ha-kyū orders contrasting parts in time.
h: **Like matched with like gives no harmony.** "if one makes yang in the qi of yang, or yin in the qi of yin, there will be no harmony, and there will be no realization." In Japanese: "陽の氣に陽とし、陰の氣に陰とせば、和する所あるまじければ、成就もあるまじ". The general rule: "It is said in the secret teachings that all things should be known as the realization of the boundary where yin and yang harmonize." ([Fūshikaden III, p. 16 (the library's translation)](/q/BiX4G5oaLGsspTH0Xku))

**Harmony is a moment between actor and audience.** When the audience is ready and the actor enters at the right time and lifts his voice, "the hearts of the ten thousand, as well as the actor's behavior, will harmonize and become deeply intimate" (萬人の心、してのふるまひ、和合してしみじみとなれば) ([p. 15 (the library's translation)](/q/BiX4G5oaLGsspTH0Xkt))

**Jo-ha-kyū orders a whole day.** The question "能に序破急をば、何とか定むべきや" is answered from musical practice. As pieces are sectioned into jo, ha and kyū, so is the programme. "One should determine this by the mood of the Noh." The opening piece should be plain and auspicious; technique comes later. ([pp. 16–17](/q/BiX4G5oaLGsspTH0Xkv))
tr: **Native terms.** *wa suru* 和する, "to harmonize, blend", as yin and yang meet; *wagō* 和合, "coming together as one", for actor and audience; *jōju* 成就, "realization, success", which is what harmony produces. *Jo-ha-kyū* 序破急 is a word for form in time, not for harmony.

**What it means in context:** harmony is produced by *supplying the opposite* of what the situation has. It is a counter-balance, not a doubling. It is also the right *timing*: the actor waits for the moment, and "what is used according to the time is the flower".

**Verdict: partly maps.** Point 1 is one of the closest statements to “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” in our Japanese material. Like added to like fails, as with Yanzi's "water added to water" and Philolaus. It differs in two ways. First, the opposites are two (yin and yang), not many, so it is complementarity more than diversity. Second, the purpose is the audience's response, and the audience is ranked: Zeami says the actor should "adopt a style that meets the heart of the noble" ([p. 16](/q/BiX4G5oaLGsspTH0Xku)). Nothing here asks whether the parts flourish. The parts are moods and moments, not persons.
an: Zeami's later treatises (*Kakyō* 花鏡, *Sarugaku dangi* 申楽談儀) develop jo-ha-kyū into a principle of all things. They are not held (see below).
The yin-yang frame is Chinese. Compare the Huainanzi on harmonizing yin and yang.
nh: **Not held:** *Kakyō* (1424) and *Sarugaku dangi* (1430). Searches for 花鏡 and 申楽談儀 returned only unrelated texts. Best public-domain edition: Yoshida Tōgo (ed.), *Zeami jūrokubushū* 世阿彌十六部集 (1909), which includes both.

q.t: Nor is it possible for harmonic proportions to be precisely found among the various voices of pipes, bells, men, and other instruments, such that precision could be given.
Thus, a precise proportion is seen only in its reason, and we cannot find the sweetest harmony in sensible things without defect, because it is not there.
so that there is order, harmony, and proportion in diversity, as we showed in the first book
so that there is nothing in the universe that does not enjoy a singularity that is not findable in any other

kb.th: For Cusanus only God has precise equality. Every created harmony is therefore approximate, and every thing is singular. The universe holds together as "order, harmony, and proportion in diversity". In society he wants one religion "in the variety of rites", which is unity of faith with diversity of practice, reached by consent.
h: **No precise harmony in sensible things.** Precise equality belongs to God alone. So "Nor is it possible for harmonic proportions to be precisely found among the various voices of pipes, bells, men, and other instruments". Further: "we cannot find the sweetest harmony in sensible things without defect, because it is not there." The most precise harmony is "proportion in equality, which a living man cannot hear in the flesh" ([De docta ignorantia II.1, scan 371](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk2CJ)).

**Harmony in diversity; every thing singular.** Species are ordered "so that there is order, harmony, and proportion in diversity", and "there is nothing in the universe that does not enjoy a singularity that is not findable in any other" ([III.1, scan 395](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk2Ch)). Elsewhere: "no one is like another in any sense, nor in imagination, nor in intellect, nor in operation, or writing, or painting, or art" ([II.1](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk2CJ)).

**Each content with its own, without envy.** God made each person "content in himself, although he admires others". Each finds his own country, customs and language sweeter, "so that there may be unity and parity without envy, as far as this can be possible" ([III.1, scan 396](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk2Ci)).

**One religion in the variety of rites.** The archangel in *De pace fidei* concedes that "a great multitude cannot exist without great diversity" ([scan 36](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk26u)). He prays: "And all will know that there is but one religion in the variety of rites. If by chance this difference in rites cannot be removed, or if it is not expedient, let the diversity be an enhancement of devotion" ([scan 37](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk26v)).

**But the goal is one faith.** God intends "that the entire diversity of religions be reduced by the common consent of all men into a single, hereafter inviolable, concord". The one truth "will lead every diversity of religions into one orthodox faith" ([scan 38](/q/BepLG3kEKIXkqLuk26w)).
an: Pico's thesis "Contradictories coincide in a universal nature" is close to Cusanus's *coincidentia oppositorum*. Whether Pico read Cusanus is debated.

The volume itself holds the *Apologia doctae ignorantiae* (scans c. 420–426), Cusanus's reply to Johannes Wenck, who attacked the coincidence of opposites as a poison (snippet: "Nor does it follow from the coincidence of opposites in the Maximum, as this opponent elicits, that this is a venom", scan 425). Not read here.

A modern reader's handwritten note pasted into scans 36–37 (signed W.D.) cites Robert Flint: the phrase *una religio in rituum varietate* may be the origin of "sensible men are all of the same religion".
nh: **Not held:** *De concordantia catholica* (searches for the title and for 'concordantia catholica' found nothing). *De docta ignorantia* is held only inside this volume, not as a separate edition.

Svātmārāma, Haṭhayogapradīpikā|||Indian.a: The text says Mūla Bandha brings prāṇa, apāna, nāda and bindu into unity, and the commentary calls this the perfection of yoga (yoga-saṃsiddhi). The commentary glosses nāda as the anāhata-dhvani, the unstruck sound heard in deep meditation. It describes apāna joining prāṇa and entering the suṣumṇā, nāda appearing, and both breaths rising above the heart, where sound and bindu unite and reach the head.

k.g: the unstruck sound heard in deep meditation

q.t: Through Mūla Bandha the Root Lock, the prāṇa upward-moving breath, apāna downward-moving breath, nāda internal sound, and bindu the point of spiritual potency attain unity. This bestows the perfection of yoga; of this there is no doubt. || 64 ||

Leon Battista Alberti, On the Art of Bui.a: Alberti takes the method of definition from music and from nature, citing the saying of Pythagoras that nature is self-similar in all its parts. He defines harmony as a consonance of voices pleasing to the ears and lists the consonances with their ratios: diapente as sesquialteral, diatesseron as sesquitertian, diapason as double, and the tone as sesquioctave. He then describes the arithmetic, geometric and musical means, which architects used for the whole building and its parts.

q.t: The matter stands thus: those numbers by which it comes to pass that that concinnity of voices most pleasing to the ears is rendered, these same numbers cause the eyes and the mind also to be filled with marvelous pleasure.

For just as in a lyre, when deep voices respond to high ones, and the middle ones, intent upon the harmony between them, resonate, there arises from the variety of voices a certain sonorous and marvelous equality of proportions, which in the greatest degree delights and detains the mind: so it happens also in all other things that serve to move and hold the minds.
Arithmeticists establish that this number six is the mean here: which indeed, placed between those two extremes set out—four and eight—is at an equal interval from both.
love is the perpetual knot and connection of the world, and the immovable support and firm foundation of the whole machine of its parts
For fire does not flee water out of hatred for the water, but out of love for itself

And the unity of the parts is born from the Love that is among them: and this can be seen in the humors of our bodies, and in the Elements of the World: through the concord of which (according to what Empedocles the Pythagorean ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher said) the World and our body consist: and through discord, it disperses. And the concord in these arises from natural Love.

kb.th: For Ficino harmony is attunement by likeness: the heavens are built by harmonic ratio, and a song, a medicine or a mind that is made like a star receives that star's influence. Love is the knot that holds the world together.
h: Song acts on spirit because both are air and spirit. The "very matter of musical harmony is much purer and more similar to the heavens than the matter of medicine", and a song "can be called a kind of aerial and rational animal" ([De vita III, p. 159](/q/BeeKBJZ6CDdsJRSMWuV)). Such a musical spirit "properly touches and acts upon the human spirit, the mediator between the body and the soul" ([p. 160](/q/BeeKBJZ6CDdsJRSMWuW)).

Harmony is what makes lower things receptive to the heavens. "Since, indeed, the heavens are composed according to a harmonic ratio / and move harmonically". He applies this harmony "through seven levels of things", from images and medicines up to the contemplative mind ([p. 162](/q/BeeKBJZ6CDdsJRSMWuY)).
Not every planet sings: "musical harmonies pertain only to these four planets. The remaining three planets, however, have voices indeed, but not songs." ([p. 160](/q/BeeKBJZ6CDdsJRSMWuW)).

The soul is not a harmony. "In every body composed of many parts, there is some harmony of those parts... Thus, if harmony itself were the soul, any composite body would be alive" ([Theologia Platonica, p. 215](/q/BfLPe7by4nNX62Ce7AF)).

Delight is itself a judgement made in number. Following Augustine, he writes: "unless the sense of delight were itself imbued with certain numbers, it could in no way assent to equal intervals and reject disordered ones" ([p. 392](/q/BfLPe7by4nNX62Ce7D6)).

"love is the perpetual knot and connection of the world". No member of the world hates another, and "fire does not flee water out of hatred for the water, but out of love for itself" ([De amore III, p. 551](/q/BhMCivLShuQxCW5iZ8x)).

q.t: these three worlds are one world. This is not only because they all relate back to one principle and to the same end, or because they are tempered by appropriate numbers and gathered by a certain harmonic kinship of nature and an orderly series of steps; but because whatever exists in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one.
because there is no multitude that is not one, they are bound together by a certain "discordant concord" and tied by multiform chains.
just as the natures themselves are intermingled within each other, yet have obtained distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws
The "ipsaity" of each thing is then most [itself] when all things are in it in such a way that all things are [themselves] within it.

kb.th: Pico, "Count of Concordia", makes harmony a method. The three worlds are one because each contains all the others, and they are bound "by a certain discordant concord". The schools of philosophy are to be harmonised because each has something the others lack. The soul is tuned like a scale, and music heals the body through the soul.
h: **Three worlds, one world, by discordant concord.** The angelic, celestial and elemental worlds "are one world". This is not only because they are "tempered by appropriate numbers and gathered by a certain harmonic kinship of nature", but because "whatever exists in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one" ([Heptaplus, scan 33](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAgL)). And "because there is no multitude that is not one, they are bound together by a certain "discordant concord"" (*discordi quadam concordia*). Yet the natures "have obtained distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws" ([scan 34](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAgM)).

**Contradictories coincide.** "Contradictories coincide in a universal nature." "The "ipsaity" of each thing is then most [itself] when all things are in it". In intellect "the greatest mixture coincides with the greatest simplicity" ([900 Theses, scan 31](/q/BhN8F7HLlfyVXsPMQSF)).

**The soul is tuned like a scale.** "Reason has to concupiscence the proportion of the diapason [octave]." The irascible part has to desire the fifth, and reason has to the irascible the fourth. "The triple proportion, arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic, indicates to us the three daughters of Themis, being symbols of judgment, justice, and peace." Music is judged by the intellect, not the senses ([scan 23](/q/BhN8F7HLlfyVXsPMQS7)).

**Music heals from the soul down.** "Medicine heals the soul through the body, but music heals the body through the soul" ([scan 39](/q/BhN8F7HLlfyVXsPMQSN)). "Nothing is more effective than the hymns of Orpheus in natural magic, if the due musical intention of the mind … have been applied" ([scan 43](/q/BhN8F7HLlfyVXsPMQSR)).

**Man has no fixed place.** God tells Adam: "We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your own, no gift peculiar to you alone". He was made to "share whatever had been private to each individual" ([Oratio, scan 227](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAjT)). "Who would not admire this chameleon of ours?" ([scan 228](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAjU)).

**Concord of the schools.** "It is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Portico or Academy", because "every single family has something distinctive that it does not share with the others" ([Oratio, scan 235](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAjb)). He writes: "I make the philosophy of both concordant" (Plato and Aristotle) ([De ente et uno, scan 173](/q/Bek54kKPvxbgmgrhAib)).
an: Ficino's *De vita* III supplies the musical-spirit doctrine behind the Orphic theses.
Cusanus's *coincidentia oppositorum* is the nearest parallel to point 2.
Pope Innocent VIII's commission condemned thirteen of the theses in 1487, and Pico's *Apologia* defends them.
nh: **Not held / never written:** the *Concordia Platonis et Aristotelis* that Pico planned (named in *De ente et uno*, scan 173) was never finished.

We distribute this harmony, which makes one capable of receiving higher things, through seven levels of things in the higher realms.
