q.t: it must be considered and maintained that Pythagoras did not reject the fifth hammer, but rather took up a sixth.
the first hammer was of four pounds weight, the second six, the third eight, the fourth nine, the fifth twelve, and the sixth contained sixteen pounds of weight
yet are so concordant that they sing together a most sweet melody, although it is inaudible to us because of the sheer magnitude of the sound
a certain fitting-together and a tempering—as if of high and low voices—producing, as it were, a single consonance

kb.th: Harmony is consonance by ratio, handed down from Boethius and the Pythagoreans. In practice it is a mediated mixture of unlike sounds, and singers and organists quietly bend it off the exact ratio.
h: He tells the smithy story uncritically and extends it. Boethius has Pythagoras discard a fifth hammer, but Gaffurius says "Pythagoras did not reject the fifth hammer, but rather took up a sixth" ([Theorica, p. 43](/q/BeqTUEnW9jkTzvLlpWd)). This gives hammers of 4, 6, 8, 9, 12 and 16 pounds ([p. 44](/q/BeqTUEnW9jkTzvLlpWe)).

He gives the standard world music and human music. The planets "are so concordant that they sing together a most sweet melody, although it is inaudible to us". Soul and body are joined by "a tempering, as if of high and low voices, producing, as it were, a single consonance" ([p. 32](/q/BeqTUEnW9jkTzvLlpWS)).
The scale is made of mutually unlike members: "each one rejects similarity to the others and they are entirely different from one another" ([p. 160](/q/BeqTUEnW9jkTzvLlpYW)).

Harmony grows with mediated variety: "the more the intermediate interval between the extremities is increased and variable, the more this kind of mixture will perceive the nature of harmony" ([Practica III.2, fol. 48r](/q/BhPbc8HZH7BPz51bIs1)).

Exact ratios are bent in practice. Organists let the fifth be diminished by "a small, hidden, and in some way uncertain quantity, which is indeed called "participated" by them" ([fol. 50v](/q/BhPbc8HZH7BPz51bIs6)). In a sixth, the middle note must be "relaxed slightly (as we are taught by the experiment of instruments)" ([fol. 48v](/q/BhPbc8HZH7BPz51bIs2)).

Sameness is forbidden and dissonance is nearly excluded. Consecutive perfect consonances are banned, and "at least one imperfect concordance... must be established as a mediator" ([fol. 50v](/q/BhPbc8HZH7BPz51bIs6)). Dissonances "achieve no stable place in songs (unless in the fastest passage of temporal measurement)" ([fol. 50r](/q/BhPbc8HZH7BPz51bIs5)).
an: Francisco de Salinas, De musica (1577), ch. XXX: says Gaffurius read Ptolemy, Aristides and Bryennius "so confusedly that it seems he read them rather than understood them". He also notes that Gaffurius conceded the 81:80 ratio's power "for tempering all musical harmonies" (read, pp. 223–224).

Bartolomé Ramis de Pareja: Gaffurius rebuked his 5:4 and 6:5 thirds (as reported by Salinas, read). Ramis's Musica practica (1482) may be the held "Practical Music" 695575b457e3b773024f224c (not checked).
Vincenzo Galilei, the hammer test (, secondary).
Zarlino builds 5:4 and 6:5 into the senario.
nh: **Not held:** De harmonia musicorum instrumentorum opus (1518), the work Salinas attacks. Searches by title found only Fogliano, Volcyr and Luscinius.

q.t: For all things correspond to each other in turn and through mutual harmonies, though with different and varying numbers.

believing that nature possesses nothing older or more fitting, whether in things already produced or those yet to be produced, than harmony—by which all parts of this world-machine are made harmonious.
We have judged that this all-encompassing concert can be contained within three diapasonic … Canticles. Thus, each Canticle will be completed by eight Tones … , namely a perfect octave.
Wherever they are out of tune, however, they must be rejected like useless strings.

kb.th: For Giorgi the whole world is one concert in three "diapasonic" canticles. All things correspond through harmonic numbers, the elements are joined by "consonant contrariety", and man is the bond in whom many strings sound as one consonance. But the concert is built by exclusion: authorities that are out of tune are thrown out "like useless strings", and dissonant matter is shed at the resurrection.
h: All things correspond "through mutual harmonies, though with different and varying numbers". He says nature has nothing older or more fitting "than harmony, by which all parts of this world-machine are made harmonious" ([Prologue, scan 12](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJHA)).

The book is literally an octave, built three times over: "three diapasonic … Canticles … each Canticle will be completed by eight Tones …, namely a perfect octave". Ancient authorities are admitted only where they agree with this design: "Wherever they are out of tune, however, they must be rejected like useless strings" ([Prologue, scan 14](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJHC)).

The elements form a harmony of opposites. Each element keeps one quality of its own and shares its other quality with its neighbour, "in an agreement and consonant contrariety" (*consonanti cōtrarietate*). As a result they "rest with great sweetness in their compounds" ([First canticle, scan 136](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJJA)).

The Tabernacle is a model of the world. Each plank has two tenons, just as each element has two qualities joining it to its two neighbours. And as the Levites take the Tabernacle down and put it up again, so the lower world is "now dissolved … and now, by a certain change, are composed again, yet by the power of the supreme bond, so that the worldly tabernacle remains always one" ([scan 200](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJKC)). The Latin for "by a certain change" is *uicissitudine quadam*.

Man is "the most harmonious bond of all things" ([scan 14](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJHC)). His members stand in octaves and fifths, and "the portions of the whole man, agree in one and the same soul … just as the strings of instruments, or various melodies, come together in one consonance" ([Third canticle, scan 705](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJSL); see also [scan 275](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJLP)).

Dissonance is shed. The final concert comes "when all the noisy and dissonant matter, which by its own nature tends toward dissolution, is laid aside" ([scan 837](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJUT)). The evil spirit, "having fallen from harmony, could not endure any true concord" ([scan 13](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJHB)).
an: **Agrippa**, *De occulta philosophia* II.24–28 (1533), has the demons who cannot bear "any true concord" nearly word for word, and the list of musical cures in Giorgi's order. See and agrippa.md.
**Bruno** made *vicissitudine*, Giorgi's passing word for the world's continual change, into the centre of his physics (bruno.md).
**Fludd and Kircher** inherited the world-monochord. **Mersenne** attacked Giorgi together with Fludd.
The book was placed on the Tridentine Index; the library translation notes this at scan 6. That is not verified here.
nh: **Not read:** the second canticle (Christ as the head who retunes all things), the long numerological chapters, and the third canticle's chapters on the soul–body consonance after scan 705. Chapter XXX of the first canticle, "the admirable concord of disordered things" (index at scan 228), was not found and is the obvious next read on dissonance.

q.t: It remains now to see how all things have friendship and enmity among themselves.
Thus, among the elements, fire is opposed to water, and air to earth, yet they otherwise agree among themselves.
Led by this opinion, Heraclitus … proclaimed that all things come to pass through strife and friendship.

The inclinations of enmities are the opposite: for such inclinations are like a natural hatred, and just as anger, indignation, and a certain commanding contrariety, so that a thing flees its contrary or repels it, as if they were fleeing from its face.

kb.th: Agrippa's world is held together by sympathy and antipathy. Every thing has friends and enemies, and the magus works with both. Musical harmony is the strongest sympathy because the universe is itself a harmonic composition. But concord needs a shared foundation: strings made from a wolf and from a lamb will never consonate.
h: "It remains now to see how all things have friendship and enmity among themselves." Fire is opposed to water "yet they otherwise agree", and Agrippa cites Heraclitus that "all things come to pass through strife and friendship" ([I.17, p. xxii](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbYU)).

Enmity is "a certain commanding contrariety, so that a thing flees its contrary or repels it" ([I.18, p. xxiii](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbYV)). It is also medicine: "rhubarb has an inclination … against bile; theriac … against poison". His list of enmities includes that "the lamb has an enmity and harmfulness toward the wolf" ([p. xxiv](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbYW)).

The universe "consists of a harmonic composition", and song "easily penetrates the aerial spirit of the listener (which is the bond between soul and body)" ([II.25, p. clvii](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbaf)).

Concord needs "compatible foundations". Strings "made from the sinews of a wolf and a lamb" cannot "be brought into any consonance, because their foundations are discordant", while "the various voices of many men harmonize, because they share a single foundation according to their species" ([II.25, p. clvii](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbaf)).
"Saturn, Mars, and the Moon have more of a 'voice' than a harmony." Only Jupiter, the Sun, Venus and Mercury have harmonies ([II.26, p. clviii](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbag)).

The soul's harmony is proportion, as the body's is. Reason stands to desire as an octave, to anger as a fourth, and anger to desire as a fifth ([II.28, p. clxx](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbas)). Grace is the soul's first mover: "when it is absent, the entire harmony falls into dissonance" ([p. clxxi](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbat)).
an: **Giorgi.** II.28 ends with demons who, "having fallen from that celestial harmony … cannot endure any true concord … and they flee far away" ([p. clxxi](/q/u06HI37aLb3oUJFH1RaKiXhbat)). This runs almost word for word with Giorgi's 1525 prologue: *ab harmonia illa … collapsus/i … concentum aliquem verum … inimicum … sustinere nequ-* ([scan 13](/q/BejoHHw2iV73HXnZJHB)). The list of cures (Terpander, Arion, Ismenias, David and Saul) follows the same order.. The direction of the borrowing is not established here.
**Ficino**, De vita III: the spiritus mechanism and the four singing planets.
**Fludd and Kircher** systematized the same correspondences. **Mersenne** attacked the occult-music tradition.

Leone Ebreo, Dialogues of Love|||Hebrew.a: Leone Ebreo's speakers report Pythagoras's view that each sphere and planet has its own voice, and that their harmonic concordance preserves the universe in weight, number and measure. Because love and friendship cause all concordance, the greater concordance of the heavens implies greater love there. Sophia suggests the concord is an effect and sign of love. Philo says beauty appears in proportionate and concordant things but is beyond their proportion, and that proportion and concord are also found in bad things, such as the greedy man and the swindler.

q.t: Since love and friendship are therefore the cause of all concordance, and since in celestial bodies there is a greater, firmer, and more perfect concordance than in all inferior bodies, it follows that among them there is a greater and more perfect love, and a more perfect friendship, than exists in these lower bodies.
What demonstration of true love and of perfect affection of one for another is greater than seeing such a sweet conformity, established and continued in such great diversity?

So, if you consider it well, you will find that although beauty is found in proportionate and concordant things, beauty is something beyond their proportion; wherefore it is found not only in proportionate composites, but even more so in simple things.

For it is well worth noting that the reason why two opposites come together is somewhat unbelievable to both philosophers and theologians; nevertheless, it is proven, namely through Christ and the Devil
that nothing stands in unity between God and the Devil, nor with His saints or angels; they may well exist beside one another, but not one within the other.
Just as the course of the stars is tempered [original: complexionieret; formed according to a specific elemental temperament or "complexion"], so also are those lines tempered which are like unto it.

kb.th: Paracelsus rarely says "harmony". He says one body and three things, a "concordance", a company. His wholeness is functional: sulphur, salt and mercury each have their own office in one body. Health is their staying together and disease is their coming apart. Man carries a free firmament of his own, parallel to the heavens but not ruled by them.
h: The microcosm has its own heaven. "so man is also constellated within him". The firmament in man is not "governed by other creatures. Rather, it is solely a powerful, free firmament, without any binding" ([Paramirum, p. 28](/q/BhbmkgbHy2VoQyn7w1w)).

The three principles "coalesce among themselves and are one, and each has its own office for completing the body … there is only one body, but three things" ([Opus Paramirum I, Latin 1658, p. 48](/q/u19vXlxpHUynRh5sMgELH6Kslw)).

Disease is the parts coming apart. "For as long as the three are united and not separated, health stands well. But where they separate … one rots, the other burns, and the third pulls another way." Its end is "the destruction of the whole kingdom" ([Opus Paramirum I, German 1589, p. 58](/q/BjolUep7BQ0KSedIKoD)).

The body is a society. It is "ein solche Gesellschafft … vñ ein solche Concordantz": strike one part and each part trembles for itself. Yet "one part cannot leave the other, but each takes care of the other" ([Surgical books, p. 497](/q/BeorpX7KxHRMQv5h0qL)).

Opposites can be together without being one. That "two opposites come together is somewhat unbelievable to both philosophers and theologians" ([Astronomia magna IV.9](/q/Ber6tBQk7TBiiBKODbv)). God and the Devil "may well exist beside one another, but not one within the other" ([next page](/q/Ber6tBQk7TBiiBKODbw)).
an: **Fludd and Boehme** took up the Paracelsian microcosm and its strife of principles. See and the Boehme page in this job.

**Galenists** attacked his rejection of "contraries cure contraries". the library holds *Medical Nights* (1616, 69b51d67261c58d63664a3a3), ch. LXXI: "That contraries are cured by contraries, not by likes".
**Sendivogius** and the 17th-century chymists built on the tria prima.

q.t: Fourth, by what skill false beliefs about God or the gods might be drawn toward the true one without civil unrest
if a prince, or anyone else, unwisely loosens the bonds of old beliefs from the mind before binding them with a new religion, the harmony of the people and the common bond is undermined
For those things which belong to only one religion, I refrain from passing down, because they are all—even the most excellent—mutually ridiculous (except where they agree in general terms)
Let it be a conviction for all that there is a God, the author of all things, from whom we should fear dire things and hope for the opposite.

kb.th: For Postel, *concordia* means the whole world brought into one faith by persuasion, without bloodshed. Rites and names may differ for a time, but only *until* (quoad, donec) the one truth absorbs them. His harmonia proper is Trinitarian: the whole present undivided in every part.
h: **The concord of the world is conversion without sedition.** Book IV is to show "by what skill false beliefs about God or the gods might be drawn toward the true one without civil unrest" ([argumenta, scan 6](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfjx0)). A prince who loosens old beliefs before binding the people to the new one undermines "the harmony of the people and the common bond" (*popularis concordia & uinculum commune*) ([Book IV, p. 326](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk2M)).

**What all religions share is a thin minimum.** Book III's "common canons of all persuasions" begin: "Let it be a conviction for all that there is a God, the author of all things". Postel keeps only what they share "in general terms", because the particulars of each religion are "all, even the most excellent, mutually ridiculous" ([Book III, p. 290](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk1m)). Inside one law, local rites may stay: every province and sacred place has "its own tutelary gods … it is right that they be worshiped by their own accepted rite". Even so, "a province is far more happily consistent when it obeys a single persuasion" ([p. 288](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk1k)).

**Rites are tolerated *until*.** Muslim converts who will not give up their worship "should be tolerated rather than abolished, until through constant preaching of the Gospel they reach the sincerity of doctrine and worship". To avoid offending them, the Christians should remove "for a time" the images of the saints ([Book IV, p. 340](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk2a)). For newly converted Indians, "that vanity is to be gradually driven out, unless it contains sin within itself", though worship once offered to an idol may be "ascribed to Christ" ([p. 353](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk2n)). Persuasion, not force.

**Harmonia is the whole in each part.** Book II closes with a "harmony of the universe and of all things placed in the quaternary", a list of over twenty fourfold series, each modelled on the Trinity: "not three worlds, but one, in each part and in the whole" ([p. 259](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk1H)). In the republic, priest, prince and judge each hold the whole of a single peace: "only one peace is required in the republic … this is the good and the goal of human society" ([p. 260](/q/BgRAg6TjkELHyaLfk1I)).

**Later, the excuse widens, but the goal stays one.** In 1547 everyone who lived by conscience "under whatever absurdity of religion" belongs to the law of nature. Christ "does not impute" their false worship "provided that what is worshipped is done for Him … and provided that one stands with one's neighbor" ([De nativitate, p. 98](/q/BhNfH8dgM1nMDXcaFBa)). "In every nation he who does good is acceptable to him", and yet the aim remains that all "be reintegrated in one under the one God" ([p. 152](/q/BhNfH8dgM1nMDXcaFCS)). In 1551 he tells Catholics and Protestants: "Allow among you that each one live according to his own rite, until Christ unites all". He proposes that all be called "Jesuan" instead ([Panthenosia, p. 131](/q/BhNfHGm1JkG3fm1kS2t)).

**One life of the whole, a thousand lives of the parts.** The final union is modelled on a body. If each part spread out by itself, we would each be a head and the universe would be *dissidium*. In the body, though, *tunc fit una uita totius mille uitae partium*, and *unius enim partis minutio* diminishes the whole ([De nativitate, p. 173, Latin](/q/BhNfH8dgM1nMDXcaFCn); the library's English for this leaf was served one leaf early and is now withheld, so the Latin is quoted).
an: **Cusanus**, *De pace fidei* (1453): the nearest model, "one religion in the variety of rites". Postel keeps the reduction and makes the variety provisional.
**Postel on himself**: *Panthenosia* (1551) rereads the *Concordia* as written "before we truly knew the indwelling spirit of Christ". There he now grants the Qur'an "some perfection".
**Comenius** later asks for concord by consent of all and a common language. Postel's 1544 concord is the prince's, not the people's.
Bodin's *Colloquium heptaplomeres*, often read as a reply to concord-by-conversion, is not held or read here.

Girolamo Fracastoro, On the Sympathy and.a: Fracastoro explains that a unison string moves another because strings stretched similarly suit the same waves (undationes) of air. Strings of dissimilar tension have cycles that hinder one another, so only a similar tension gives the needed proportion. In chapter 14 he calls the concord between the senses and their objects wonderful when tempered. Sounds that are too loud, sharp, deep, harsh, confused, uniform or unmusical are received with distress and can disturb the organ.

q.t: Furthermore, one unison note sets another unison in motion, because strings that are stretched similarly are naturally suited both to create and to receive similar waves [original: "undationes"] of air. Those, however, which are stretched differently are not fit to be moved by the same cycles [original: "circulationibus"], but one cycle hinders the other.
When a string on a lute is struck, we see another string tuned to the same pitch move, even if it is not nearby.
Truly wonderful is that concord which exists between the senses and their objects, provided they are tempered.

kb.t: The Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1554–58; ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861)
kb.th: The world in the Popol Vuh begins with a conversation. Several creator gods speak, deliberate, worry, find each other, and join their words and their thought. Only then does the earth rise. Their first humans fail because they cannot hold together. But the gods want humans who will honour and feed them, so the whole they build is a hierarchy of makers and worshippers.
h: **Creation follows joined words.** K'iche': "X-e cha cut, ta x-e naohinic, ta x-e bizonic: x-e riqo quib; x-qui cuch qui tzih, qui naoh." ([p. 8 [scan 306]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiipwMjagraD1dbXhp4)) Brasseur's French: "Et ils parlèrent: alors ils se consultèrent et méditèrent: ils se comprirent; ils joignirent leurs paroles et leurs avis." ([p. 9 [scan 307]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiipwMjagraD1dbXhp5)) the library's AI English of the K'iche' page reads "They spoke, then they consulted, then they were troubled: they met; they joined their words and their advice." (the library's translation) Then the earth is made.

**The first humans fail because they do not cohere.** The mud-man "était sans cohésion, sans consistance, sans mouvements, sans force, inepte et aqueux" ("was without cohesion, without consistency, without movement, without force, inept and watery"; our English), and the gods undo him. ([printed p. 49 [scan 317]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiipwMjagraD1dbXhpF))

**Humans are made to honour the gods.** The aim, in Brasseur's French: "essayons de faire des (hommes) obéissants et respectueux qui (soient nos) soutiens et nourriciers." ("let us try to make obedient and respectful (men) who will be our supporters and nourishers"; our English) (same page)
tr: **Native terms:** *cuch* ("to join, gather": *x-qui cuch qui tzih, qui naoh*, "they joined their word, their thought"); *tzih* (word); *naoh* (thought, wisdom); *bizonic*. No word in the passages read is rendered "harmony" by Brasseur.
**What it means here:** agreement reached between distinct agents through talk, which still includes worry. The good outcome is a world that "stands" and creatures that cohere and speak.

**Verdict: partly maps.** The creation scene is the best held text in this group for a whole made *by* distinct parts: several gods, each named, must talk and agree before anything exists, and the text keeps their worry in the account. The failed mud-man shows the opposite of a whole: something with no cohesion falls apart in water. It does **not** map on the guard clause. The humans are made to be "obedient and respectful" supporters of the gods, and the many failed creations are destroyed, not helped to flourish. The text's whole is a cosmos of makers and servants.
an: Ximénez's own Spanish version, ed. Scherzer 1857, is in the library, as is the Ximénez manuscript (Ayer MS 1515). Neither was read.
A second Brasseur 1861 record and Lewis Spence's 1908 English summary are in the library. Spence is a retelling, not a translation.
Modern translations (Recinos 1947; Tedlock 1985; Christenson 2003) are in copyright and not in the library.

q.t: It is truly marvelous how Nature has ordered one consonance after another in such a way.

Without this harmony, the world would not endure at all; it would either be utterly annulled or, with things returning to their first state (if one may say so), the confusion of ancient Chaos would be seen once more.
Or rather that it is a certain artful union of diverse sounds, reduced to concordance.
for Harmony arises from nothing other than the diversity of things that are put together and are opposite to one another

kb.th: Harmony is an artful union of diverse and opposed sounds, set by the ratios of the senary (1–6). Dissonance is admitted inside the composition but kept outside the privileged number.
h: The senary holds all the simple consonances: "Within this number are contained all the forms of the simple consonances possible to be found". This includes the thirds, 5:4 and 6:5 ([Istitutioni I, p. 23](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY6D)). On the major third he writes: "It is truly marvelous how Nature has ordered one consonance after another in such a way." ([III, p. 161](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY8R)).
The same number holds the world together: "Without this harmony, the world would not endure at all... the confusion of ancient Chaos would be seen once more" ([p. 23](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY6D)).

Harmony comes from diversity. Counterpoint is "a certain artful union of diverse sounds, reduced to concordance", "for Harmony arises from nothing other than the diversity of things that are put together and are opposite to one another" ([III.1, p. 147](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY8D)).

Dissonance belongs in the composition, but under rule: "Dissonance makes the Consonance that immediately follows it seem more delightful". Compositions of consonances alone "would be almost imperfect", yet dissonances are "an incidental feature" ([p. 173](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY8d)). A cadence has no grace "if it is without the Dissonance" ([p. 250](/q/BeoftPgcQGTkyBzgY9s)).

Dissonance is still kept out of the number. Dissonances have rational ratios but "cannot be said to be so, nor to have such reasons, because their ratios are contained among numbers other than those placed between the aforementioned parts" ([Dimostrationi, p. 74](/q/BeqTUp3nagI9QqQqgoU)).
an: Vincenzo Galilei, Dialogo (1581): attacks the syntonic tuning Zarlino said is sung "according to the pleasure of the Reverend Master Gioseffo Zarlino". In that tuning, D–F is a dissonant 32:27 a comma short of 6:5, which the senses "accept it without resistance" (read, pp. 6, 10).
Galilei, Discorso intorno all'opere di Zarlino (1589): not held in the library.
Rameau inherits the senario as the corps sonore's partials 1–6. That link is a common reading and was not checked here.
nh: **Not held:** Sopplimenti musicali (1588), Zarlino's reply to Galilei. Complete Works vol. 2 (69ac83c8f37088db5191839c, 1589) only promises it ("perhaps I will speak in my Sopplimenti", p. 266), so it appears to be the Dimostrationi, not the Sopplimenti. Also not held: Galilei's Discorso (1589).

Not read: Zarlino's justification of the sixths (8:5, outside the senario "in act"), and Istitutioni III on the major vs minor third as the basis of mode. The passage known as "discordia concors" was not found under that phrase.

Jean Bodin, Six Books of the Commonwealt.a: Bodin reads the numbers 1 to 4 as God's harmonic proportion and takes them as the pattern for a royal State governed harmonically, with discord arising once one passes to 5. He sets Law, Equity, Execution of the law and the Magistrate's duty at 4, 6, 8, 12, joined by the harmonic fourth between 6 and 8. He also says a little discord mixed among the concords gives them more grace, and he matches the three daughters of Themis to arithmetic, geometric and harmonic justice.

q.t: For 2 to 3 makes the fifth, 3 to 4 the fourth, two to four the octave; and again, one to two makes the octave, 1 to 3 the twelfth, which contains the fifth and the octave, and 1 to 4 the double octave, which contains the entire system of all the tones and concords of music. Whoever tries to pass on to 5 will make an unbearable discord.

This is what the good musician does to make the consonance of the fourth, the fifth and the octave more agreeable: he slips in some discord beforehand, which makes the consonance I have mentioned wonderfully sweet.

But it is not enough to have arranged these four points in Geometric proportion, and partly in Arithmetic, unless they are coupled together by Harmonic proportion. This unites and joins the two middle numbers, 6 and 8, the second to the fourth, and the first to the third. From this results a melodious harmony composed of the fourth, the fifth, and the octaves
In this, however, he seems to come closer to the truth than the Pythagoreans
must be divided into twelve equally proportional parts, which will be twelve equal Semitones
Although this occurs with some imperfection of the consonances and intervals, it happens without great offense to the ears.
To know this belongs to the Theorist, and not to the Practitioner

kb.t: Francisco de Salinas, De musica libri septem (Salamanca 1577)
kb.th: A blind organist and Salamanca professor who held that sense and reason must agree. He is the Renaissance theorist who says out loud that the ratio school owns the *perfect* instrument while Aristoxenus owns the instruments people actually play.
h: **Aristoxenus is closer to the truth than the Pythagoreans, for real instruments.** He "erred greatly" about the perfect instrument by refusing numbers, "In this, however, he seems to come closer to the truth than the Pythagoreans", because lutes, lyres and viols follow his equal division. Their tempered consonances are off, "which can easily be perceived by the sense of hearing" ([III.23–24, p. 214, scan 228](/q/Beogg5pcZeVMx3ey07o)).

**Twelve equal semitones on the viol.** Makers must divide the octave "into twelve equally proportional parts, which will be twelve equal Semitones" (*in duodecim partes æquè proportionales*), using the mesolabium ([III.31, p. 173, scan 187](/q/Beogg5pcZeVMx3ey079)).

**The ear tolerates temperament; the theorist knows the error.** Players who judge by sense alone know the comma "in name only". Tempering "happens without great offense to the ears" (*citra magnam aurium offensionem*), and "To know this belongs to the Theorist, and not to the Practitioner" ([III.32, p. 174, scan 188](/q/Beogg5pcZeVMx3ey07A)).
an: Zarlino and Vincenzo Galilei argued over the same temperaments. Mersenne later gave correct numerical values for equal semitones (not claimed here).

q.t: the other singers united their voices until the whole chorus was in action, and often the bystanders, to the numbers of thousands, would ultimately join in the words of some familiar song, keeping time by concerted movements of the hands and feet.
He composes songs himself and learns those of others, and is always ready to impart either to the fellows of his craft.
To-day there are peace, and goodfellowship; therefore let all join hands and rejoice in the dances,
In the life of this world there is no beginning anew, therefore rejoice, for all good ends.

kb.t: Nahua song, "flower and song", as recorded by Daniel G. Brinton (Ancient Nahuatl Poetry, 1887)
kb.th: Brinton's edition shows Nahua song as a collective practice: one singer starts, the chorus joins, and thousands of bystanders join the words and keep time. The worthy singer shares songs with his fellows. The song texts dwell on flowers and on the shortness of life. The held text gives no Nahua theory of harmony. The European writers it quotes judge Nahua music by whether it plays "in accord".
h: **The whole crowd joins the song.** "the other singers united their voices until the whole chorus was in action, and often the bystanders, to the numbers of thousands, would ultimately join in the words of some familiar song, keeping time by concerted movements of the hands and feet." Brinton is paraphrasing Mendieta. ([§ 5, p. 21 [scan 27]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFtD))

**The worthy singer shares.** Brinton gives Sahagún's portrait: the good singer "composes songs himself and learns those of others, and is always ready to impart either to the fellows of his craft"; the bad one will not communicate what he learns and "is at once envious and boastful". ([§ 2, p. 13 [scan 19]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFt5))

**Peace now, because life is short.** In a song attributed to Nezahualcoyotl, known through a Spanish version: "In the life of this world there is no beginning anew, therefore rejoice, for all good ends." Then: "To-day there are peace, and goodfellowship; therefore let all join hands and rejoice in the dances," ([§ 9, p. 44 [scan 50]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFta))

**Flowers open the song.** Torquemada's Nahuatl opening line, quoted by Brinton: "Xochitl mamani in huehuetitlan", rendered "There are fresh and fragrant flowers among the groves". ([§ 9, p. 44 [scan 50]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFta))

**The outsiders' ear.** Brinton reports Baker's verdict: "The teponaztli, he states, could yield but two notes, and could not have been played in accord with the huehuetl." Travellers found the chanting "harsh, strident and disagreeable to the European ear". ([§ 6, p. 24 [scan 30]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFtG); [p. 21 [scan 27]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsnhUNXNKYvjjUFtD))
tr: **Native terms:** *cuicatl* (song), *xochitl* (flower), and the paired phrase *in xochitl in cuicatl*, "flower and song", which modern scholars (Garibay, León-Portilla) treat as the Nahua term for poetry and art. The pair was **not found printed** in the pages of Brinton read here; it appears only in a library AI note.
**What it means here:** song is something a whole community does together, at fixed festivals, for gods and lords. Flowers stand for song and for beauty that does not last.

**Verdict: does not map** as a concept, and **partly maps** as practice. There is no Nahua harmony theory in the held text. What maps is the practice: a leader, then a chorus, then a crowd, with two drums of different kinds. But the crowd joins *the same words in the same time*, which is closer to union than to diversity. The flower-and-song theme is about transience and joy, not about parts and wholes. The European claim that the drums could not play "in accord" shows the outside ear, not a Nahua standard.
an: Sahagún, *Historia general* (Florentine Codex), Book X ch. 8, is Brinton's source on singers. The Codex is in the library in three volumes and the 1905 Paso y Troncoso facsimile.
The *Cantares mexicanos* facsimile (Peñafiel 1904) is in the library. It is the source manuscript for Brinton's songs.
Ángel María Garibay and Miguel León-Portilla built the modern reading of *in xochitl in cuicatl* as Nahua "philosophy". Both are in copyright and not in the library.

Vincenzo Galilei, Dialogue on Ancient an.a: In this dialogue, Galilei has Bardi describe stretching two strings and dividing one by a bridge, so that the whole and the parts sound the consonance or dissonance of a proportion. He says the Fifth and Fourth between 3:2 and 4:3 were a work of nature. The Fourth is called a middle interval between consonance and dissonance, third among the five consonances drawn from the numbers one to six, and nature is said never to pass between extremes without touching the middle.

q.t: When the two strings are then struck together, you will hear the whole (representing the larger number) and from the parts (representing the smaller) the dissonance or consonance contained in the proportion thus applied to those strings.

Furthermore, the sound that issues from its extremes is, in its simplicity of nature, truly such that it does not offend the hearing as dissonances do; yet it does not have the quality of delighting it like the other consonances. Thus, it can deservedly be called "middle" between the two.
Confused and in some way even contrary things seem to be the binding agents, even when they come from the same category of binder

Regarding the good, consider how the universe is composed of contraries: for some living creatures, good things are found beneath the waves, for others on dry land; for these in the mountains, for those in the fields; for some in the depths, and for others on high.
it is desired and sought after by many, because it flourishes through a diverse kind of bonds.

kb.th: For Bruno concord exists only where there is contrariety. Everything is "from contraries, through contraries, in contraries, and toward contraries", one contrary is the principle of the other, and the world's unity is the turning of opposites into each other (*vicissitudine*). We delight in a voice that "results from the harmony of many", and there is "no delight without contrariety".
h: "concord is not achieved except where there is contrariety" ([Spaccio, Dialogue I, scan 79](/q/Bh9OzFULDIBRyHw8AYh)). Everything is "from contraries, through contraries, in contraries, and toward contraries: and where there is contrariety, there is action and reaction, there is motion, there is diversity, there is multitude, there is order … and there is vicissitude" ([scan 80](/q/Bh9OzFULDIBRyHw8AYi)).

"one contrary is the principle of the other, and that therefore transmutations are circular". "Love is a hate, and hate is a love in the end." "In the greatest poisons are the best medicines" ([De la causa V, p. 288](/q/BejgTOg3pxq9OAd9Ssv)).

The highest good lies in "the unity that enfolds the whole". "we delight in the voice, not in a single one, but in an enfolding one that results from the harmony of many" ([De la causa V, p. 289](/q/BejgTOg3pxq9OAd9Ssw)).

"if there were no bitterness in things, there would be no delight … separation is the cause of us finding pleasure in union". The dialogue concludes: "There is, then, no delight without contrariety" ([Eroici furori I.2, scan 59](/q/BeiyPoFPqhfzsGOctnn)).

The same bond binds by contraries (Cupid's one fire drives to joy and sadness, hope and despair; [De vinculis IX](/q/BgOaXCFPz7y2dUTcPeY)). No single bond binds diverse things, because "the universe is composed of contraries: for some living creatures, good things are found beneath the waves, for others on dry land". The absolute good "flourishes through a diverse kind of bonds" ([De vinculis X–XII](/q/BgOaXCFPz7y2dUTcPeZ)).

The soul is not a product of harmony. It is the "principle and intrinsic cause of harmony, temperament, and symmetry, which derive from it", against "certain fools under the name of philosophers" ([Spaccio, Epistle, scan 39](/q/Bh9OzFULDIBRyHw8AY3)).
an: **Cusanus** gave him the coincidence of opposites and the vocabulary of enfolding. In the Spaccio he praises "that philosopher who arrived at the principle of the coincidence of opposites" (scan 79). See the Cusanus page in this job.
**Heraclitus** and the Pythagorean pairs of opposites stand behind point 1.
**Giorgi** already used *vicissitudo* for the world's continual undoing and remaking. On Bruno's side the dependence is not shown.
He faulted **Aristotle** for "saying that contraries cannot actually coexist in the same subject" (De la causa V, scan 294).

Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic|.a: Della Porta names the hidden properties of things as sympathy and antipathy, which he also calls consensus and dissensus, and describes some things as joined in mutual marriage and others as hostile in blind discords. He explains the magnet's attraction and repulsion by likeness and sympathy on one side and discord of natures on the other. In the chapter on mixtures he states that good operations depend on proportion of weights and right harmony.

q.t: It must also be most carefully observed that the correct dose of a mixture be understood and the ratio of weights be discovered, because the goodness of operations in all things exists only in optimal proportion and right harmony.

From hidden properties, there also exists in animals, vegetables, and all species (if I may say so) a certain compassion, which the Greeks call sympathia sympathy and antipathia antipathy, but we more commonly call consensus and dissensus. For some things are associated with each other by a mutual marriage and are bound together as if by a treaty.

In truth, it is one and the same stone which, from one side, by a certain likeness and sympathia natural agreement snatches the iron to itself not unwillingly, and from the contrary and opposite side, by a dissimilarity and mutual discord of natures or antipathia natural aversion, drives it away and rejects it.
The new method is not constrained by the generation of "separating by eight." There are four methods of generation, whether rotating left or rotating right; all are cyclical without end.

kb.th: The traditional generation of pitches by thirds is a rough approximation. The exact method makes every one of the twelve steps the same irrational ratio, the twelfth root of two, so that the cycle closes on itself.
h: **Three-part loss and gain is only approximate.** "These, along with such ratios as … "if the circle is round, the circumference is three and the diameter is one," are all just rough approximations. They are not the refined principles." ([Lülü jingyi, "Do not use three-part loss and gain", scan 114](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8xu))

**Adjacent pipes are related by 2^(1/12), computed by successive root extraction.** He takes the diagonal of a one-chi square (√2), then a square root, then a cube root. "Applying the cubic root method to divide it, one obtains 1.059463094359295264561825 feet. This is the ratio of the Yingzhong double-octave scale." ([scan 116](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8xw); √2 step on [scan 115](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8xv)). Here 倍律 means the doubled, octave-lower pipe, not a "double-octave scale" as the library translation has it.

**Closure is the point.** "Since the twelve pitches begin with Huangzhong and end with Yingzhong, returning to the beginning in an endless cycle, this is a natural truth." ([scan 116](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8xw)) Working backwards from Zhonglü gives Huangzhong at exactly ten cun, "returning to the origin" (還元) ([scan 139](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8yJ)).

**A later Qing reader called his method ordinary root extraction.** "The milü is in fact the method of roots and powers found within the Shuli Jingyun. It was disguised under the name of gougu." ([leaf "Corrective Regulations", scan 56](/q/BhqLuRMtGl4iWvTS8wy))
an: The Huainanzi's three-part generation, which he rejects.
The Qing "Corrective Regulations" leaf.
Simon Stevin and Marin Mersenne reached equal temperament in Europe at about the same time.

William Gilbert, On the Magnet|||Renaiss.a: Gilbert describes one magnet turning another into its own order, so that opposite poles attract and like poles repel until the two agree according to nature. He argues that repulsion comes from action, and he dismisses the antipathy of the sympathy-and-antipathy writers. He also treats the Moon and the Earth as agreeing in a double proportion of motion through a magnetic confederation, which he calls their true symmetry and harmony.

q.t: Nor is this truly a contrariety, but a supreme concord, and a true and genuine conformation of magnetic bodies in the nature of things, provided they have been divided and separated: for it is necessary that parts so divided be raised some distance from the whole, as will appear later.

But a magnet also seems to repel a magnet; for the pole of one magnet repels the pole of another magnet which does not agree with it according to nature. By repelling, it turns it in a circle so that they may agree as much as possible according to nature.

Therefore, the Moon and the Earth agree among themselves in a double proportion of motion; and the Earth is moved in the space of twenty-four hours, with a diurnal motion; because the Moon has a motion proportional to the Earth, while the Earth agrees with the Lunar motion in a sub-double proportion.

kb.th: Maier set alchemy to music. In *Atalanta fugiens* each of fifty emblems carries a three-voice fugue: one voice flees, one pursues, and a third, steady voice holds them together. In his prose he says two different things about harmony. Sometimes it is the joining of contraries, and sometimes it is likeness, with "like rejoicing in like".
h: **The fugue is a chase held by a steady voice.** "As this Atalanta flees, so one musical voice always flees before another, and the other follows, like Hippomenes. Yet in the third, they are stabilized and confirmed, which is simple and of a single value, like a golden apple." ([preface, p. 9](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXKD)). So many fugues are fitted "to one simple voice" ([p. 10](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXKE)). In his allegory the chase is volatile Mercury, which golden sulphur fixes.

**A world of one element could not live.** "For if there were only one element, no mutation of it into another, no generation or corruption would occur; indeed, all things would be one immutable thing". So the Creator built the world "from diverse and contrary natures... so that one might pass into another through affinity" ([Discourse VII, p. 38](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXKg)).

**But "the harmony of all nature" is likeness.** "This is the harmony of all nature, that like rejoices in its like, and imitates its tracks as much as it can in all things from a certain tacit consent and conspiracy." ([Discourse II, p. 18](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXKM)).

**The coniunctio is mutual gift that ends in fusion.** "The Sun without the Moon is not of great estimation... the Sun receives from the Moon multiplication and the propagation of the species." The mixed subjects pass "through various colors" until "they arrive at one color and essence" ([Discourse XXX, p. 131](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXMB)).

**Perfection is nearness to the unison.** In *Symbola* the octave is the rule of the other intervals "because they are closer and more equal to the unison". Gold is "pure and homogeneous", and "that which is equal and certain in all respects stands as the measure for the other, unequal thing" ([Book V, pp. 232](/q/BejVnndJ5CZhPCM3KH8)–[233](/q/BejVnndJ5CZhPCM3KH9)). Yet gold is perfect because in it "one quality is ensnared and held by its opposite".

**Music's place.** The preface ranks optics, painting and music just after the intellectual sciences. It repeats the story that Terpander's song calmed the Spartans' civil strife "that they returned to friendship". The book "joined Optics with Music and sense with intellect" ([p. 8](/q/Bhbn6QMPHnh9PDLvXKC)).

"Thus, to the whole world, all things are joy and utility, since all things exist for the sake of the whole; but the whole exists for the sake of God, for His glory." Mixtures of contraries are "more imperfect" and "sustain internal unhappiness" ([De sensu I.5, p. 15](/q/BgOdMsggYURbGuztwZb)). "From such sympathy and antipathy, it is declared that there is sense and consensus in the world." ([p. 30](/q/BgOdMsggYURbGuztwZq)).

The finished harmony is an organ: one breath sounding through many pipes, each with its own tone. Contrariety also has a dark side. When each property steps "into its selfehood", strife marks the Fall.
h: **Yes and No.** "The No is a counter-strike … to the Yes, or to the Truth, so that the Truth might be revealed and be something in which there is a contrary, in which eternal love is active, perceptible, willing, and something that can be loved." If all powers were "only One Power... no understanding could exist. For understanding originates in the distinctness of multiplicity, where one property sees, tests, and wills another." The 1656 English says the same: "If there were no Anger-Fire, there could be alſo no Light-Fire, and the Eternall Love would be hidden" ([Mysterium Magnum, p. 540](/q/BejYwGwo5A8PHBdxxY2)).

**Strife reveals; likeness heals.** "And were there not an everlasting mixing …, there would be an eternal peace in nature. But in that case, nature would not be manifest; it becomes manifest in strife" (*in streit wird sie offenbar*). On the same page, the sick essence "cannot be better helped than with equality" ([Signatura ch. II, p. 17](/q/BejYvIVfgvEIDeWRa0Q)).

XVI, scan 386](/q/BejYvIVfgvEIDeWRa6M)). The angelic kingdoms are each "a particular instrument, but all together into one Music... Every string of this instrument raises and gladdens the other". Gaspar Ens, Thaumaturgus mathematicus|||.a: Ens describes an experiment with a lute in which two strings tuned in exact unison sit among discordant ones. When one is struck, the other trembles perceptibly and the rest stay still. Altering the tension of one string stops the effect. He attributes the tremor to hidden sympathy, and to strings equally tensioned and consonant in unison receiving motion through the nearby air and trembling in the same measure.

q.t: I ask now, whence does this tremor arise? If not from some hidden sympathy? Galileo, Two New Sciences (on sympatheti.a: Salviati explains consonance by pulses of two tones that are commensurable in number on the eardrum. Kenelm Digby, Discourse on the Powder of.a: Digby describes agitated air, or sound, moving the vaporous spirits of a person bitten by the Tarantula. The effect is greater when the sound is proportioned to the nature and temperament, the balance of humors, of the wounded.

q.t: These spirits are consequently moved by this agitated air, that is to say, by this sound; and this all the more effectively as this agitation, or sound, is proportioned to the nature and temperament the balance of humors of the wounded.

Theatrum sympatheticum|||Renaissance & E.a: One tract says musical sound within the airy spirits of brain and heart causes a motion proportional to the nature and the musical beat. Its examples are Timotheus moving Alexander, a struck lute moving another's strings, and droplets dancing in rhythm. Another tract says the stars imprint sympathetic and antipathetic force on bodies constellated to them.

q.t: We also see that sounds, which are nothing but motion of the air, cause a similar motion in water. As, for example, when a sharp sound, which is made while the lips of a glass vessel are rubbed with a finger, excites a certain gyration and dance of certain droplets of water, just as if it were dancing in rhythm.

I shall say furthermore that a sympathetic and antipathetic force is imprinted by the stars upon physical bodies, which they exert upon certain bodies constellated to them, and they either destroy or recreate them; and, to spare myself innumerable examples, why do the olive and the oak, the vine and the cabbage, differ with such great contrariety?

Christiaan Huygens, the \"sympathy\" of.a: In the letter, Huygens reports two clocks hanging a foot or two apart whose pendulums beat together without varying. He attributes this to a kind of sympathy, proposes an imperceptible agitation of the air as its cause, and notes that the pendulums move in opposite directions. Hung fifteen feet apart, the clocks differed by 5 seconds in a day, and a table placed between them left the agreement unchanged.

q.t: When I made the pendulums swing out of rhythm, I found that within half an hour they always returned to harmony. They kept this pace constantly afterward for as long as I let them run.
Musical harmony is composed of voices that are very different, and even contrary to one another; and yet, this contrariety is brought back into consonance
the entire world consists of contraries—for without contraries, neither truth, nor order, nor indeed the very essence of the world could exist.
This Panharmony should win universal agreement for our works, our opinions, and our words—just as it does for divine works—so that any apparent dissonance vanishes.
We desire that men finally at some point be freed from dissensions, so that sects and hatreds may cease.

kb.th: Comenius built pansophia, universal wisdom, on harmony. The world "consists of contraries", as music consists of contrary voices, and wisdom brings them back into consonance. His social version of the same programme aims at concord through shared knowledge, a common language and the hearing of every opinion, until dissent and dissonance "vanish".
h: **Contraries are needed and must be brought back into consonance.** "Musical harmony is composed of voices that are very different, and even contrary to one another; and yet, this contrariety is brought back into consonance". "the entire world consists of contraries, for without contraries, neither truth, nor order, nor indeed the very essence of the world could exist." But the first requisite of harmony is "that nothing be dissonant" (*ne quid sit dissonans*), and Panharmony aims "so that any apparent dissonance vanishes" ([Prodromus §XIII, p. 68](/q/Bg5XfEiexP4hbL8jSB3)).

**Hear everyone.** "We desire that men finally at some point be freed from dissensions, so that sects and hatreds may cease." This cannot happen "unless the opinions of all are heard, and compared calmly, and measured against those same laws which they have set for themselves on both sides" ([Prodromus §7, p. 56](/q/Bg5XfEiexP4hbL8jSAp)).

**Concord through sameness of view.** "Nor is there reason to despair of a greater harmony among mortals, if there were a greater consensus, that is, the same perceptions regarding the same things." Those who struggle against providence "must at last be forced into order against their will" ([Dilucidatio, p. 130](/q/Bg5XfEiexP4hbL8jSC3); Latin *concordia... consensio, hoc est, iidem de rebus iisdem sensus*).

**One language, many languages.** Comenius hopes the scattered languages may be "reduced to unity and harmony" ([Via lucis, p. 79](/q/BhHiif3IsX7rP4lpNpS)). One way is Zeuxis' way: select the best of each language and reduce it "harmoniously into this one: so that from many sweetnesses one might be made". He prefers a language built from the things themselves. Meanwhile, "nations also keep and cultivate their own peculiar languages" ([p. 80](/q/BhHiif3IsX7rP4lpNpT)).

**The world is "a meer harmony".** "THus we have seen that the created World is a meer harmony." ([Physicks, Epilogue, p. 238](/q/u0cqUc9SbZDfs1eSy1nwZcVOFM)). "the world be- ing made up of a thousand thousand parts, and particles of parts, is nevertheleffe one, and undivided in it selfe" ([p. 239](/q/u0cqUc9SbZDfs1eSy1nwZcVOFN)).
an: Mersenne, named in *Via lucis* (scan 107) as already building a philosophical language, holds that diversity is imperfection. Leibniz took over both the universal character and the harmony of things.
Aristotle's objection to Plato's unity is the natural critique of point 3.

William Holder, Natural Grounds and Prin.a: Holder says tension determines the measure of vibrations, so harmony comes under mathematical calculation of proportions among chord lengths, vibration times and intervals. He cites Galileo's doctrine of pendulums for the sympathy of consonant strings. On a bass viol, unison and octave strings vibrate when a lower string is struck, and dissonant strings stay quiet. He lists the ratios 2 to 1, 3 to 2, 4 to 3, 5 to 4, 6 to 5 and 5 to 3 as a variety of consonances within one Diapason.

q.t: Tension, determines the Measure of the Vibrations which it makes. And thus, Harmony comes under mathematical Calculations of Proportions, of the length of Chords, of the Measure of Time in Vibrations; of the Intervals of Tuned Sounds.
GALILEO, from this Doctrine of Pendulums, easily and naturally explains the so much admired sympathy of Consonant strings; one (though untouched) moving when the other is struck.

You may see here, within the space of three Intervals from the Unison, viz. 3d, 5th, and 8th, what a Concourse there is of Consonant Rations, to variegate and give (as 'twere) a pleasant Purling to the Harmony within that Space: For now, all this Variety is form'd within one System of Diapason, justly bearing that Name.

I hold that the Dualists are wrong regarding the first point, and that they would be right regarding the second, where Mr. Diroys blames them without cause; or rather that one can reconcile the evil or the lesser good in some parts with the better in the whole.

kb.t: Gagaku and Japanese music theory: the Kangen ongi (late 12th c.) and Kaibara Ekiken (c. 1710)
kb.th: Japanese writing about court music took over the Chinese frame. The modes correspond to the Five Phases and the five organs, and music is the harmony of Heaven and Earth that "harmonizes those above and below". Harmony in the body is pictured as good government: the heart rules, the organs obey. When they do not obey, that is discord.
h: **The harmonized body is a well-ruled state.** The *Kangen ongi* 管絃音義 (in the Gunsho ruijū's music section) ties each gagaku mode to a phase, an organ and a Buddhist precept. It quotes Zhiyi's *Shidai zenmon*: "If the heart practices the true law, all subordinates follow, and the rule is just and peaceful. Thus the five organs are harmonized, the six galleries are in accord, and the Four Elements are at peace." (故「五臟調和」). The contrary case: "If the heart practices illegal acts, the servants rebel and harm each other." ([Gunsho ruijū 12, p. 12 (the library's translation)](/q/Bjei9OjaEs4Z7jWUslY))

**The "level mode" is named for balance.** The treatise explains *hyōjō* 平調 by its high and low tones being "evened": "而二音均平之上". It quotes "平理未有偏頗", "the principle of levelness has no bias". ([p. 12](/q/Bjei9OjaEs4Z7jWUslY)) (partial: my reading of the kanbun; the library's gloss is faulty)

**Ekiken: the root of music is harmonious joy.** The sages modelled music on the harmony of Heaven and Earth; it "harmonizes those above and below" (和二上下一). "Therefore, music takes harmonious joy as its foundation, and sound and appearance as its ornamentation." ([Ekiken zenshū 2, *Gakusetsu*, p. 296 (the library's translation)](/q/BeuQkSan7LlmksSUrqi))

**Ekiken: nature's music, and the mean of feeling.** Birdsong, insects, the deer's cry and leaping fish, "these are all natural impulses that cannot be suppressed", the natural music of things. "Therefore, the way of creating music lies in balancing likes and dislikes and not losing the heart of harmony and joy." ([Preface to a wagon inscription, p. 297 (the library's translation)](/q/BeuQkSan7LlmksSUrqj))
tr: **Native terms.** *chōwa* 調和 ("tuned and harmonized", of the organs); *wa* 和 and *waraku* 和樂 ("harmonious joy", Ekiken); *kinpei* 均平 ("evened, level", of two tones); *chōshi* 調子 (mode/tuning; it appears in the treatise's mode names but was not studied here).

**What it means in context:** in the *Kangen ongi*, *chōwa* is the state of a body whose parts obey a ruler. In Ekiken, *wa* is a calm, joyful disposition, and the job of music is to keep feeling within bounds ("balancing likes and dislikes").

**Verdict: does not map** in the main, and partly maps in one respect. The body has five different organs and five different tones, so diversity is assumed. But their harmony is defined by obedience to the heart-king, and discord means subordinates rebelling. That is harmony as rank and order. Ekiken's *waraku* is the mean of feeling, close to the Yueji and to the Sona simile's evenness, not diversity in wholeness.
an: Both rest on the Yueji. Ekiken restates it rather than adding to it.
The *Kangen ongi* passage on the organs is itself a quotation from the Tiantai master Zhiyi. Buddhist meditation literature is the channel here, not Confucian ritual.
nh: **Not found in the library:** *Kyōkunshō* 教訓抄 (1233), *Taigenshō* 體源抄 (1512) and *Gakkaroku* 楽家録 (1690). Searches for 楽家録 and 雅楽 returned nothing relevant. Best public-domain editions: *Nihon koten zenshū* / *Kokusho kankōkai* printings (e.g. *Gakkaroku*, Kokusho kankōkai 1906; *Kyōkunshō* in *Zoku gunsho ruijū*).

The mind hears harmony and dissonance in affections, finding "a harmonious and a disso- nant, as really and truly here as in any musical num- bers" ([Inquiry p. 37](/q/Bem9nVCXWIKfEQM5C01))

kb.th: Harmony is the governing whole: chords fixed by the mode dictate the melody of every voice. Dissonance drives a chain of chords toward the perfect cadence, where nothing is left to desire. All of it should follow from one evident principle, though taste may bend the rules.
h: Reason over experience: "Music is a science that must have certain rules. These rules must be drawn from an evident principle, and this principle can hardly be known to us without the help of Mathematics." ([Preface p. 11](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFut)), yet "Good taste, which dictates most of these rules, even obliges us sometimes to depart from them." ([p. 138](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFxY))

Melody from harmony: voices "will form a good harmony together only with difficulty, not to say that it is impossible, if this order is not dictated to them by the rules of harmony." ([II.19, p. 138](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFxY)); "the song depends absolutely on the chords fixed by the mode." ([II.21, p. 143](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFxd))

Dissonance chains forward: without the leading note "this dissonant chord must be followed by another dissonant one, and so on by a chain, until one hears this leading note, which then determines the conclusion" ([II.14, p. 217](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFyp))

Closure as goal: the perfect cadence "satisfies in such a way that one has nothing left to desire" ([p. 54](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFwC)); without it "the soul cannot be satisfied." ([p. 146](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFxg))

Even cheerful music needs dissonance: "as one cannot dispense with intermingling dissonant chords in them, one must ensure that the dissonances are born in them naturally" ([II.20, p. 141](/q/Biw8j3PGu1cpL8xDFxb))

q.t: THE Figures that excite in us the Ideas of Beauty, seem to be those in which there is Uniformity amidst Variety.

what we call Beautiful in Objects, to speak in the Mathematical Style, seems to be in a compound Ratio of Uniformity and Varie- ty; so that where the Uniformity of Bo- dys is equal, the Beauty is as the Variety; and where the Variety is equal, the Beauty is as the Uniformity.
the Want of that most perfect Uniformity observable in the latter, is com- pensated by the greater Variety in the o- thers, so that the Beauty is nearly equal.
Harmony often raises Pleasure in those who know not what is the Occasion of it: And yet the Foun- dation of this Pleasure is known to be a sort of Uniformity.

kb.th: Harmony is one case of original beauty: an immediate pleasure of an internal sense, occasioned by uniformity amidst variety, and linked to its objects by God's choice rather than by necessity.
h: Beauty in figures is occasioned by uniformity amidst variety. "THE Figures that excite in us the Ideas of Beauty, seem to be those in which there is Uniformity amidst Variety." ([p. 15](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14Kjdt))

Beauty is a compound ratio of the two. "what we call Beautiful in Objects, to speak in the Mathematical Style, seems to be in a compound Ratio of Uniformity and Varie- ty; so that where the Uniformity of Bo- dys is equal, the Beauty is as the Variety; and where the Variety is equal, the Beauty is as the Uniformity." ([p. 16](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14Kjdu)), and less uniformity "is com- pensated by the greater Variety in the o- thers, so that the Beauty is nearly equal" ([p. 17](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14Kjdv)).

Harmony is original beauty founded on coincidence of vibrations, and a composition needs unity of key: "the Dissonance which would arise from tacking Parts of different Tunes together as one, altho both were separately agreeable." ([p. 26](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14Kje4))

The pleasure is immediate. "the Pleasure does not arise from any Knowledge of Principles, Proportions, Causes, or of the Usefulness of the Object; but strikes us at first with the Idea of Beauty" ([p. 10](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14Kjdo))

The link is contingent: "possibly the DEITY could have formed us so as to have receiv'd no Plea- sure from such Objects, or connected Plea- sure to those of a quite contrary Nature." ([p. 94](/q/BeqWVCMyhlvTh14KjfA))
an: Helmholtz, *Sensations of Tone*: also holds that knowing the cause does not make a chord more harmonious, and attacks Euler for having the mind perceive ratios as such.
Shaftesbury, Hutcheson's acknowledged source for the moral sense.
Hume, Reid, Kant on taste.

David Hume, Treatise of Human Nature II.a: Hume defines sympathy as a lively idea converted into an impression, and says a strong sympathy with another's uneasiness produces love or tenderness, while a weak one produces hatred or contempt. He compares the passions to a string instrument whose vibrations keep sounding after each stroke. Contrary passions can be present together and form a third affection when they do not exactly clash.

q.t: Now if we consider the human mind, we shall find that, with regard to the passions, it is not of the nature of a wind instrument of music, which, in running over all the notes, immediately loses the sound after the breath ceases; but rather, it resembles a string instrument, where after each stroke the vibrations still retain some sound, which gradually and imperceptibly decays.

It is certain that sympathy is not always limited to the present moment, but that we often feel through communication the pains and pleasures of others which do not yet exist, and which we only anticipate by the force of imagination.
Contrary passions are not capable of destroying each other, except when their contrary movements exactly clash and are opposite in their direction, as well as in the sensation they produce.
For it is certain that the perception of perfection produces pleasure
a musical harmony will please us if we perceive the order of the sounds constituting it; but it will displease us when we do not see clearly why each sound is arranged in its particular place.
then it will displease us, and we will be affected by a feeling almost of pain while perceiving those things.
It can happen, therefore, that some notice an order which others do not feel, from which the same thing can please some and displease others. Both, however, can be deceived

kb.th: Harmony pleases because we perceive order in it, and the order is objectively present in the ratios. Easy order gladdens, hard order saddens, and both are sweet. Variety is a second requirement, set alongside order.
h: "For it is certain that the perception of perfection produces pleasure" ([p. 29](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wC)). Applied to music: "a musical harmony will please us if we perceive the order of the sounds constituting it" ([p. 31](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wE))

The greatest sweetness comes from an order of orders: "we shall feel the highest degree of sweetness if, in addition, we recognize the order which those very things hold among themselves." ([p. 31](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wE)). Order disturbed brings "a feeling almost of pain" ([p. 32](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wF))
Taste differs, but it can be mistaken: "the same thing can please some and displease others. Both, however, can be deceived" ([p. 31](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wE))

Sad music is still sweet. Musical "sadness is placed only in the more difficult perception of perfection or order, and for this reason, it differs from joy only by degree." ([p. 33](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wG))

Variety is needed too: if one system "is retained for too long, it must necessarily produce boredom rather than delight. Since music requires variety as well as sweetness in tones and consonances" ([p. 252](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs101))

Consonance and dissonance differ by degree and by use: their nature "must not be sought in the ease of perception alone, but must also be regarded in relation to the whole method of composition." ([p. 62](/q/BgOYCinqC2EgzHxs0wl))
an: Descartes, letter to Mersenne, 1630, is the contrary view, that beauty is relative to judgment.
Leibniz, PNG §17, is the precedent for pleasure as the unconscious perception of numerical order.
Helmholtz later replaced the perception of ratio with roughness from beats (; not re-read here).
nh: Lettres à une princesse d'Allemagne (1768 ed. cited) is **not held**. It is cited only in other books (e.g. Lomonosov's Works, 69af380405844800f9d80d60).

q.t: a third sound is produced by the collision of the two volumes of air moved by the two given sounds
A listener placed exactly in the middle between the two players will hear this third sound much more clearly than if they were standing close to either individual player.
Therefore, the harmonic system reduces the diverse to the same; multiplicity to unity
It is physically impossible, because in its own way it is a unity, and it is within the circle. It possesses its own pleasantness by itself

kb.th: Harmony is unity. Its physical sign is the "third sound" that two sustained notes produce together. The harmonic system "reduces the diverse to the same", yet dissonant chords are unities in their own way, and they show their diversity only by comparison.
h: **The third sound.** Two loud sustained sounds produce a third, lower one. It is heard best "exactly in the middle between the two players", five or six paces apart, and Tartini puts it down to "the collision of the two volumes of air". The unison and the octave give none. ([p. 13](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdPf), [p. 14](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdPg)). His cause is wrong, and his printed pitch for the fifth is an octave too high.

**Harmony reduces the diverse to the same.** One string sounds three harmonics, and organ pipes of different pitch "form a single sound". "Dunque il sistema armonico riduce il diverso allo stesso; la moltiplicità alla unità." ([p. 13](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdPf))

**Dissonance is not unpleasant in itself.** A well-disposed chord of the ninth or seventh "in its own way it is a unity, and it is within the circle. It possesses its own pleasantness by itself". Only when it is compared with the major or minor third "does it reveal its diversity". ([p. 90](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdQu))

**Two unities.** "The principle of the harmonic nature is unity as the whole; the principle of the arithmetic nature is unity as the minimal part." The dissonances have their principle "in duality". ([p. 91](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdQv))

**Against equal temperament.** He praises Vallotti's unequal tuning for its "chiaro oscuro" of more and less perfect chords, which an equal temperament would erase. He calls the search for one temperament on which "the nations (discordant among themselves in this)" could agree a desperate case. ([p. 100](/q/BgOYCQfhTYxrGpQFdR4))
an: Helmholtz explains combination tones by nonlinearity, not air collision.
Chladni (1802) reports Romieu's 1753 priority claim for the same phenomenon (Akustik scan 248, seen in search only).
Riemann's harmonic dualism echoes the major/minor = harmonic/arithmetic opposition (Riemann not held; see not held).

Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentimen.a: Smith treats approval of another person's emotion as the discovery that one sympathizes with it, so that agreement or disagreement of sentiments decides propriety. He says the sufferer and the spectator need only reach concord, not unison. He describes joy, grief and love as naturally musical, and the voice of anger as harsh and discordant.

q.t: It is evident, however, that these two sentiments may correspond with each other enough to maintain social harmony. Although they will never be perfectly identical [original: "unisons"], they may be in agreement [original: "concords"], and this is all that is needed or required.

Joy, grief, love, admiration, and devotion are all passions that are naturally musical. Their natural tones are all soft, clear, and melodious; they naturally express themselves in rhythmic phrases [original: "periods"] marked by regular pauses, and for that reason, they are easily adapted to the regular, repeating melodies of a tune.

On the contrary, in these situations, a person who either feels no such emotion as I do, or feels something that is not at all proportional to it, cannot avoid disapproving of my feelings because they clash [original: "dissonance"] with his own.

Franz Anton Mesmer, Memoir on the Discov.a: Mesmer compares organized bodies to a needle. A magnetized needle, after oscillations proportioned to the impulse, returns to its original position, while an unmagnetized one settles only by chance. He holds that the harmony of organic bodies, once disturbed, is restored only through a universally acting, definite Principle, which he is convinced exists.

q.t: It is in this way that the harmony of organized bodies, once disturbed, must experience the uncertainties of my first supposition, if it is not recalled and determined—

Just as uncertainly, according to my first assumption, will the once-disturbed harmony of organic bodies be restored, if it does not happen through a universally acting, definite Principle [original: "Principium"; the author refers to a vital force or "life principle" common in 18th-century medical philosophy], of whose existence I am convinced. This alone can restore this harmony to its natural state.

so that the number of circles is placed above the line, and the number of lines is placed below it.
we do not calculate this ourselves (in the sense that we worry about the numbers by which the time or space ratios can be expressed), but nature calculates for us in a sense
uniformity; thus, one also finds pleasure in less simple, or dissonant ratios, if they have a relationship to something simpler

kb.th: Vibration can be made visible: sand on a bowed plate traces its nodal lines. Most sounding bodies are not harmonic, so the harmonic series cannot be the ground of harmony. What pleases is proportion that nature "calculates for us", and consonance alone wearies.
h: **The sand method.** He holds the plate at a point that is to stay at rest, and then: "After scattering some sand on the surface, one strokes with the" bow at the edge. Sounds are written as fractions, "so that the number of circles is placed above the line, and the number of lines is placed below it." ([1787 p. 38](/q/BgOcHbJcS37JxxgiAey), [p. 49](/q/BgOcHbJcS37JxxgiAf9)) (this upgrades)

**Most bodies are inharmonic.** Plates and bells have higher tones "for the most part in unharmonic and irrational ratios". Had that been known, no one would have thought of "deriving all principles of harmony" from the string's overtones. ([1787 p. 71](/q/BgOcHbJcS37JxxgiAfV))

**Consonance alone wearies.** The simplest ratios please in themselves, but used alone they "would weary us with their uniformity". Dissonant ratios please when they relate to "something simpler" and pass into it, because "nature calculates for us". ([1802 pp. 292–293](/q/BgOY57OBXlB0LK6FyFI))

**The whole needs a trained listener.** A fugued chorus enchants the connoisseur, but for those "not capable of grasping the path of the various voices and their agreement into a harmonious whole" it is pointless or unpleasant. ([1802 p. 293](/q/BgOY57OBXlB0LK6FyFJ))
**Euler's degrees fail the test of experience**, and Descartes' "neither with too much ease, nor with too much difficulty" is preferred. ([1802 p. 293](/q/BgOY57OBXlB0LK6FyFJ))
an: Euler is the target. Helmholtz later makes the same objection.
Rameau's corps sonore is the implicit target of point 2.

Immanuel Kant, Critique of Judgement|||M.a: Kant says harmony and melody take the place of the structure of language, and that music expresses an aesthetic Idea by balancing tones in proportion to one another. The mathematical form, the ratio of air vibrations in a set time, grounds the claim of Taste on everyone. He also describes a harmony of the mental faculties that can be determined only by feeling and that must be universally communicable, which grounds the assumption of a common sense.

q.t: Therefore, the way these sensations are structured—through harmony and melody—takes the place of the structure of language. By balancing these sounds in proportion to one another, music expresses an aesthetic Idea: a vast, wordless wealth of thought centered around a specific theme that creates the dominant emotion of the piece.

This harmony can only be determined by feeling, rather than by following rules or concepts. Since this harmony itself must be capable of being shared with everyone [original: "universal communicability"], our feeling of it must also be shareable.
Among the moderns, one replaced the lack of rhythm with harmony
Architecture adheres to music, and a beautiful building is a simultaneous concert of harmony and harmonic connections frozen in space.

This multiplicity in unity is related to the whole, so that internal, different contrasts are brought into unity within the whole; harmony is therefore the unity of different tones, it is the reflection of all particular units into an absolute unity of the whole.

kb.t: F. W. J. Schelling (1775–1854), Philosophie der Kunst (lectures, in a student's notes)
kb.th: Harmony is multiplicity in unity: different tones, and their inner contrasts, are brought into the unity of the whole, which reflects the particular into the absolute. The moderns put harmony where the ancients had rhythm. Architecture is music "frozen in space".
h: **Harmony is the unity of different tones.** "Diese Vielheit in der Einheit wird auf das Ganze bezogen, so daß innere differente Kontraste zur Einheit im Ganzen gebracht werden; Harmonie ist also Einheit verschiedener Töne". "Among the moderns, one replaced the lack of rhythm with harmony". ([the library p. 143](/q/BhEvqaGd0lZ958NdPDD), [p. 142](/q/BhEvqaGd0lZ958NdPDC))
**Frozen music.** "A beautiful building is a simultaneous concert of harmony and harmonic connections frozen in space." ([the library p. 238](/q/BhEvqaGd0lZ958NdPEk))
nh: The printed *Philosophie der Kunst* (Sämmtliche Werke I.5, 1859), the source of the standard "erstarrte Musik" wording: not held.
**Novalis**: no work found in the library (see not held).

q.t: in a manner nearly similar to that which constitutes in sound the sensation of a beat, when two strings, forming an imperfect unison, are heard to vibrate together
We are now to apply the same principles to the alternate union and extinction of colours.
The same constitution of the human mind, which fits it for the perception of harmony, appears also to be the cause of the love of rhythm
discords are occasionally mixed with concords, in order to obtain an agreeable variety of expression

kb.th: Light behaves like sound. Colour fringes are the optical counterpart of the beat that two strings make in imperfect unison. In music, the faculty that perceives harmony is the same one that loves regular recurrence, and discord is added only for variety.
h: **Interference is the beat of light.** Thin-plate colours and diffraction fringes come "from the effect of the interference of double lights, in a manner nearly similar to that which constitutes in sound the sensation of a beat, when two strings, forming an imperfect unison, are heard to vibrate together". The task is to apply this to "the alternate union and extinction of colours". ([p. 464](/q/BgOcNFr0JqMmUrEb55C))

**Harmony, rhythm and habit share one cause.** "The same constitution of the human mind, which fits it for the perception of harmony, appears also to be the cause of the love of rhythm", and even of attachment to familiar persons and places. Rhythm is broken only for contrast, as "discords are occasionally mixed with concords, in order to obtain an agreeable variety of expression". ([p. 392](/q/BgOcNFr0JqMmUrEb542))
an: Helmholtz takes the beat as the mechanism of dissonance itself.
Young's 1800 *Outlines of experiments and inquiries respecting sound and light* (Phil. Trans.), where he first argued from sound to light, was not found in the library.
