q.t: then the need for totality, which is innate to our organ, leads us out of this limitation; it sets itself in freedom by producing the opposite of the individual forced upon it, and thus produces a satisfying wholeness.
One may well call these combinations characterless, as they lie too close to one another for their impression to become significant.
both, however, will always have something general and, in this sense, something characterless about them
the last place to which it can lead them remains the totality, which they achieve more or less, but thereby at the same time miss the character that the picture might otherwise have had

kb.t: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Zur Farbenlehre (1810)
kb.th: Colour harmony is totality. The eye, given one colour, demands its opposite across the colour circle, and the diametric pairs are "the actually harmonic opposites". But a complete totality is generic. Character comes from a part that stands out from the whole without dissolving into it, and neighbouring colours are "characterless".
h: **The need for totality.** "Yellow demands red-blue / Blue demands red-yellow / Purple demands green". "Das Bedürfniß nach Totalität, welches unserm Organ eingeboren ist" frees the eye from the single colour "and thus produces a satisfying wholeness". These are "eigentlich harmonischen Gegensätze". ([§§ 810–813, pp. 303–304](/q/BhBfo00muL2fq1RjXwh))

**Neighbours are characterless, and skip-one pairs are characteristic.** Adjacent colours "lie too close to one another for their impression to become significant", though they "cannot produce a bad effect". The characteristic arises only "als ein Theil aus einem Ganzen heraustritt,... ohne sich darin aufzulösen". ([§ 827, p. 309](/q/BhBfo00muL2fq1RjXwn); [§ 817, p. 305](/q/BhBfo00muL2fq1RjXwj))

**Totality alone is generic.** A colouring with all colours in equilibrium "will always have something general and, in this sense, something characterless about" it. Modern painters reach "the totality" by instinct and "miss the character that the picture might otherwise have had". ([§§ 886–887, p. 327](/q/BhBfo00muL2fq1RjXx5))
an: Runge's colour sphere (1810) and Chevreul's law of simultaneous contrast (1839) are the obvious comparisons. Neither was searched.
Schopenhauer's *Ueber das Sehn und die Farben* (1816) builds on Goethe. Not searched.

q.t: While following tones seem to move further and further away from the tonic, or numbers seem to become only more different through arithmetic progression, a return, a surprising correspondence, suddenly reveals itself.
thus [entering] into a specific ratio by means of a leap.

In this way, the simple numbers of specific gravities—numbers which have a conceptless immediacy in themselves, and therefore can show no order—would appear as the final results of ratios in which the underlying specifying rule would be recognizable.

kb.t: G. W. F. Hegel (1770–1831), Wissenschaft der Logik (1812)
kb.th: Measure is the unity of quality and quantity. On a quantitative scale, a qualitative node appears suddenly. The musical scale is the example: as tones move away from the fundamental, "a return, a surprising correspondence" breaks in, like an *actio in distans*.
h: **Harmony as a nodal point.** "Indem folgende Töne vom Grundtone sich immer mehr zu entfernen... scheinen, thut sich vielmehr auf einmal eine Rückkehr, eine überraschende Uebereinstimmung hervor", which was not prepared by the step before. The same holds for chemical combining proportions, where products exist only at particular ratios, entered "by means of a leap". ([p. 311](/q/BhEyNNUPjF2yIIxqCiz), [p. 312](/q/BhEyNNUPjF2yIIxqCj0))
nh: *Vorlesungen über die Ästhetik* (ed. Hotho, 1835–38): not found.

q.t: Therefore, in harmony, the ground bass is to us what inorganic nature—the crudest mass upon which everything rests and from which everything rises and develops—is to the world.
Indeed, the impure dissonances that provide no definite interval can be compared to the monstrous births resulting from the crossing of two animal species

On all these paths, the melody expresses the multifaceted striving of the Will; but through the final rediscovery of a harmonic interval, and even more so the tonic, it also always expresses satisfaction.
could have no other expression than the sustained tonic, the effect of which would soon be unbearable

kb.th: Music copies the Will itself. Harmony is the whole scale of the Will's objectification, with the bass as inorganic nature and the melody as human striving. Dissonance is the Will's striving, and its return to the tonic is satisfaction. A pure harmonic system is arithmetically impossible, which is the musical sign of the Will's conflict with itself.
h: **Harmony as grades of nature.** "In harmony, the ground bass is to us what inorganic nature... is to the world". The middle voices are plants and animals, and "impure dissonances" are like monstrous crossbreeds. ([p. 293](/q/BgOavTXovZl0Yk2u8ja))

**Dissonance is striving, and the tonic is satisfaction.** Melody wanders through every tone, "including the dissonant seventh", and returns. The sustained tonic alone would "soon be unbearable". ([p. 295](/q/BgOavTXovZl0Yk2u8jc))
**Music is perfect only as a full-voiced whole.** "The melody itself intervenes in the harmony as an integral part, just as the latter does in the former". ([p. 300](/q/BgOavTXovZl0Yk2u8jh))

**Dissonance is essential, and temperament hides it.** The world is "a constant battlefield". Correspondingly, "ein vollkommen reines harmonisches System der Töne ist nicht nur physisch, sondern sogar schon arithmetisch unmöglich", and music "kann bloß die ihr wesentlichen Dissonanzen... durch Temperatur, verstecken". ([pp. 300–301](/q/BgOavTXovZl0Yk2u8ji))
an: He cites Chladni's *Akustik* for the temperament point ( is from the same book).
Tartini, a century earlier, valued the unequal temperament's light and shade. Schopenhauer sees only concealment.
Nietzsche's *Birth of Tragedy* (on musical dissonance) was not searched.

q.t: It is a league of diverse groups, each of which practices some SPECIES within a GENUS passion.
It employs discords as usefully as accords; a very precious property and well worthy of examination.
This is the image of musical relations; a tone does not harmonize at all with its contiguous neighbors
a regime that may be termed a true industrial hell, compared to the continuous charm of the passionate series

kb.th: Social "Harmony" is the passional series: a league of diverse groups, each cultivating a variety of one passion. Rivalry between neighbouring groups ("discords") drives it as much as sympathy at a distance ("accords"). Work alternates every two hours, and inequality of class is kept as one of the springs of the series.
h: **The series uses discord.** A series "is a league of diverse groups, each of which practices some SPECIES within a GENUS passion". The cabalist passion "employs discords as usefully as accords". Each group is at odds with its neighbours on the scale: "This is the image of musical relations; a tone does not harmonize at all with its contiguous neighbors". ([p. 142](/q/BnDZkMOkS22FpbMVDuw), [p. 149](/q/BnDZkMOkS22FpbMVDv3))

**Alternation against monotony.** Doing "the same thing from morning to evening, all year and all his life" is "a true industrial hell". The series runs on "two contrary impulses, one of sympathies, the other of antipathies". ([pp. 149–150](/q/BnDZkMOkS22FpbMVDv4))

**Inequality as a spring, with a floor.** "Cupidité, disparates, inégalités, cabales, sont des moyens et non pas des obstacles; ce sont les ressorts, les parties constituantes d'une série contrastée." The peacock's graded eyes mean Association "cannot be reconciled with our philosophers' dreams of equality and leveling". Yet all three classes get "a MINIMUM, or guaranteed well-being". ([p. 26](/q/BnDZkMOkS22FpbMVDt4); [*Quatre mouvements* p. 423](/q/BnDa2UXSvIryI8MSIIp))
an: Considerant and the Phalanstère experiments: not searched. *Le nouveau monde industriel* (1829, held, [6ad5489590dd8591ceb2eaba](/book/6ad5489590dd8591ceb2eaba)) and *La fausse industrie* (held): not read.

q.t: The solution given by this geometer assumes that any function can always be developed into series of sines or cosines of multiple arcs.
Whatever the function φx may be, or the form of the curve representing it, the integral has a determined value
as if to attest to the unity and simplicity of the plan of the universe
which no longer bears any perceptible imprint of the initial arrangement

kb.th: Any function can be resolved into a series of sines. Mathematical analysis unites the most diverse phenomena, and the order of heat, if we could sense it, would strike us like "harmonic resonances". That order is the erasure of every initial inequality.
h: **Any function as a sine series.** Bernoulli's string solution "assumes that any function can always be developed into series of sines or cosines of multiple arcs". The best proof is to compute the coefficients, which exist "whatever the function φx may be". ([§§229–230, p. 249](/q/BgOelbnou1SJZZy24hF))

**Analysis unites the diverse.** "Elle rapproche les phénomènes les plus divers, et découvre les analogies secrètes qui les unissent" ([p. xiv](/q/BgOelbnou1SJZZy24d6)). The order of heat, if grasped by the senses, would make "une impression comparable à celles des résonances harmoniques" ([p. xv](/q/BgOelbnou1SJZZy24d7)).

**The order is the erasure of difference.** "Toutes les inégalités s'effacent rapidement et disparaissent", and the final law "no longer bears any perceptible imprint of the initial arrangement". ([pp. xv–xvi](/q/BgOelbnou1SJZZy24d8))
an: Ohm (1843) and Helmholtz build the theory of tone on the series. Ohm is not held; see not held.

Frédéric Bastiat, Economic Harmonies|||M.a: Bastiat uses the vocabulary of harmony and dissonance for the social order. He says that error and vice remain possible, and that the dissonances tend to disappear because error brings disappointment and vice brings punishment. He links these harmonic laws to Newton and to the psalmist's praise of the heavens, and he describes the natural social order as moving toward a rising common level and greater equality.

q.t: For harmony to be without dissonance, man would either have to have no free will or he would have to be infallible. We say only this: the great social tendencies are harmonic, in that, since every error leads to a disappointment and every vice to a punishment, the dissonances tend incessantly to disappear.

It seems to me that I perceive, in the play of the natural laws of society, sublime and comforting harmonies. What I see, or believe I see, must I not try to show to others, in order to rally around a thought of concord and fraternity many wayward intelligences and many embittered hearts?

It is in this that the truly marvelous harmony of the natural social order consists. I cannot describe this harmony without fighting against ever-recurring objections, and without falling into tiresome repetitions.
It is better to rend them apart, and to let the heaven stand far above us, and the earth lie under our feet.
He from the first had refused to consent to his mother being torn from her lord and children
The god of hurricanes and storms dreads also that the world should become too fair and beautiful

kb.t: Maori cosmogony, the children of Rangi and Papa, in Sir George Grey (Polynesian Mythology, 1855)
kb.th: In this account the world begins when the children of Heaven (Rangi) and Earth (Papa), cramped in darkness between their clasped parents, debate what to do and agree to force them apart. Light and life come from separation, not union. One brother never consents, and his anger lives on in the world as wind and storm.
h: **The children debate, then separate their parents.** "Let us now determine what we should do with Rangi and Papa, whether it would be better to slay them or to rend them apart." Tane-mahuta answers: "It is better to rend them apart, and to let the heaven stand far above us, and the earth lie under our feet." ([p. 2 [scan 24]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmSWWwdCRI2b6aJ6u))

**One brother dissents, and the dissent stays.** Tawhiri-ma-tea, father of winds and storms, "from the first had refused to consent to his mother being torn from her lord and children". He makes war on his brothers. "The god of hurricanes and storms dreads also that the world should become too fair and beautiful" ([p. 5 [scan 27]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmSWWwdCRI2b6aJ6x))
tr: **Native terms:** the held English gives *Rangi*, *Papa* (*Papa-tu-a-nuku*), *Po* (the ages of darkness), and the gods' names. No Maori word for harmony, balance or concord appears in the passages read.

**What it means here:** order arises by *differentiating* a fused pair: sky above, earth below, children in the space between. The ordered world keeps conflict in it: Tawhiri's storms keep attacking the forests and the sea.

**Verdict: partly maps, in an unexpected direction.** The myth agrees with “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” that fusion without distinction is a failure state: the clasped parents mean darkness, and nothing can grow. It is close to "homogenization" as the first enemy. It also keeps dissonance inside the whole: Tawhiri is never reconciled. But the text does not call the result a harmony, and the separation is violent and against the parents' will. It is a story about differentiation and lasting conflict, not about parts that strengthen each other.
an: John White, *The Ancient History of the Maori* (1887–90), gives Maori-language versions of the same traditions. Vol. 1 is in the library, with other volumes; not read.
Edward Shortland, *Maori Religion and Mythology* (1882), and Grey's song collection *Ko nga Moteatea* (1853) are in the library; not read.
nh: The Maori text of this story (Grey 1854) was not found in the library.

k.g: intervals that sound stable and pleasant
pulsing fluctuations in loudness caused by interference between two frequencies

q.t: the condition of consonance is that two of the lower partial tones of the notes combined shall be of exactly the same pitch; when they are not, disturbance arises from beats.
The relation of whole numbers to consonance became in ancient times, in the middle ages, and especially among Oriental nations, the foundation of extravagant and fanciful speculation.

Whether one combination is rougher or smoother than another, depends solely on the anatomical structure of the ear, and has nothing to do with psychological motives. But what degree of roughness a hearer is inclined to endure as a means of musical expression depends on taste and habit
hence the boundary between consonances and dissonances has been frequently changed.

kb.th: Consonance is a fact of the ear: partials coincide, and when they do not, beats disturb. The system of scales and harmony built on that fact is a historical, aesthetic achievement, not a law of nature.
h: The answer to Pythagoras' enigma is the ear plus Fourier: "the condition of consonance is that two of the lower partial tones of the notes combined shall be of exactly the same pitch; when they are not, disturbance arises from beats." He calls the older number speculation "the foundation of extravagant and fanciful speculation." ([p. 229](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaK3))

Roughness is fixed, but tolerance for it is not: "what degree of roughness a hearer is inclined to endure as a means of musical expression depends on taste and habit" and so "the boundary between consonances and dissonances has been frequently changed." ([p. 234](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaK8))

Scales are not natural law. In 1865 the system "nicht auf unveränderlichen Naturgesetzen beruht, sondern dass es die Consequenz ästhetischer Principien ist" ([1865 p. 358](/q/BgOY5zmbhAzVUhkmVCM)). The English softens this: "does not rest solely upon inalterable natural laws, but is also, at least partly, the result of esthetical principles" ([p. 235](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaK9)).

The ear as a set of sympathetic resonators. The nerve endings are joined to an apparatus "which may be put in sympathetic vibration under the influence of external vibration" ([p. 142](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaIe)). He hedges this with "probably".

Yet just intonation is "natural": "Any other Third is only a more or less unsatisfactory substitute for the natural major Third." ([p. 315](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaLR)). Tempered thirds "simply sound out of tune and wrong." ([p. 314](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaLQ))
Against Euler: "Euler's system gives no explanation of the reason why a consonance when slightly out of tune sounds almost as well as one justly tuned" ([p. 231](/q/BgxPvZxw3dRO3oTuaK5))
an: (existing) objects that roughness does not explain everything.
Euler, *Tentamen*, is the target here.
Stumpf's fusion theory and the later critics of Helmholtz's resonance-place theory of hearing.

q.t: and—given a cultivated musical taste—generally cannot well tolerate octave or fifth progressions

It is true that a soft piece of music can, under certain circumstances, please us better than a loud one, and certainly better than the loudest possible one. But this is because, under the given circumstances, the weaker motion is more harmonious with the rest of the system of our movements, and any movement of a certain kind that is too strong (or continued for too long) brings disharmony into a part of our system as a whole.
The rectangle formed according to the Golden Section, along with those rectangles closest to it, does indeed possess an advantage in aesthetic appeal over the remaining rectangles.

kb.t: Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801–1887), Vorschule der Aesthetik (1876)
kb.th: The principle of the unified connection of the manifold. Pleasingness grows as a clear feeling of unity runs through a greater manifold. Its two extremes, endless uniformity and characterless splotching, displease unconditionally, and in any case one judges which way the balance fails "by the feeling of monotony or fragmentation".
h: **Unity through the manifold, with an optimum.** "Die Wohlgefälligkeit [wächst] um so mehr..., ein je intensiveres oder deutlicheres Gefühl der Einheit sich durch eine je grössere Mannichfaltigkeit durch erstreckt; nur dass Conflicte hindern, beides zugleich ins Unbestimmte zu steigern." The extremes, a uniform surface without end and a splotching with no common character, "unbedingt missfallen". The best middle range varies with the person and their state. ([p. 76](/q/BgScokEy0rfa9lMpV2s))

**Monotony or fragmentation as the test.** In each case one can judge "nach dem Gefühle der Monotonie oder Zersplitterung", that is, by the feeling of monotony or fragmentation, which side has been violated. Higher relations of unity let the manifold grow, but only up to the limit of comprehensibility. ([p. 77](/q/BgScokEy0rfa9lMpV2t))
In music, cultivated taste "cannot well tolerate octave or fifth progressions", because they are too uniform.
an: It continues Hutcheson's compound ratio and Leibniz, but replaces the product with an inverted U.
Birkhoff's *Aesthetic Measure* (1933, M = O/C) is the later formalisation. Not in the library (not searched).

q.t: We are therefore justified in asserting that simple tones and vibrations of a circular type are indissolubly connected. This law was discovered by Ohm.
It is impossible to suppose that the ear would hear as separate tones simple components of extremely nearly the same frequency.
It will be advisable to consider these necessary exceptions to the universality of Ohm's law a little more in detail.

We have now to consider the more difficult subject of consonance among pure tones; and we shall have to encounter considerable differences of opinion, not only as to theoretical explanations, but as to matters of observation.

kb.t: Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, 1842–1919), with G. S. Ohm's law
kb.th: The ear hears a simple tone wherever a simple (pendular) vibration is present, and only there. This is Ohm's law, and it makes the ear a Fourier analyser. The law has exceptions at near-unison, and by the 1890s the consonance of pure tones was disputed on the data, not only in theory.
h: **Ohm's law.** Whenever a simple vibration is present the tone is heard, and when it is absent it is not: "simple tones and vibrations of a circular type are indissolubly connected. This law was discovered by Ohm." ([I § 27, p. 18](/q/BgOeXlaUx0bUxn6xHBF))

**Its exceptions.** "It is impossible to suppose that the ear would hear as separate tones simple components of extremely nearly the same frequency." Such components beat, and their phase matters. ([II § 386, p. 443](/q/BgOeT5UFTSG9UQU2p1r))

**Consonance of pure tones is disputed.** After quoting Helmholtz he writes: "the more difficult subject of consonance among pure tones... considerable differences of opinion, not only as to theoretical explanations, but as to matters of observation." ([II § 395, p. 463](/q/BgOeT5UFTSG9UQU2p2B))
an: Helmholtz builds on Ohm. Seebeck's objection to Ohm (1843–44) and König's beat-tone observations are reported in vol.
nh: **Ohm**, "Über die Definition des Tones, nebst daran geknüpfter Theorie der Sirene" (*Ann. Phys.* 59, 1843): not found. The law is cited here only through Rayleigh.

q.t: Biké hozóni signifies his trail of terrestrial beauty, his happy trail, feet, or footprints. But, liberally translated, the two expressions joined mean a happy old age,
In different connections, it has been found advisable to translate these words with different English equivalents.
It is said that, if a single syllable is omitted or misplaced, the ceremony terminates at once; all the preceding work of nine days is considered valueless
Sána nagaí means literally: he wanders or travels in old age; or we might say, old age wanders.

kb.t: Navajo hózhó, as recorded by Washington Matthews (The Night Chant, 1902)
kb.th: In the Night Chant the good state the ceremony restores is *hozóni* (modern spelling *hózhó*). Matthews renders it "beauty", "happily", "a happy old age". It surrounds the walker on every side and is wished on the whole kin group. The ceremony reaches it by exact repetition of a fixed form. It is a wellbeing word, not a word for unlike parts making a whole.
h: **Hozóni means beauty, happiness, a happy old age.** Matthews explains the closing formula *sána nagaí, biké hozóni*: "Biké hozóni signifies, his trail of terrestrial beauty, his happy trail, feet or footprints. But, liberally translated, the two expressions joined mean a happy old age". He adds that he translates the words differently in different places. ([par. 915, p. 279 [scan 299]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmMlwqWa6DbXEaMh9))

**Beauty is a surround.** One of the ceremony's prayers ends: "With beauty all around me, I walk." It is followed by "It is finished in beauty", said four times. ([par. 613, p. 145 [scan 165]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmMlwqWa6DbXEaMez))

**It is asked for the whole kin group.** In the interlinear prayer, *hozógo* ("in beauty") is asked for "my female kindred", "my young men", "my young women", "my chiefs", "us", the corn, and before, behind, below, above and around. Only then does the speaker ask for goods, horses and sheep. ([par. 981, p. 302 [scan 322]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmMlwqWa6DbXEaMhW))

**The ritual must be exact.** Of the most important song: "It is said that, if a single syllable is omitted or misplaced, the ceremony terminates at once; all the preceding work of nine days is considered valueless". ([par. 617, p. 145 [scan 165]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRmMlwqWa6DbXEaMez))
tr: **Native term:** *hozóni / hozógo / hozó* in Matthews' spelling; *hózhó*, *bik'eh hózhóón* in modern orthography. Matthews glosses it "beauty", "happily", "beautiful", "happy". He never glosses it "harmony" on the pages read.

**What it means here:** the state of a person, and of everything around them, when things go well: health restored, a long life, a "happy trail" behind. The ceremony that restores it is a fixed sequence that must not vary by one syllable.

**Verdict: does not map** onto “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”, and partly maps onto “Wellbeing, peace and sustainability as nested harmonizing”. Hózhó is a wholeness word. It names the person inside a good surround, and it is extended to the whole kin group. But nothing in Matthews makes *difference among parts* the source of that state. The route to it is exact repetition, which is order and fidelity, not variety. Modern books often translate hózhó as "harmony" or "balance".
an: Matthews' later *Navaho Myths, Prayers and Songs* (1907, ed. Goddard) is in the library but was not cited. **the library text problem:** its "translation" layer is an AI rewording of an English book. It inserts glosses Matthews never wrote, e.g. "Hózhó refers to beauty, harmony, and health" (scan 25). Do not quote that layer as Matthews.

Gladys Reichard, *Navaho Religion* (1950), and Gary Witherspoon, *Language and Art in the Navajo Universe* (1977), are the standard sources for "hózhó = harmony/balance". Both are in copyright and not in the library.

q.t: The performers in the hula were divided into two classes, the olapa—agile ones—and the ho'o-paa—steadfast ones.
The part of the ho'o-paa was indeed the heavier, the more exacting duty.
Well with me, well with us both.

kb.t: Hawaiian hula and pono, as recorded by Nathaniel B. Emerson (Unwritten Literature of Hawaii, 1909)
kb.th: Emerson describes the hula troupe as two complementary classes: the young, moving *olapa* and the older, seated *ho'o-paa* who keep time and carry the chant. A prayer to Laka asks for *pono*, which he renders "well", for the singer and then for "us both", singer and goddess. The held text shows a whole made of unlike roles, and a word for rightness shared by two. It has no word for harmony as such.
h: **Two kinds of performer.** "The performers in the hula were divided into two classes, the olapa, agile ones, and the ho'o-paa, steadfast ones." The young olapa dance; the ho'o-paa are "of greater experience and of more maturity", handle the heavier instruments, keep time, and lead or carry the song. "The part of the ho'o-paa was indeed the heavier, the more exacting duty." ([ch. IV, scan 38, printed p. 28](/q/BiX2CM8jMUJXPSa3M5m))

**Pono for me, pono for us both.** The altar-song to Laka ends: "A pono au, a pono kaua." ([Mele Kuahu, l. 10, scan 45, printed p. 33](/q/BiX2CM8jMUJXPSa3M5t)) Emerson translates the line: "Well with me, well with us both." ([scan 46](/book/69e00fdcc47b5c9f8821241b?page=46))
tr: **Native terms:** *pono*; *kaua*; *olapa* and *ho'o-paa*, the two performing classes; *mele* (chant). No term rendered "harmony" was found in the pages read.

**What it means here:** *pono* is the right condition of a person and of a relationship: here, between a devotee and the goddess of the hula. The troupe is a whole made of two unlike roles, young and old, moving and still.

**Verdict: partly maps.** The olapa/ho'o-paa division is a clear case of distinct parts with distinct duties making one performance, and Emerson stresses that the less visible part is the heavier one. That fits “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” as practice. *Pono* fits “Wellbeing, peace and sustainability as nested harmonizing” (wellbeing, right relation) better than “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”: it is rightness, not diversity. The relation it names is also hierarchical (devotee and goddess, novice and master), so do not read it as a relation of equals.
an: David Malo, *Moolelo Hawaii* (written c. 1840; tr. Emerson as *Hawaiian Antiquities*, 1903), is the main Native Hawaiian source for *pono* in government and religion.
Abraham Fornander, *An Account of the Polynesian Race*, vol. 2 (1880), is in the library; not read. Kalākaua, *The Legends and Myths of Hawaii* (1888), is in the library; not read.
Mary Kawena Pukui's work on *pono* and *lōkahi* (unity) is in copyright and not in the library.

q.t: The rules of Native harmony are very difficult to detect. They certainly exist. When you hear a chorus of beautiful voices singing in two or three parts, you at once perceive great differences between their system of harmony and ours.
One will notice a curious succession of fourths and sixths, quite unusual in our music.
In 5 and 6 boys answered to men and girls to women in the usual antiphonic way.
The use of European instruments will raise them to that higher level in the course of time.

kb.t: Henri A. Junod on Thonga music (The Life of a South African Tribe, vol. 2, 1912)
kb.th: Junod reports that Thonga (Tsonga) choruses sing in two or three parts, that boys answer men and girls answer women, and that timbila (xylophone) players play with both hands. He says "Native harmony" certainly exists but is hard to detect. He then judges it by the European scale and expects European instruments to "raise" it.
h: **Part-singing with its own system.** "The rules of Native harmony are very difficult to detect. They certainly exist. When you hear a chorus of beautiful voices singing in two or three parts, you at once perceive great differences between their system of harmony and ours." He adds: "One will notice a curious succession of fourths and sixths, quite unusual in our music." and that timbila players "invariably play with two hands". ([Part V, C, p. 268 [scan 276]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlosPmSQphEf9K8bk))

**Call and answer between age and gender groups.** "In 5 and 6 boys answered to men and girls to women in the usual antiphonic way." ([p. 256 [scan 264]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlosPmSQphEf9K8bY))

**Measured by the European scale.** Junod holds that the seven-note scale is "given" to the human ear. Singers who are a fraction of a tone off "are not yet true on the note", and "The use of European instruments will raise them to that higher level in the course of time." ([p. 267 [scan 275]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlosPmSQphEf9K8bj); [p. 266 [scan 274]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlosPmSQphEf9K8bi))

**Thirty xylophones, one anthem.** At a reception for a Portuguese official, "thirty timbila played the National Portuguese Anthem". Junod congratulates the administrators who taught them. ([p. 255 [scan 263]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlosPmSQphEf9K8bX))
tr: **Native terms in the held text:** *timbila* (xylophone; Junod says the Chopi are the "masters"), *bunanga* (trumpet band), *shitiringo* (flute). Junod gives **no Thonga word** for harmony, concord or part-singing in the pages read. "Native harmony" is his European term.
**What it means here:** for Junod, "harmony" means simultaneous pitches that form chords, judged against European rules.

**Verdict: partly maps, as practice only.** Two or three different vocal lines sung at once, and antiphony between social groups, are diversity inside one musical whole. That is the strongest held African evidence for “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” as something people *do*. It is not evidence of a Thonga *concept* of harmony. Junod's own frame cuts the other way: he wants the parts to converge on one European scale and one European tune. The thirty timbila playing the Portuguese anthem "in perfect tune" are, in idea 1's terms, homogenization celebrated as progress.
an: Erich von Hornbostel, "African Negro Music" (*Africa* 1, 1928), and later A. M. Jones, *Studies in African Music* (1959), described African multipart music without the evolutionist frame. md`).
Hugh Tracey, *Chopi Musicians* (1948), is the classic study of the timbila orchestras Junod mentions. In copyright.
Junod's vol.

Frances Densmore, Teton Sioux Music|||Na.a: Densmore explains the tonic chord of a major key as comprising the first four overtones of the fundamental tone. She cites Helmholtz that partial tones exist in nature, shown by a sympathetically vibrating membrane. She classifies songs by whether adjacent accented tones have a simple chord-relation: harmonic, melodic, or melodic with a harmonic framework. Nineteen percent are harmonic in structure.

q.t: This chord is based on the laws of acoustics and comprises, if the chord is major, the first four overtones of the keynote or fundamental tone. It is understood, of course, that the tone produced by a stretched string or other body capable of strong sympathetic vibration is a compound, not a simple sound.

Thus, if adjacent accented tones have a simple chord-relation to each other, the song is classified as having a harmonic structure; if such a chord-relation does not exist, it is classified as having a melodic structure, while an intermediate type is classified as melodic with a harmonic framework.

We must try to realize that when traditional law is put into action, it seems to result in a constant struggle to adapt the common law of nations [original: ius gentium] to natural law [original: ius naturae], thereby achieving that essential balance which seems to be the ultimate goal of law throughout the world.

kb.t: The Guoyu, "Discourses of the States": Shi Bo in the Zhengyu (compiled c. 5th–4th c. BCE; speech set c. 774 BCE)
kb.th: Shi Bo tells Duke Huan of Zheng that the Zhou king is doomed because he discards *he* and takes up *tong*. Harmony produces things and sameness cannot continue. A single sound has nothing to hear, and a single colour makes no pattern.
h: **Harmony begets, sameness ends.** "夫和實生物，同則不繼" ("Harmony truly begets things; sameness does not continue"). *He* is defined as "以他平他", balancing one thing with another that is different. (Guoyu, Zhengyu, Shi Bo's speech; [Wikisource](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/國語/卷16))

**Variety is needed for sense and pattern.** "聲一無聽 … 物一無文 … 味一無果": one sound, nothing to hear; one thing, no pattern; one flavour, nothing to eat. Wei Zhao's gloss adds that five sounds must mix to be listenable and five colours to form a pattern. ([Wikisource](https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/國語/卷16))
tr: **Native terms:** *he* 和 against *tong* 同. Shi Bo's definition is 以他平他謂之和: "using an other to level an other". *Ping* 平 (to level, balance) is the operative verb, as in Yanzi.

**What it means here:** a productive meeting of *different* things. Wei Zhao glosses it cosmologically ("when yin and yang are harmonised, the myriad things are born"). In the speech it is also political: the king "discards he and takes up tong" (去和而取同), which in context means keeping men who agree with him.

**Verdict: maps on the first half, more strongly than Yanzi.** "Harmony begets things" makes difference *generative*, not just tolerable. This is the closest classical Chinese statement of "the parts and the whole strengthen each other", because the whole (new things) comes *from* the meeting of others. It does not map on the guard clause. The beneficiary is still the ruler and his line, and "levelling" (*ping*) means the others are brought into balance, not left to flourish on their own terms.
an: Yanzi's soup (Zuozhuan, Zhao 20) is the better-known version of the same argument: (see zuozhuan.md).
Analects 13.23, "harmonious but not the same".
Xunzi, by contrast, says music "unites the same" (樂合同) and uses *tong* approvingly: (see xunzi.md).
nh: **Not held in the library.** No edition of the Guoyu (國語, with or without Wei Zhao's 韋昭 commentary) was found. Searches for 國語, 國語 韋昭 and the phrase 以他平他謂之和 returned only quotations of the Guoyu in other works (the Shiji, Wang Yinglin's *Yuhai*, the *Gezhi jingyuan*). The Ming anthology *Jingji leibian* has a section on he and tong, but it reprints the Zuozhuan and Liu Liang, not Shi Bo.

kb.t: Lüshi chunqiu, the music chapters "Great Music", "Extravagant Music", "Appropriate Sound" (c. 239 BCE)
kb.th: Music arises from measure and is rooted in the Great One (太一). Sound comes from he (和), and he comes from shi (適), "the fitting". The fitting is the mean between too loud and too soft, too high and too low. Rulers use the One to make the realm harmonious, and "the One commands, the Two obey."
h: **Music comes from the One.** 音樂之所由來者遠矣，生於度量，本於太一 … 離則復合，合則復離，是謂天常: "Music's origin is far back. It is born of measure and rooted in the Great One … parting, they rejoin; joined, they part again. This is called the constancy of Heaven." (my reading) ([大樂, in 經濟類編 卷46, p. 3](/q/Bl0UffJsddeKOtJ9pTf))

**Sound comes from he, he from the fitting.** 聲出於和，和出於適: "sound issues from harmony; harmony issues from the fitting". And 凡樂天地之和，陰陽之調也: "all music is the harmony of heaven and earth, the attunement of yin and yang". (p. 4; p. 5)

**The fitting is the mean.** 太鉅太清太小太濁皆非適也 … 衷也者適也，以適聽適則和矣: "too loud, too high, too soft, too low: none is fitting … the mean is the fitting; when a fitting mind listens to fitting sound, there is harmony". The gong of the Yellow Bell is "the root of sound, the mean of high and low". ([適音, p. 11](/q/Bl0UffJsddeKOtJ9pTn))

**Extravagance is a vice of size and number.** The tyrants' music 以鉅為美，以衆為觀 … 不用度量: "took hugeness as beauty and multitude as spectacle … and did not use measure". It made the people resentful. (侈樂, p. 8)

**The One rules the Two.** 一也者制令，兩也者從聽 … 知一則明，明兩則狂: "the One commands, the Two obey … knowing the One is clarity, making much of the Two is madness". (大樂, p. 6) All quotations are from a Ming anthology (Feng Qi's 經濟類編) that reprints the three chapters in full. They are untranslated in the library, and the English is my reading. All five claims are "partial".
tr: **和 he**: harmony or attunement of sound, mind and cosmos. It is defined by **適 shi**, "the fitting", and **衷 zhong**, "the mean". In "Appropriate Sound" he is what happens when moderate sound meets a level mind (心必和平, p. 10).
**調 tiao**: tuning or attunement (陰陽之調).

**Verdict: does not map.** Here he means *moderation and fit*: a mean between extremes, set by a pitch standard and a calm heart. Plurality is not its content. Plurality (兩, the Two) comes out of the One and is ruled by it, and "multitude" (衆) in sound is named as a vice. The nearest Western neighbour is the Aristotelian mean, not diversity in wholeness. The cyclic image in point 1 (parting and rejoining) is the closest the text comes to “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”, and it describes alternation, not a standing whole.
an: The Yueji shares the formula "the airs of an age of good order … of disorder", in almost the same words. It is quoted at the end of 適音 (p. 11).
Mozi's "Against Music" is answered directly: 世之學者有非樂者矣，安由出哉 ("some scholars condemn music; where does that come from?", p. 5). Not yet a claim.
Huainanzi carries the 太一 cosmology on.

kb.t: The Upaniṣads (Chāndogya c. 7th–6th c. BCE; Maitrī/Maitrāyaṇī much later)
kb.th: The chanted syllable Om joins unlike partners (speech and breath), and musical tone comes from breath. But the Upaniṣads' image of the final whole is honey, in which the juices of many trees can no longer tell themselves apart, and the "sound-brahman" is a ladder to the soundless.
h: **Om is where a couple is joined.** "The Rik indeed is speech, Sâman is breath, the udgîtha is the syllable Om. Now speech and breath, or Rik and Sâman, form one couple." "And that couple is joined together in the syllable Om. When two people come together, they fulfil each other's desire." ([Chāndogya I.1.5–6, tr. Müller, p. 2 [scan 114]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu6k))

**The Sāman comes from tone, and tone from breath.** "'What is the origin of the Sâman?' 'Tone (svara),' he replied. 'What is the origin of tone?' 'Breath,' he replied." ([Chāndogya I.8.4, p. 16 [scan 128]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu6y))

**In the True, the parts lose their distinctness.** Bees "make honey by collecting the juices of distant trees, and reduce the juice into one form," and "as these juices have no discrimination, so that they might say, I am the juice of this tree or that", so creatures merged in *sat* do not know it. ([Chāndogya VI.9.1–2, p. 101 [scan 213]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlE6p1aSOPvppKu8L))

**Sound-brahman leads to the soundless.** "Verily, there are two Brahmas to be meditated upon: sound and non-sound. Now, non-sound is revealed only by sound." ([Maitrī 6.22, tr. Hume, p. 437 [scan 459]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wp9)). Beyond the varied sound, people "disappear" in the soundless brahman: "There they are unqualified, indistinguishable, like the various juices which have reached the condition of honey." ([p. 438 [scan 460]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1WpA))

**The inner sound has many forms.** With the ears closed, practitioners "hear the sound of the space within the heart. Of it there is this sevenfold comparison: like rivers, a bell, a brazen vessel, a wheel, the croaking of frogs, rain, as when one speaks in a sheltered place." ([Maitrī 6.22, p. 437 [scan 459]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wp9))
tr: **नाद *nāda* / शब्दब्रह्म *śabda-brahman*** (sound; "sound-brahman"). Sound is a real form of the absolute, but the lower one. **Verdict: does not map.** The text gives no relation among sounds, such as consonance or a whole of tones. Sound matters as a means of ascent, and its variety is something to pass beyond.

**मिथुन *mithuna*** (couple, pair), in Chāndogya I.1: speech and breath are joined in Om "as two people come together". **Verdict: partly maps.** It is a union of two unlike partners who complete each other. But it is a pair joined in one syllable, not a many-part whole.

**सत् *sat*** (being, the True) and the honey simile. **Verdict: does not map; it disagrees.** The whole is reached when the parts can no longer say whose juice they are. That is what “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” calls homogenization, and the text presents it as the highest truth.
an: Śaṅkara's Advaita reads the honey and the soundless brahman as non-difference (not traced in the library; the library holds his *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* and Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary).
Kashmir Śaiva thought, including Abhinavagupta, keeps the One but treats the world of difference as its real self-expression. See abhinavagupta.md and.
Saṅgīta theory takes the sound-brahman as its metaphysical ground.
nh: **Nādabindu Upaniṣad**: not in the library as a text (only named in Weber's *History of Indian Literature*). The best PD edition would be the Adyar *Yoga Upaniṣads* (ed. A. Mahadeva Sastri, 1920) or the T. R. Srinivasa Ayyangar translation (*The Yoga Upaniṣads*, Adyar 1938).
**Müller's SBE 15** (Upanishads II, with the Maitrāyaṇa) was not found in the library, so Hume (1921) was used for the Maitrī.

kb.t: Dong Zhongshu (attrib.), Chunqiu fanlu (c. 179–104 BCE; composite)
kb.th: Things of a kind move each other. A plucked gong string sets off the other gong strings because "their number is so", not because of a spirit. Dong generalizes this to omens and kings. Separately, he makes he (和) the greatest virtue of heaven and earth, meaning the year's balance points and a regimen of moderation for ruler and body.
h: **Like answers like, and the zither is the proof.** 試調琴瑟而錯之，鼓其宮則他宮應之 … 非有神，其數然也: "tune zithers and set them apart: strike the gong, and the other gong answers … it is not a spirit, their number makes it so". (Wikisource reading; the library witness below)

**The premise is likeness, not unlikeness.** 百物其去所與異而從其所與同，故氣同則會，聲比則應: "all things leave what is unlike them and follow what is like them; so like qi gathers and matched sounds answer". ([同類相動, 卷13, p. 80](/book/6a3c74ac39b4508b04e58529?page=80); chapter head [p. 79](/q/Bl0aQ3KYmKXXdndgHeR))

**He is the greatest virtue.** 天有兩和以成二中: "Heaven has two he to complete two zhong". The two he are the spring and autumn mid-points (east and west), and the two zhong are the solstitial centres. 和者天地之所生成也，夫德莫大於和，而道莫正於中: "he is that by which heaven and earth generate and complete; no virtue is greater than he, no way more correct than the centre". ([循天之道, 卷16, p. 151](/book/6a3c74ac39b4508b04e58529?page=151); [p. 152](/q/Bl0aQ3KYmKXXdndgHfc))

**Zhong-he is a regimen.** 能以中和理天下者其德大盛，能以中和養其身者其壽極命: whoever rules the world by zhong-he has abundant virtue, and whoever nourishes the body by it lives out his span. The text then turns to timing sexual intercourse by yin and yang (p. 152–153).
tr: **感應 ganying / 同類相動**, "stimulus and response", "like kinds move each other": resonance. It is the physics of sympathetic strings, and it is explicitly *like with like*.

**和 he / 中和 zhonghe**: in ch. 77, he is a calendrical term. It names the equinoctial balance where yin and yang are equal, paired with zhong, the solstitial extreme where one of them peaks. By extension it means moderation in governing and in the body. The Shijing line 不剛不柔 ("neither hard nor soft") is quoted as its gloss.

**Verdict: does not map.** Dong's resonance runs the opposite way from “Harmony is diversity in wholeness”. Things "leave what is unlike" and "follow what is like" (同). That is close to the *tong* that the Zuozhuan and Analects set against he, and the direct inverse of Philolaus, for whom like things "had no need of harmony". Dong's he is balance and timing, the mean of a cycle. Neither sense is diversity in wholeness.
an: Huainanzi has the same zither case.
Wang Chong's *Lunheng* attacked the omen theory built on ganying.
Zhu Xi's 中和 is ethical, not calendrical (see zhu-xi).
nh: No English translation of the Chunqiu fanlu was found in the library.

kb.th: The world is beautiful the way a poem is, by ordered contraries, and its parts flourish in their own places. Yet what delights the senses in music is equality and likeness, which is number.
h: **The world is a poem adorned with antitheses.** God orders the ages "like a most beautiful poem" from contraries, the wicked included. "so the beauty of the age is composed by a certain eloquence not of words, but of things, through the opposition of contraries" ([City of God XI.18, Dombart 1877, scan 498, p. 486](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHq)). Latin: "ordinem saeculorum tamquam pulcherrimum carmen etiam ex quibusdam quasi antithetis honestaret" ([scan 497, p. 485](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHp))

**Each part flourishes in its place and contributes to a common whole.** Fire, cold and wild beasts offend us only because they are inconvenient to us. "they flourish in their own places and natures and are disposed in a beautiful order, and how much they contribute to the beauty of the universe of things for their own portions as if to a common commonwealth" ([City of God XI.22, scan 502, p. 490](/q/BhDwQoHG3TUAzPb4KHu))

**What pleases the senses pleases by equality.** In sound, form, light, colour, smell and taste: "Nihil eni ẽ horũ p̃stantiu q̃ nob nõ eq̃litate aut similitudine placeat. ubi autẽ eq̃litas aut similitudo ibi nũerositas" ([De musica VI.13.38, 15th-c. MS, scan 104](/q/BhNl3G6Fzzirc8jmjUW)). In plain Latin: nothing pleases us except by equality or likeness, and where there is equality or likeness there is number. Partial: OCR only, no the library translation.

**Music is "scientia bene modulandi".** The dialogue presses on what the word "bene" adds to the definition: "deinde qd sit sic bene modulari non enim frustra e definitioni additu" ([De musica I.2, MS scan 11](/q/BhNl3G6Fzzirc8jmjT1)). Partial: search snippet only.

**The felt power of singing is a moral risk.** He wept at the Church's songs, approves of them for weaker minds, and still judges it sin to be moved more by the singing than by the words. "Thus vacillate I between dangerous pleasure and tried soundness" ([Confessions X.33, English tr., scan 248, p. 220](/q/Bh9WQOkskerTjM43ofQ))
an: Heraclitus and *De Mundo* before him, on concord from opposites.
Boethius makes the same "likeness is friendly" move.
Medieval music theory took "scientia bene modulandi" as the standard definition, through Cassiodorus, Isidore and Regino. Leibniz's best-possible-world harmony takes over the theodicy.

kb.t: Mataṅga, Bṛhaddeśī (c. 6th–9th c. CE; known here only through quotation)
kb.th: Mataṅga is known in the library only through what the Saṅgītaratnākara and its commentary quote from him. In those fragments the world is made of sound, the note "shines by itself", and a melody-type (*jāti*) is born from a collection of microtones, notes and scales. The tradition he belongs to pictures the melodic whole as a kingdom with a king, a minister and an enemy.
h: **The world is composed of sound.** Kallinātha quotes Mataṅga for this: "There is no dance without Sound; therefore, the world is composed of Sound." ([Saṅgītaratnākara, comm. on 1.2.1–3, p. 23 [scan 55] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONvj))

**The note shines by itself.** "स्वय हि राजते यस्मात्तस्मात्स्वर इति स्मृतः", "Because it shines by itself, it is known as Svara (self-shining)." ([comm. quoting Bṛhaddeśī, p. 84 [scan 116] (the library's translation)](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONwi))

**A melody-type is born from a collection.** "श्रुतिस्वरग्रामसमूहाज्जायन्त इति जातय", "They are called Jatis because they are born from the collection of micro-tones" (and notes and scales). Alternatively, they are called jātis because rasa is born from them, or because they are "pure or mixed" like the castes (*jāti*) of men. ([comm. quoting Bṛhaddeśī, p. 171 [scan 201]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONy5))

**Consonance at 13 or 9, counted inclusively.** The commentator explains "Matanga’s definition of Consonance as "an interval of thirteen or nine" actually means an interval of twelve or eight", because Mataṅga counts the starting note. ([comm. on 1.3.46–51, p. 93 [scan 125]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONwr))

**The tradition's political image of a melody.** In the verse Mataṅga's systematiser Śārṅgadeva writes, the vādī is "the King", the saṃvādī "the Minister", and "The "Dissonant" (Vivadi), because of its contrary nature, is called the Enemy by the brave." The commentary: the other roles can be swapped, "however, the use of a Dissonant note would destroy the Jati or Raga". ([1.3.50 with comm., p. 93 [scan 125]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOdOjWF69ADTpqONwr))
tr: **नाद *nāda*** (sound). For Mataṅga as quoted, the world is *nādātmaka*, made of sound. **Verdict: does not map by itself.** The claim says what the world is made of. It says nothing about how the parts relate.

**जाति *jāti*** (birth, kind, melody-type; also caste). A whole "born from the collection" (*samūha*) of śrutis, svaras and grāmas, and the source of rasa. **Verdict: partly maps.** This is a genuine parts-to-whole definition: the melody-type is born from a collection of parts, and rasa is born from it. But Mataṅga's own analogy is caste, with "pure or mixed" kinds. The social model behind the word is classification by birth.

**संवाद / विवाद *saṃvāda / vivāda*** (speaking-together / speaking-apart). Consonance is literally "agreement" and dissonance "dispute". **Verdict: partly maps, then turns against.** Consonance is defined by interval count, as in Bharata. In the polity image, though, the consonant note is the loyal minister and the dissonant one is the enemy who destroys the rāga. There is no room for dissonance that serves the whole.
an: Bharata, whose consonance count Mataṅga keeps.
Śārṅgadeva and his commentators Kallinātha and Siṃhabhūpāla, who quote him throughout vol. 1: see sarngadeva.md. The commentator corrects his counting (item 4).
Abhinavagupta, near-contemporary in Kashmir, writes the rasa theory that jāti is said to produce. See abhinavagupta.md.
nh: **The Bṛhaddeśī itself is not in the library.** Everything above is second-hand, through the commentary printed with the Adyar Saṅgītaratnākara. The Bṛhaddeśī survives incomplete. The PD edition needed is K. Sāmbaśiva Śāstrī (ed.), *Bṛhaddeśī of Mataṅga Muni*, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 94 (1928). The modern critical edition (Prem Lata Sharma, IGNCA 1992–94) is in copyright.

kb.th: In the Latin *De radiis*, one "celestial harmony" of star-rays reaches every place in a different mixture. That harmony produces the differences between things, and every individual mirrors the whole of it.
h: **Celestial harmony makes things different, not alike.** Every star sends its rays to every place, and each place receives its own blend, so the one harmony keeps producing differences. "in every place there is a different tenor of rays which is derived from the total harmony of the stars." ([De radiis §27, scan 174](/q/BhDa8p2rKowaFwdHD0I))

**Each part carries the state of the whole.** Anything in the elemental world, however small, is a state of the whole celestial harmony, so one individual known completely would reveal all of it. "one would foresee the entire condition of celestial harmony as if through a mirror; since every thing of this World is thus an example of the one harmony." ([De radiis §56, scan 179](/q/BhDa8p2rKowaFwdHD0N))

**Everything radiates.** The thesis is widened from the stars to all things: fire, earth, medicines, colour and sound all send out rays. "the collision of bodies also makes a sound, diffusing itself everywhere through rays of its own mode" ([De radiis §58, scan 180](/q/BhDa8p2rKowaFwdHD0O))

**Rays that agree add up; rays that disagree cancel.** When different things' rays fall on one thing, they temper each other, "increasing the species of the effect if they agree, and diminishing their effects if they disagree" ([De radiis §65, scan 180](/q/BhDa8p2rKowaFwdHD0O))
an: The Latin West read *De radiis* as the theory behind magic. In the library, Wimpina's *De erroribus philosophorum* (1493) says that to hold "the opinion of Alkindi" accuses the Author of nature; Pietro d'Abano argues against "the son of Alkindi"; Ficino (*De triplici vita*), Agrippa, Trithemius and Roger Bacon cite him.
Ficino's tempering of soul and body by music belongs to the same Latin sympathy tradition.
The doctrine that the four oud strings act on the four humours, usually credited to al-Kindī, is held in the library only in the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ.
nh: **Not held:** al-Kindī's music treatises (e.g. *Risāla fī ajzāʾ khabariyya fī l-mūsīqī*, *Kitāb al-muṣawwitāt al-watariyya*, the treatise on the composition of melodies). Nothing in the library lets us verify his strings–humours–elements–seasons–zodiac correspondences or what he says about the effects of the modes. The Arabic original of *De radiis* is lost; the library has the Latin only.

kb.th: Not in the library. Every statement on this page is unverified.
h: Israel's music was held in high esteem, with David and Samuel as its masters and the Levites as its performers in the Temple.
Hebrew poetry and chant were bound to the words. Ha-Levi criticizes the adoption of Arabic quantitative metres for Hebrew because they distort the language.
tr: Likely terms are Hebrew **niggun ניגון** (melody) and **shir שיר** (song), and the Judaeo-Arabic original's Arabic music vocabulary (*laḥn*, *taʾlīf*). None was checked.

**Verdict: not assessable.** If the model-knowledge account is right, ha-Levi's interest is in the fit between music and sacred text and in national tradition, not in diversity in wholeness. That is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
an: Later Jewish writers cited the *Kuzari* constantly. the library has many such citations (Menasseh ben Israel, Buxtorf, Eisenmenger, Gabbai). None was checked for the music passage.
nh: **Not held:** no edition of the *Kuzari* was found under "Kuzari", "Cuzari", "כוזרי" or "Hirschfeld". Best public-domain editions: Hartwig Hirschfeld, *Kitab al Khazari* (London: Routledge, 1905; English), and Buxtorf's Latin *Liber Cosri* (Basel, 1660) with Ibn Tibbon's Hebrew. Both are candidates for acquisition.

q.t: If the heart practices the true law, all subordinates follow, and the rule is just and peaceful. Thus the five organs are harmonized, the six galleries are in accord, and the Four Elements are at peace.
If the heart practices illegal acts, the servants rebel and harm each other.

kb.t: Gagaku and Japanese music theory: the Kangen ongi (late 12th c.) and Kaibara Ekiken (c. 1710)
kb.th: Japanese writing about court music took over the Chinese frame. The modes correspond to the Five Phases and the five organs, and music is the harmony of Heaven and Earth that "harmonizes those above and below". Harmony in the body is pictured as good government: the heart rules, the organs obey. When they do not obey, that is discord.
h: **The harmonized body is a well-ruled state.** The *Kangen ongi* 管絃音義 (in the Gunsho ruijū's music section) ties each gagaku mode to a phase, an organ and a Buddhist precept. It quotes Zhiyi's *Shidai zenmon*: "If the heart practices the true law, all subordinates follow, and the rule is just and peaceful. Thus the five organs are harmonized, the six galleries are in accord, and the Four Elements are at peace." (故「五臟調和」). The contrary case: "If the heart practices illegal acts, the servants rebel and harm each other." ([Gunsho ruijū 12, p. 12 (the library's translation)](/q/Bjei9OjaEs4Z7jWUslY))

**The "level mode" is named for balance.** The treatise explains *hyōjō* 平調 by its high and low tones being "evened": "而二音均平之上". It quotes "平理未有偏頗", "the principle of levelness has no bias". ([p. 12](/q/Bjei9OjaEs4Z7jWUslY)) (partial: my reading of the kanbun; the library's gloss is faulty)

**Ekiken: the root of music is harmonious joy.** The sages modelled music on the harmony of Heaven and Earth; it "harmonizes those above and below" (和二上下一). "Therefore, music takes harmonious joy as its foundation, and sound and appearance as its ornamentation." ([Ekiken zenshū 2, *Gakusetsu*, p. 296 (the library's translation)](/q/BeuQkSan7LlmksSUrqi))

**Ekiken: nature's music, and the mean of feeling.** Birdsong, insects, the deer's cry and leaping fish, "these are all natural impulses that cannot be suppressed", the natural music of things. "Therefore, the way of creating music lies in balancing likes and dislikes and not losing the heart of harmony and joy." ([Preface to a wagon inscription, p. 297 (the library's translation)](/q/BeuQkSan7LlmksSUrqj))
tr: **Native terms.** *chōwa* 調和 ("tuned and harmonized", of the organs); *wa* 和 and *waraku* 和樂 ("harmonious joy", Ekiken); *kinpei* 均平 ("evened, level", of two tones); *chōshi* 調子 (mode/tuning; it appears in the treatise's mode names but was not studied here).

**What it means in context:** in the *Kangen ongi*, *chōwa* is the state of a body whose parts obey a ruler. In Ekiken, *wa* is a calm, joyful disposition, and the job of music is to keep feeling within bounds ("balancing likes and dislikes").

**Verdict: does not map** in the main, and partly maps in one respect. The body has five different organs and five different tones, so diversity is assumed. But their harmony is defined by obedience to the heart-king, and discord means subordinates rebelling. That is harmony as rank and order. Ekiken's *waraku* is the mean of feeling, close to the Yueji and to the Sona simile's evenness, not diversity in wholeness.
an: Both rest on the Yueji. Ekiken restates it rather than adding to it.
The *Kangen ongi* passage on the organs is itself a quotation from the Tiantai master Zhiyi. Buddhist meditation literature is the channel here, not Confucian ritual.
nh: **Not found in the library:** *Kyōkunshō* 教訓抄 (1233), *Taigenshō* 體源抄 (1512) and *Gakkaroku* 楽家録 (1690). Searches for 楽家録 and 雅楽 returned nothing relevant. Best public-domain editions: *Nihon koten zenshū* / *Kokusho kankōkai* printings (e.g. *Gakkaroku*, Kokusho kankōkai 1906; *Kyōkunshō* in *Zoku gunsho ruijū*).

kb.th: He (和) is the state of feelings that, once aroused, each hit their proper measure, "with nothing perverse or contrary". In conduct it is the "unhurried, unforced" ease with which ritual is performed. That ease belongs inside ritual: without ritual it is self-indulgence.
h: **He is feeling without discord.** On Zhongyong ch. 1 (喜怒哀樂之未發謂之中，發而皆中節謂之和): 發皆中節，情之正也；無所乖戾，故謂之和, "when they arise and all hit the measure, that is the correctness of feeling; with nothing perverse or contrary, it is called he." (my reading) ([quoted in 大學衍義, vol. 16, p. 37](/q/Bl0Uxe9Ch3jPiR2fBSv))

**He is ease inside ritual.** On Analects 1.12 (禮之用，和為貴), Zhu Xi glosses he as 從容不迫, "unhurried and unforced". In conversation he adds: 若離了禮說從容不迫，便是自恣, "to speak of ease apart from ritual is self-indulgence"; and 有禮而不和，則尚是存得那本之體在；若只管和，則併本都忘了, "ritual without he still keeps the root; he alone forgets the root altogether." ([朱子語類 卷22, p. 118](/q/Bl0cpAyimC4ZSAO53ig))
**Zhang Zai's cosmic harmony is the same he.** 此以太和狀道體，與發而中節之和無異 ([張子全書, p. 80](/q/Bl15zIrFQzUg2SuP1VI)).

**The school ties it to fixed rank.** His disciple Huang (presumably Huang Gan) explains why ritual is strict: 天高地下，萬物散殊，分之一定而不可移, "heaven high, earth low, the myriad things dispersed and distinct, their portions fixed and immovable." ([論語纂疏 卷1, p. 79](/q/Bl0WEtjJ50JT3EFT5yh))
tr: **和 he**, in the Zhongyong sense: the right measure of each emotion as it arises. It is defined negatively, as 無所乖戾, "nothing perverse or discordant".
**從容不迫 congrong bupo**: an ease of manner, the absence of strain in doing what ritual requires.

**中和 zhonghe**: the pair. Zhong is the unaroused centre (無所偏倚, "leaning to no side"), and he is the measured response. "Extend zhong-he and heaven and earth take their places, the myriad things are nourished."

**Verdict: does not map.** Zhu Xi's he is a property of one person's response: each feeling fits its occasion and none clashes. It is the absence of discord, not discord held inside a whole. In society it is the ease with which a person fits an order whose distinctions are "fixed and immovable". Diversity is present only as rank, and he is consent to it. That is the case the guard clause of “Harmony is diversity in wholeness” warns about.
an: Gao Gong (Ming) objected that "unhurried" only means "not hasty". For him he is 情意之流通, "the free flow of feeling": 高下散殊，天地之禮也；周流同化，天地之和也 ([問辨錄, p. 96](/q/Bl0WPiaVcTMKaGyWgvg)).. That restores the Yueji pairing, and it pushes he toward union (同化), not plurality.
Zhu Xi on Zhang Zai's Taihe: (see zhang-zai).

kb.t: Ṣafī al-Dīn al-Urmawī, Kitāb al-adwār and al-Risāla al-sharafiyya (c. 1216 – 1294)
kb.th: Ṣafī al-Dīn founded the "Systematist" school of Arabic and Persian music theory. His seventeen-step division of the octave was meant to cover several regional scale systems at once. His own texts are not in the library, so this page rests on Farmer (1929).
h: **One scale for several systems (as Farmer reports).** "This scale, which proceeded by steps of two limmas and a comma, was clearly founded on the old ṭunbūr al-khurāsānī scale, and nominally, at any rate, embraced the Pythagorean, Zalzalian, and Persian systems." Farmer attributes it to Ṣafī al-Dīn only "probably" ([Farmer, *History of Arabian Music*, p. 206 [scan 230]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogpqCyU3YVWOkBhwc))

**His authority shaped the later tradition.** Qutb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī and the later theorists "all prostrate themselves before the authority of Ṣafī al-Dīn 'Abd al-Mu'min, even when they have to disagree with him." ([p. 203 [scan 227]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogpqCyU3YVWOkBhwZ))
tr: In the Arabic theory of intervals the usual terms are **mulāʾim ملائم** / **talāʾum تلائم** ("fitting, agreeable", consonant), **ittifāq اتفاق** ("agreement"), and **munāfir منافر** / **munāfara منافرة** ("repugnant", dissonant).
**taʾlīf تأليف** ("composition, joining") is the older word for putting notes together. It is closer to Greek *harmonia* as "fitting together".

**Verdict: partly maps.** *Mulāʾim* is a relation between two notes, so it is graded consonance. That is "ratios as one manifestation" (idea 5), not diversity in wholeness. The Systematist scale is a different matter. If Farmer is right, it is a single frame designed to hold several regional systems, which is a real case of diversity in wholeness at the level of theory. Farmer says "nominally", so this should not be overstated.
an: Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī (see qutb-al-din-shirazi.md), ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Marāghī and al-Lādhiqī built on him and argued with him (Farmer).
His predecessors are al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā.
nh: **Not held:** *Kitāb al-adwār* and *al-Risāla al-sharafiyya fī l-nisab al-taʾlīfiyya*. Searches for الأدوار, "Safi al-Din" and "Urmawi" found only Farmer and unrelated texts. Best public-domain editions: Carra de Vaux, *Le traité des rapports musicaux* (Paris, 1891; French translation of the *Sharafiyya*). Rodolphe d'Erlanger, *La musique arabe* vol. 3 (1938) translates both. It is in copyright in some jurisdictions and is not held.

kb.t: Quṭb al-Dīn al-Shīrāzī, Durrat al-tāj (music section) (1236 – 1311)
kb.th: Quṭb al-Dīn was a polymath (astronomer, physician and philosopher) whose Persian encyclopaedia includes a major treatise on music in the Systematist line of Ṣafī al-Dīn. None of it is in the library.
h: **Systematist authority.** Farmer calls him Ṣafī al-Dīn's "greatest pupil" and the *Durrat al-tāj* "one of the most authoritative works on the "Systematist" theory of music." ([Farmer, *History of Arabian Music*, p. 227 [scan 251]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogpqCyU3YVWOkBhwx))

**Deference with disagreement.** He is among the later theorists who defer to Ṣafī al-Dīn "even when they have to disagree with him" ([p. 203 [scan 227]](https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeogpqCyU3YVWOkBhwZ))
tr: He uses the same Arabic terms as Ṣafī al-Dīn for consonance (**mulāʾim ملائم**) and dissonance (**munāfir منافر**). In Persian, the general word for proportion and fit is **tanāsub تناسب**.

**Verdict: not assessable from the library.** The likely answer is the same as for Ṣafī al-Dīn: consonance is a graded relation between pairs of notes (partly maps, at the level of ratio only). Treat that as a hypothesis.
an: He built on Ṣafī al-Dīn (see safi-al-din.md). Later Timurid theorists (ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Marāghī) built on both. Not in the library.
nh: **Not held:** *Durrat al-tāj li-ghurrat al-Dībāj*. Searches for "Durrat al-taj" and "Qutb al-Din Shirazi" found nothing. The music section exists in Persian lithographs and modern editions. No public-domain English or French translation is known to me. Its music section is summarized in d'Erlanger, *La musique arabe* (not PD everywhere; not held).

q.t: This pleasure requires a certain proportion between the object and the sense itself.
We say that the parts of the whole object are less different among themselves, between which there is a greater proportion.
That proportion must be Arithmetic, not Geometric, the reason for which is that there are not so many things to be noted in it, since the differences are everywhere equal.
which are incommensurable. And therefore, as I judge, they can by no means be perfectly known by the sense simultaneously

kb.th: Harmony is a fit between an object and a sense: consonance is what the ear can take in easily, but that ease is not beauty. Beauty is a relation to a judgment that varies from one hearer to the next.
h: Pleasure needs a proportion between the object and the sense. When the parts of an object stand in a greater proportion, they differ less, and the sense takes them in more easily. "This pleasure requires a certain proportion between the object and the sense itself." ([p. 1](/q/BhI8eaAwF31xcf5TJAE))
The proportion must be arithmetic. Incommensurable parts cannot be held by the sense at all: "they can by no means be perfectly known by the sense simultaneously" ([p. 2](/q/BhI8eaAwF31xcf5TJAF))

What pleases most is a middle difficulty, and variety pleases too. The most pleasing thing is not "which is perceived most easily by the sense, nor even that which is perceived with most difficulty"; and "variety is most pleasing in all things" ([p. 2](/q/BhI8eaAwF31xcf5TJAF))
The fifth is "the most pleasing of all consonances". The octave can be used alone only because "the two voices are heard as if they were one" ([p. 11](/q/BhI8eaAwF31xcf5TJAO))
A syncopated dissonance builds expectation, so that "that which has been awaited for longer is more pleasing when it finally arrives" ([p. 22](/q/BhI8eaAwF31xcf5TJAj))

Beauty and pleasantness have no fixed measure: "because human judgments are so different, one cannot say that the beautiful or the pleasant have any fixed measure." Also: "the same thing that makes some want to dance can give others the urge to cry." He traces this to memory, using the example of a dog whipped to a violin ([AT I 133](/q/Bem7gUNYAmgxyHUUOYB))
an: Leonhard Euler, Tentamen (1739), ch. II §11: agrees that taste varies, but holds that order is objective and that a listener can be wrong about it.
G. W. Leibniz, Ultimate Origination: makes the same point about discord and expectation, folded into a theodicy.
Marin Mersenne, who asked the question in the letters.

kb.t: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and Herbert Spencer (1820–1903) on the origins of music
kb.th: For Darwin, preference for melody is selected: female birds choosing "the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty". Spencer (known here only through Croce) made music the natural language of the passions, there to increase sympathy.
h: **Darwin: song is shaped by sexual selection.** "The severest rivalry between the males of many species to attract by singing the females". Females, "by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect". ([p. 89](/q/BilNa4DQTy8jFYQCkEG))

**Spencer, through Croce.** "Music is explained as the natural language of the passions, aimed at increasing sympathy between men". Croce dismisses Spencer's aesthetics as among "the first crude attempts". ([Croce p. 448](/q/BhCwoBfLVeXFYtSynCo)) (second-hand)
nh: **The Descent of Man** (1871), the chapters on music and the voice: not held. The claim that human music descends from courtship song is therefore not verified here.
